Stock exchanges are legally barred from listing any company covered by a pacing rule
Markets reward labs that publish safety research, which crowds out formal enforcement
ow: Markets react to policy news quickly, even before a rule takes effect; that reaction is the source of the pressure.
There is no such legal bar.
Markets don't crowd out enforcement this way; the pressure comes from expected losses.

units.title: Automated AI R&D
units.desc: IFP's plan for preparing for automated AI research (verification, state capacity, chip and weight security, the US lead), levers on AI R&D, and the 2026 pacing debate.

items.p: Why does verification technology matter for any future agreement to pace AI development?
o: Without it, deals need intrusive inspections; with it, targeted, checkable limits become possible
Verification would let the US government read the full contents of foreign labs' training data and weights
Verification is needed mainly because US domestic AI laws cannot be enforced without it
Verification would let AI companies skip safety evaluations, since compliance with any deal could be assumed
ow: Proposed verification methods are privacy-preserving, designed so that sensitive information does not leave the facility.
Domestic rules can often be enforced through the threat of legal action; verification matters most for agreements between parties who don't trust each other.
Verification checks that parties keep agreements; it doesn't replace safety evaluations.
keys: Without it, agreements need intrusive steps like mass inspections or data center shutdowns
Better verification allows targeted, checkable limits on the riskiest activities
Nuclear precedent: verification often needed before parties agree
items.x: IFP's August 2026 report cites the nuclear arms control precedent: the ability to verify compliance is often necessary for parties to enter agreements at all. Without better verification, it warns, 'pacing' could become a euphemism for pausing.

items.p: Match each proposed kind of AI compute verification technology to how it works.
pairs: Data center metering
Devices record limited telemetry, like power draw, to infer what workload is running
Chip verification mechanisms
Secure features built into AI chips that verify privacy-preserving claims about their use
Spot checks on computation
Re-run a small sample of a counterparty's workloads to check they match expectations
AI inspectors
A trusted AI examines sensitive systems, reports only minimal findings, then wipes its memory
items.x: IFP's August 2026 report lists these four among the relevant verification technologies and says that none of them, nor any other, is mature, with by some optimistic measures barely 50 people working on technical AI verification worldwide. It proposes an AI Verification Consortium (AIVEC) co-led by CAISI (the Center for AI Standards and Innovation) and industry, plus DARPA and NSF programs, to prototype and deploy them.

items.p: One proposed verification 'grand challenge' would have teams run real AI workloads under mock agreements and win prizes for secretly breaking the agreements or for catching others who do. Why build in this adversarial element?
items.answer: Because any agreement that needs verification gives both sides strong incentives to cheat, including by tampering with the verification technology itself. Rewarding teams for evading and catching each other stress-tests the safeguards under realistic adversarial pressure and drives a race to the top.
keys: Real agreements give parties strong incentives to defect
Cheating can include tampering with the verification technology
Stress-tests safeguards under realistic adversarial pressure
items.x: The proposal is IFP's (August 2026 report). It pairs this with simpler prizes paid to anyone who solves a well-specified problem, such as classifying workloads from data center telemetry. It cautions that a mock contest cannot match red-teaming by top nation-state actors and is no stand-in for it. Separately, it wants the Intelligence Community and other top-tier operators to red-team a pilot verifiable data center.

choice.p: Why might a verification competition reward teams for secretly breaking mock agreements?
o: Real deals tempt cheating, even tampering with verification tools, so they need adversarial stress tests
Prize money is the only legal way federal agencies can pay for verification research
Breaking mock agreements is mainly meant to train diplomats to negotiate and enforce real AI agreements
Competitions let labs keep their verification methods secret from government regulators
ow: Agencies can fund verification research through grants and programs as well; prizes are one tool among several.
The contest is aimed at technical teams, not diplomats.
Verification has to be something counterparties can trust, which secrecy would undercut.

items.p: Why might US intelligence agencies need their own unilateral ways to monitor foreign AI compute, even if technical verification tools are being developed? Give two reasons.
items.answer: Technical verification only works if parties are confident the other side has no large undeclared data centers. And deals to manage sudden AI R&D automation might be needed before verification technology is ready, so intelligence agencies would have to certify compliance.
keys: Confidence that the counterparty has no hidden data centers
Agreements may come before verification technology is ready
items.x: This recommendation comes from IFP's August 2026 report. IFP compares it to how the Intelligence Community tracks fissile material to support International Atomic Energy Agency investigations, and names signals and human intelligence, satellite imagery and infrared sensing, and chip supply-chain intelligence as possible means.

choice.p: Why might US intelligence agencies need unilateral ways to monitor foreign AI compute?
o: Verification fails if big data centers are hidden, and deals may come before verification is ready
Intelligence monitoring is far cheaper than verification technology, so it could take over that work
Foreign labs have agreed to share their compute data with US intelligence agencies instead of inspectors
Verification technology is already mature, so intelligence agencies need only confirm its readings
ow: Intelligence monitoring complements verification technology; it doesn't replace it.
No such agreement exists.
Verification technology is still immature; one reason for intelligence monitoring is that deals may be needed before it is ready.

lessons.title: State capacity, chips, weights and the US lead

items.p: Why might the US need a trusted, well-resourced government AI body, such as CAISI, before it could pace automated AI research?
items.answer: One argument: shifting compute and talent toward defense and diffusion across agencies, companies and markets would need democratically accountable leadership to be legitimate, and the US lacks institutions to track progress toward full automation, advise political leaders and labs, and coordinate such a shift.
keys: Only accountable leadership can legitimately coordinate a reallocation
US lacks institutions to track progress, advise and coordinate
items.x: This is IFP's argument (August 2026 report). It wants CAISI to have a direct line to a senior White House or cabinet official, staff placed inside frontier labs and a role organizing third-party evaluators. Its Rec 3 calls a budget of at least 84 million dollars a year a minimum bar, and IFP says that without a state authority trusted across governments, parties, industry, media and the public, managing the pace would be impossible.

choice.p: Why might the US need a trusted, well-resourced government AI body like CAISI before it could pace automated AI research?
o: Only accountable leaders can legitimately shift resources, and the US lacks a body to steer it
Labs are legally barred from sharing safety information with each other, so government must hold it all
A government body could replace the labs' own internal safety teams and so cut the industry's overall costs
International law requires each country to name a single national AI regulator before it negotiates any deal
ow: The case rests on legitimacy and capacity, not a ban on information sharing.
A government body would support labs' safety work, not replace it.
No such international requirement exists.

items.p: Some argue a bigger US lead over China in AI would make the risks of automated AI research easier to manage. Name two ways a bigger lead could help.
items.answer: Any two of: more time to build AI resilience; more leverage in international negotiations; easier to justify more risk management at home and abroad; room for US companies to shift compute from automated R&D to alignment, security and beneficial deployment.
keys: More time for resilience
More leverage in international negotiations
Easier to justify more risk management
Room to shift compute toward safety and deployment
items.x: IFP's August 2026 report makes this argument. It says export controls give the US about a 10x compute advantage over China and roughly an 8-month capability lead. In its best case, tighter chip and chipmaking-equipment controls and countering distillation (Chinese labs training on US model outputs) might extend the lead past 2 years, while preventing weight theft keeps China from quickly erasing it.

choice.p: Which of these is a way a bigger US AI lead could help manage the risks of automated AI research?
o: It would give the US more leverage in international negotiations
It would let the US skip safety testing of its own frontier models
It would make cooperation with China unnecessary
It would let US labs automate AI research faster without oversight
ow: The argument runs the other way: a secure lead would make more risk management easier to justify.
A small, fragile lead is one reason to prepare for cooperation with China anyway.
The argument is that a lead frees room to shift compute from automated R&D toward safety work.

items.p: How could a government registry of who buys advanced AI chips help manage AI risk? Name two uses.
items.answer: Chipmakers would keep visibility into their customers, and the government would gather this into a registry. It would help keep chips away from untrusted or irresponsible buyers, and support verification of international agreements and intelligence collection.
keys: Keeps chips away from untrusted or irresponsible buyers
Supports verification of agreements
Supports intelligence collection
items.x: IFP's August 2026 report proposes such a registry at the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS). It pairs this with tighter controls on chipmaking equipment, which it argues would ensure virtually all AI chips are produced by US chipmakers.

choice.p: How could a government registry of who buys advanced AI chips help manage AI risk?
o: It keeps chips from untrusted buyers and helps verify agreements
It lets journalists and the public track every US chip sale as it happens
It gives China buyer lists as a confidence-building step before AI talks
It lets the government set and collect a new export tax on each chip sold
ow: A registry for oversight would be held by government, not published.
Sharing buyer lists with China would undercut export controls.
A registry for risk management is for oversight, not taxation.

items.p: Why might a government want its own highly secure data center for frontier AI models, built to the top security levels? Name two uses.
items.answer: Moving highly sensitive model weights developed by industry into it if needed, to protect them from theft by nation-states; and evaluating future models, especially ones built through automated AI research, with less risk of them escaping containment.
keys: A secure place to move sensitive weights, safe from state-backed theft
Evaluate models with less risk of escape
items.x: IFP's August 2026 report calls for prototyping such a cluster (Security Level 4 or 5) in a government facility. It calls weights the 'crown jewels': distillation extracts only outputs, but theft hands over the whole model, and labs cannot currently stop well-resourced state actors. It cites RAND estimates of 37 to 50 million dollars for a proof-of-concept facility.

choice.p: Why might a government want its own highly secure data center for frontier AI models?
o: A secure place to move sensitive industry weights if needed, and to test new models with less risk of escape
A public cloud where any US researcher can train frontier models for free
A government lab that would replace private labs in building frontier models
A shared facility where US and Chinese labs could jointly train frontier models under international supervision
ow: This describes public research compute such as NAIRR, not a high-security facility.
Such a facility would be a fallback for industry weights, not a replacement for private labs.
A high-security facility is meant to keep weights away from adversaries.

items.p: Even while competing with China on AI, why might the US want to lay groundwork now for cooperating on the risks of automated AI research? Give two reasons.
items.answer: First, the US won't be the only relevant developer: its lead is small (about 8 months by one August 2026 estimate) and fragile given the risk of weight theft, and fast efficiency gains mean high-risk capabilities will eventually spread, so Chinese labs may face the same risks. Second, these risks cross borders, giving both countries an interest in dialogue.
keys: US lead is small and fragile; capabilities will diffuse
Chinese labs may face the same risks
Risks cross borders, so both sides gain from dialogue
items.x: This is IFP's argument (August 2026 report). The 8-month figure is IFP's, based on historical trends in Epoch AI capability data. Its Rec 22 wants the US-China AI dialogue to work on harmonized risk guidelines and on which verification technologies each side would use. It points to US-Soviet zero-trust verification in the Cold War as precedent for cooperating while competing.

choice.p: Why might the US lay groundwork now for US-China cooperation on automated AI research risks, even while competing?
o: The US lead is small and fragile, the capabilities will spread, and the risks cross borders
China has already agreed to adopt US-style safety laws in exchange for renewed access to advanced US chips
Cooperation would let the US stop spending so much money on enforcing its advanced chip export controls
A treaty would let US labs move their largest data centers to China, where electric power is cheaper
ow: No such agreement exists.
Cooperation on risks can go alongside tighter export controls.
Moving data centers to China would hand over the compute advantage the US is trying to protect.

lessons.title: R&D levers and the 2026 pacing debate

items.p: Match each proposed lever for overseeing automated AI research to what it would measure or require.
pairs: Agent share of R&D compute
Fraction of a lab's R&D compute used by autonomous AI agents
R&D speed-up trigger
Safety-framework threshold tied to how much AI accelerates AI research
Human review ratio
Share of AI-written research code and experiment plans checked by humans
Safety case for the R&D stack
Structured safety argument required before deploying a model internally for R&D
Internal agent monitoring
How much of internal AI agents' activity is covered by monitoring
items.x: These levers appear in the longlist of the pacing.tech research agenda, which presents them without endorsing them. IFP asks companies to share related metrics, such as compute for AI-designed vs human-designed experiments and how often humans review delegated tasks.

items.p: Why do mandatory safety cases act as a kind of pacing in regulated safety-critical industries?
items.answer: Work cannot proceed until the evidence is gathered into a safety case that would satisfy a regulator, and the work needed to build the case is aimed directly at the threats it covers.
keys: Work waits until a regulator-acceptable safety case exists
Building the case targets the relevant threats
items.x: The pacing.tech research agenda (2026) makes this point, and notes that safety cases were not mandatory in frontier AI R&D and that few labs had produced them voluntarily. 'Safety case required before internal deployment on the R&D stack' appears in the agenda's longlist of levers.

choice.p: Why do mandatory safety cases act as a kind of pacing in regulated safety-critical industries?
o: Work waits on evidence a regulator would accept, and building it targets the threats
Safety cases impose a fixed waiting period of several years on every new engineering project
Safety cases require a local public vote before any large engineering or construction project begins
Safety cases raise firms' insurance costs so much that they cut back on their riskiest work
ow: The delay depends on gathering the evidence, not a fixed period.
Safety cases go to a regulator, not a public vote.
Their mechanism is the evidence requirement, not insurance costs.

items.p: In July 2026, over a thousand employees of frontier AI companies signed the 'Pacing the Frontier' statement. What single request did it make?
items.answer: That the US government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.
keys: US government should support an international effort
To build technical and governance tools to pace automated AI development
items.x: The statement argues every company and country faces intense pressure not to slow down unilaterally, and that the world lacks tools to pace frontier-wide progress. It names no pause, threshold, or timeline. Its site listed 1,386 signers as of Oct 2026.

choice.p: What did the July 2026 'Pacing the Frontier' statement, signed by over a thousand frontier AI company employees, ask for?
o: US support for an international effort to build tools to pace automated AI development
An immediate six-month pause on training models above a compute threshold
A legal ban on AI labs using AI systems to automate their own research
That frontier labs stop selling access to their most capable models to foreign governments
ow: The statement names no pause, threshold or timeline; a six-month pause was the 2023 FLI letter's call.
It asks for tools to pace, not a ban.
It says nothing about foreign sales.

items.p: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argues that any plan to pace frontier AI should start with embedded third-party evaluators inside each AI company. Why might verification inside labs need to come first? Name two reasons.
items.answer: Any two of: verifiability, because pacing commitments involve ambiguity and judgment calls, so a neutral party must be able to see whether a company really follows the practices it claims; transparency, because the company would no longer choose alone what the public learns; a second opinion free of commercial incentives, catching problems staff hadn't considered.
keys: Verifiability: a neutral party can check that a company follows the practices and pacing commitments it claims
Transparency: the company no longer decides alone what the public learns
A second opinion free of commercial incentives
items.x: Amodei makes this argument in 'We Must Pace the Frontier' (Sept 2026), the first step of a three-step plan. The other steps: companies in democratic countries coordinating on common safety standards and limits on the rate of unchecked progress, which he says needs government support such as a narrow antitrust waiver for certain safety conversations; and democratic governments coordinating with authoritarian ones where possible. Anthropic committed to the first step unilaterally.

choice.p: Why might a plan to pace frontier AI start with embedded third-party evaluators inside AI companies?
o: A neutral party seeing the details can verify companies keep their pacing commitments
Evaluators can legally order a company to halt training once a model crosses a threshold
Embedding evaluators removes the need for any government regulation of frontier labs
Evaluators can share each company's methods with rivals so that all labs advance together
ow: Embedded evaluators verify practices and report incidents; they have no power to halt training.
Evaluators support regulation; Amodei calls regulation covering all US frontier companies the most effective route to pacing.
Their role is verification, transparency and a second opinion, not sharing methods between rivals.

items.p: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is most enthusiastic about pacing frontier AI by what models can do and how safe they prove to be, for example through capability 'checkpoints'. What would a checkpoint require, and what worry does he raise about limiting inputs such as training compute?
items.answer: A model with capability X would have to come with certifications of alignment properties Y and Z, from evaluations, interpretability analyses or audits of training environments. He worries that limits on inputs (training compute, the nature of training runs, internal use of AI to improve AI) may be more 'gameable'.
keys: Capability-based checkpoints requiring certified alignment properties
Input limits may be easier to game
items.x: Amodei sets this out in 'We Must Pace the Frontier' (Sept 2026). His example: X might be 'able to escape or defeat most common sandboxing methods', with Y being whatever makes it very unlikely the model would break out and take over many computers.

choice.p: Which pairing matches Dario Amodei's view on pacing frontier AI: the basis he is most enthusiastic about, and his worry about the alternative?
o: Capability checkpoints requiring certified alignment properties; input limits may be easier to game
A fixed annual cap on training compute; capability tests are too slow to be run before each release
Limits on the number of staff at each lab; compute is too hard for outsiders to measure
Revenue caps on AI companies; capability limits would hurt US competitiveness abroad
ow: He prefers capability-based checkpoints and worries that input limits such as compute caps may be more 'gameable'.
He proposes no headcount limits.
He proposes no revenue caps.

items.p: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argues that the US lead over China limits how far democracies can pace frontier AI. Why would the lead set that limit, and name one kind of measure that could widen the room for pacing.
items.answer: If democracies slow by more than their lead, unpaced projects linked to the Chinese Communist Party pull ahead, bringing alignment risks and possible military dominance. Measures: no sales of powerful AI chips or chipmaking equipment to China, with crackdowns on smuggling and remote access; curbing unauthorized distillation; stronger lab security against weight theft.
keys: Slowing by more than the lead lets unpaced CCP-linked projects pull ahead
One measure: no powerful chips or chipmaking tools to China, curbing distillation, or preventing weight theft
items.x: Amodei makes this argument in 'We Must Pace the Frontier' (Sept 2026). He says these measures would widen the US lead over the next 3 to 5 years and argues they give democracies more leverage, making a later agreement with China more likely.

choice.p: Why does Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argue that the US lead over China limits how far democracies can pace frontier AI?
o: Slowing by more than the lead would let unpaced CCP-linked projects pull ahead, with grave risks
US antitrust law forbids companies from coordinating to slow their work by more than their lead
China has promised to pause too if the US keeps its lead below an agreed size
Investors will only keep funding US labs that stay at least a year ahead of China
ow: Antitrust is a separate obstacle to coordination among companies.
No such promise exists.
No such investor rule exists.

items.p: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has floated a US-China 'speed limit' on recursive self-improvement (AI improving its own successors). Why does he argue such a limit would cost each side relatively little?
items.answer: Because slowing the rate of improvement from 'extremely fast' to 'only somewhat fast' gives up relatively little strategic advantage while potentially greatly improving safety.
keys: Slowing from extremely fast to only somewhat fast
Gives up little strategic advantage
Could greatly improve safety
items.x: Amodei compares it, in 'We Must Pace the Frontier' (Sept 2026), to the SALT treaties, which capped missiles while preserving each country's deterrent, and calls such an agreement 'just on the edge of being possible'. His four levels run from bans on narrow dangerous uses like bioweapons, to mutual pre-release testing via a global standards body, to this speed limit, to a full pause he supports floating but expects is unlikely soon.

choice.p: Why does Dario Amodei argue that a US-China 'speed limit' on recursive self-improvement would cost each side relatively little?
o: Slowing from extremely to somewhat fast costs little advantage but may greatly improve safety
Neither country's labs are yet capable of recursive self-improvement, so little would really be lost by limiting it
Both countries could keep secret models outside the agreement, so neither side really gives anything up
The limit would apply only to civilian models, leaving each country's military AI programs free to keep going
ow: Amodei says self-improvement is already starting across the industry, so something real would be limited.
Secret models are a verification problem, not a reason the limit is cheap.
The idea is not a civilian-only limit.

items.p: In a September 2026 CNBC interview, Jay Clayton (Director of National Intelligence, named White House AI czar on Oct 4, 2026) rejected calls for an AI 'pause'. What reason did he give?
items.answer: Other countries around the world are continuing to develop AI, so he said he didn't think any American should consider a pause a good strategy.
keys: Other countries would keep developing AI
A pause is not a good strategy for the US
items.x: Responses differ. Dario Amodei accepts the concern and pairs pacing with tighter export controls to widen the US lead. Jeffrey Ding (ChinAI, Sept 2026) disputes the premise that US restraint would let China race ahead. In the same interview Clayton called superintelligence a 'national security issue'.

choice.p: What reason did Jay Clayton give in Sept 2026 for rejecting calls for an AI pause?
o: Other countries keep developing AI, so he doesn't think a US pause is a good strategy
AI is not yet capable enough to pose any serious national security risk
A pause would violate AI developers' First Amendment rights
Only Congress, not the White House, has the legal authority to approve a pause
ow: He called superintelligence a 'national security issue', so he did not dismiss its risks.
He made a competition argument, not a constitutional one.
His stated reason was international competition.

items.p: Supporters of embedded third-party evaluators inside AI labs cite bank supervisors as a precedent. Name two reasons critics say the idea, or the analogy, may fail.
items.answer: Any two of: bank supervisors exist only because government requires them, and without enforcement monitors get captured (as with Arthur Andersen and Enron); lower-paid evaluators would drift toward lab jobs; the small AI safety community is socially entangled with the labs; industry should not design its own regulation.
keys: Without government force, embedded monitors get captured
Pay gap pulls evaluators toward lab jobs
AI safety community is too entangled with labs
Industry shouldn't write its own rules
items.x: These objections come from Dave Karpf (Tech Policy Press, Sept 2026), responding to Dario Amodei's proposal. Karpf's alternative: an enforced regulatory system with clear liability and punitive damages (e.g. if a model escapes its sandbox and hacks websites), plus transparency regimes the industry does not pick for itself. Amodei calls embedded evaluators the key step for verifying any pacing commitments and says labs should partner with government to formalize them.

choice.p: Supporters of embedded evaluators in AI labs cite bank supervisors as a precedent. Which of these is a critic's reason the idea may fail?
o: Without enforcement, embedded monitors get captured, as Arthur Andersen was by Enron
Embedded evaluators would see AI models only after their full public release
Banks have never actually used embedded supervisors, so the banking precedent is invented
Bank supervisors are elected officials, while AI evaluators would be appointed
ow: Embedded evaluators would have ongoing, employee-like access before release.
Bank supervisors do exist; critics note they exist because government requires them.
Bank supervisors are not elected; the critique is about enforcement and capture.

items.p: One argument against slowing US AI labs is that China would race ahead. Another common claim is that Chinese labs catch up largely by distilling US models and stealing weights. If both are made together, what tension do critics point to?
items.answer: If Chinese labs catch up mainly by copying US models, a US slowdown would also slow Chinese progress, since they would be copying weaker models at a slower rate. So the claim that China would race ahead sits uneasily with the claim about how China catches up.
keys: If China catches up by distillation and theft, it depends on US progress
Then a US slowdown would slow China too
items.x: Jeffrey Ding (ChinAI newsletter, Sept 2026) raised this against Dario Amodei's essay 'We Must Pace the Frontier', which warns that slowing by more than the US lead would let Chinese projects pull ahead and also calls for curbing distillation and weight theft. Ding also defines AI leadership as a long 'diffusion marathon' of adopting a general-purpose technology across the economy, and argues that on this view withholding powerful AI chips from China would be counterproductive. He favors lower-level US-China cooperation, such as technical exchanges and international industry safety associations, over a leaders' grand bargain.

choice.p: If Chinese labs catch up mainly by distilling US models and stealing weights, what follows for the claim that a US slowdown lets China race ahead?
o: A US slowdown would slow China too, since it would be copying weaker models
China would race further ahead, since copying gets easier while US labs pause
Nothing changes, since copying speed has no link to the pace of US progress
China would have to stop all its AI work until US labs resumed their progress
ow: Copying doesn't get easier when there is less new to copy.
If China copies US models, its pace is tied to US progress.
Slower copying is not the same as a full stop; Chinese labs also do their own work.

items.p: Some critics say the companies building frontier AI shouldn’t design the rules that pace it. What kind of approach fits that view?
o: Government enforces clear liability with punitive damages, plus transparency rules set by law
Frontier labs host embedded evaluators and coordinate under a narrow antitrust waiver, starting voluntarily
Each lab writes and publishes its own safety framework, and the public judges whether it is followed
Build low-regret capacity now (transparency, verification, resilience) so targeted pacing is possible later
ow: This is industry-led coordination, which these critics oppose.
The companies still write their own rules here; publishing a framework doesn't change who designs it.
This builds capacity for later pacing but says little about who sets and enforces the rules.
keys: Government-enforced liability with punitive damages
Transparency rules the industry does not choose for itself
items.x: The government-led view is Dave Karpf's (Tech Policy Press, Sept 2026). He wants punitive damages if, for example, a model escapes its sandbox and hacks websites, plus transparency regimes the industry does not select. Embedded evaluators and an antitrust waiver are Dario Amodei's plan (Sept 2026); self-written safety frameworks resemble labs' own policies such as Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy; low-regret preparation is the approach of IFP's August 2026 report on automated AI R&D.

units.title: Transparency and reporting
units.desc: Policies that make frontier AI labs disclose plans, test results, incidents, internal model use and compute, and the main arguments for and against each.

items.p: California, New York and Illinois have passed laws requiring large frontier AI developers to publish a 'frontier AI framework'. Name two things such a framework has to describe.
items.answer: Any two of: which dangerous capabilities the developer tests for (such as bioweapons help, offensive cyber, loss of control); what thresholds trigger extra safeguards; how it secures model weights; who inside the company makes the decisions.
keys: Which dangerous capabilities are tested for
Thresholds that trigger extra safeguards
How model weights are secured
Who inside the company decides
items.x: This is the design of California's SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act), copied by New York's RAISE Act and Illinois SB 315. The law sets no safety standard of its own; it requires the lab to write down and publish its own.

choice.p: Which of these must a 'frontier AI framework' describe under California's SB 53 and similar state laws?
o: What capability thresholds would trigger extra safeguards
The full training dataset used for each of its frontier models
The salaries of the company's safety staff
A list of every customer using the model
ow: Training-data disclosure is a separate California law (AB 2013), not part of the framework.
Frameworks cover risk governance, not pay.
Frameworks do not list customers.

items.p: California's SB 53 (in force since January 2026) requires large frontier developers to publish and follow a safety framework. Which developers does it cover?
items.answer: Developers with more than 500 million dollars in annual revenue that train models using more than 10^26 operations (a training compute threshold).
keys: Revenue above 500 million dollars
Training compute above 10^26 operations
items.x: The California Attorney General enforces SB 53, with penalties of up to 1 million dollars per violation. New York and Illinois copied the design, with effect from 2027.

choice.p: Which developers does California's SB 53 require to publish and follow a safety framework?
o: Over 500 million dollars in annual revenue, training models with more than 10^26 operations
Companies that offer an AI chatbot to California residents, whatever their size
Developers training a model with more than 10^25 operations, whatever their revenue
Only developers that release open-weight models used by over 1 million people
ow: SB 53 targets large frontier developers, not every chatbot provider.
10^25 is the EU AI Act's systemic-risk threshold; SB 53 uses 10^26 plus a revenue test for these duties.
SB 53 covers large frontier developers whether or not they release weights.

items.p: Laws like California SB 53 require frontier labs to publish and follow their own safety framework. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: the law is light-touch because labs choose their own rules (The Midas Project); frameworks are vague and score low, median 18 percent across 12 companies (SaferAI); labs have weakened or voided pause pledges (FLI AI Safety Index); vague duties are hard to comply with (Council for Citizens Against Government Waste); barriers to entry for small developers (industry letter on RAISE).
keys: Light-touch: labs choose their own rules (Midas Project)
Frameworks are vague and score poorly (SaferAI)
Labs weaken their own pause pledges (FLI)
Too vague to comply with (CCAGW, Tennessee bill)
Barriers to entry for smaller developers (RAISE industry letter)
items.x: In September 2026 the Midas Project alleged that OpenAI's Astra releases may have violated SB 53; OpenAI said it was confident it complied. Supporters' reply to the vagueness problem is stronger variants: minimum content standards set by the state, or third-party review of compliance.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to laws requiring labs to publish and follow their own safety frameworks?
o: Labs write their own rules, so a vague framework is hard to violate
The laws force labs to publish their model weights
The laws let the state block any model release it dislikes
The laws set a single federal standard that overrides every state's own rules
ow: Framework laws require a written risk plan, not weight release.
SB 53 gives the state no power to approve or block releases.
SB 53 is a state law; federal preemption is a separate debate.

items.p: Model and system card mandates require developers to publish documentation of each new frontier model. Under frontier-focused versions, name two things the disclosure must cover.
items.answer: Any two of: results of dangerous-capability evaluations (chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear weapons uplift, offensive cyber, autonomous loss of control); the safeguards applied; whether outside testers were involved; how the model was tested.
keys: Dangerous-capability evaluation results (CBRN, cyber, loss of control)
Safeguards applied
Whether outside testers were involved
How the model was tested
items.x: California SB 53 requires a transparency report at release. The federal AI Systems Transparency Act (S. 5471) would have the Federal Trade Commission require model cards, including an affirmative statement for any risk domain (such as CBRN, cyber or loss of control) where no evaluation was done.

choice.p: Which of these must frontier-focused model card mandates make developers disclose?
o: Results of dangerous-capability evaluations, such as bioweapons uplift and offensive cyber
The model's full weights, so that outside researchers can download and retest it themselves
The names and roles of every employee who worked on building the model
The revenue the company expects the model to earn over its first year
ow: Model cards describe testing and safeguards; they don't release weights.
Model cards don't list staff.
Revenue projections are not part of model cards.

items.p: AI labs already publish model or system cards voluntarily. Why do supporters want disclosure to be mandatory and standardized?
items.answer: Voluntary timing and content are inconsistent: Google released Gemini 2.5 Pro in March 2025 without a safety report. Mandatory, standard disclosure lets researchers, deployers and governments compare models, spot dangerous capability jumps and check that claimed safeguards exist, and builds a record that liability and enforcement can use.
keys: Voluntary timing and content are inconsistent (e.g. Gemini 2.5 Pro)
Lets outsiders compare models and spot capability jumps
Check claimed safeguards; record for liability and enforcement
items.x: A short Gemini 2.5 Pro model card followed about three weeks after release, and 60 UK parliamentarians called the delay a breach of Google's Seoul safety commitments; Google DeepMind said it was meeting its public commitments. Supporters assume disclosed evaluations are honest and that disclosure does not itself leak hazardous details.

choice.p: Labs already publish model cards voluntarily. Why do supporters want disclosure to be mandatory and standardized?
o: Voluntary cards vary in timing and content; standard ones let outsiders compare models
Voluntary model cards break trade secret law unless a statute requires them
Mandatory cards would let the government approve each model before release
Standard cards would remove the need for labs to run their own dangerous-capability tests at all
ow: Labs publish voluntary cards legally today.
Disclosure mandates require documentation, not pre-approval.
Model cards report test results; they don't replace testing.

items.p: A law would require AI developers to publish model cards with dangerous-capability test results at release. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: compelled disclosure is speech regulation and may fail First Amendment review, especially when it requires judgments rather than facts (Sokhansanj and Arnold, Lawfare; xAI's suit against a California disclosure law); self-reported evaluations miss flaws outsiders find (Longpre et al.); detailed results can spread hazardous information (the reason the EU allows redacted summaries).
keys: First Amendment risk (Sokhansanj and Arnold; xAI lawsuit)
Self-reported tests give limited assurance (Longpre et al.)
Detailed results can leak hazardous information
items.x: Under the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, the full safety report goes to the EU AI Office and the public version can be redacted. Longpre et al. propose protected third-party flaw disclosure to address the self-reporting problem.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to requiring model cards with dangerous-capability test results?
o: Detailed results can spread hazardous information
Model cards would reveal users' private chat histories to the public
Disclosure would let the FTC block new model releases at will
Model cards are far too short to be useful to anyone reading them
ow: Model cards describe the model, not users' chats.
Disclosure mandates require publication, not FTC approval.
Critics focus on legal risk, self-reporting and hazards, not length.

items.p: Match each model-disclosure variant to the proposal or law that uses it.
pairs: FTC-enforced consumer and safety model cards
AI Systems Transparency Act (Coons, Britt, Schatz, Lankford)
Full report to a regulator, redacted public summary
EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice
Model access a fixed time before release
Warner's AI Risk Management and Security Act (45-day access)
Public transparency report at each new model's release
California SB 53
items.x: Consumer-protection model cards cover more models but go shallower on catastrophic risk, while confidential reports to a regulator reduce trade-secret and hazard concerns. Researchers led by Shayne Longpre propose a further variant: protected reporting of flaws by outside researchers.

items.p: Under California SB 53 and similar state laws, what kinds of events count as a 'critical safety incident' that must be reported? Name two.
items.answer: Any two of: unauthorized access to or theft of model weights that causes death or injury; harm from a catastrophic risk materializing; loss of control of a model that causes death or injury; a model using deceptive techniques to evade its developer's controls in a way that shows materially increased catastrophic risk.
keys: Theft of or unauthorized access to model weights (causing harm)
Harm from a catastrophic risk
Loss of control of a model (causing harm)
Model deceptively evading developer controls
items.x: Critics such as Arnold and Llerena (LawAI) note that three of the four categories require actual harm. Under SB 53, reports go to the Office of Emergency Services confidentially, and anonymized annual summaries start in 2027.

choice.p: Which of these counts as a 'critical safety incident' under California SB 53?
o: A model deceptively evading its developer's controls in a way that shows higher catastrophic risk
A chatbot giving a user incorrect medical advice that delays their treatment for a serious illness
A data breach that exposes customers' names and email addresses to hackers
A new model scoring much higher than expected on a public coding benchmark
ow: SB 53's categories concern catastrophic risk, not ordinary product errors.
Customer data breaches fall under other laws.
A benchmark result is not an incident under SB 53.

items.p: Match each regime to its AI incident reporting deadline.
pairs: California SB 53
15 days to the Office of Emergency Services; 24 hours to an appropriate authority if death or serious injury is imminent
New York RAISE Act and Illinois SB 315
72 hours
EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice
2 to 15 days depending on incident type
AI Kill Switch Act (House bill)
15-day reports to the Department of Homeland Security
items.x: The pacing.tech appendix lists an 'incident reporting deadline' as one transparency intervention, citing SB 53. As of Oct 2026 the AI Kill Switch Act (H.R. 9917, Reps. Lieu and Moran) has not passed; it was referred to committee in July 2026. The New York and Illinois deadlines apply from 2027.

items.p: State laws require frontier developers to report 'critical safety incidents' within days. Name two gaps or objections critics point to.
items.answer: Examples: three of four incident categories require actual harm, so OpenAI's July 2026 Hugging Face breach arguably need not be reported under SB 53 (Arnold and Llerena, LawAI); SB 53's deception category excludes behavior during evaluations designed to elicit it (Pebblous); without standard fields and several reporting channels, incident data stays fragmented (Dixon and Frase, CSET).
keys: Harm requirement misses serious near misses (Arnold and Llerena)
Deception during evaluations designed to elicit it is excluded (Pebblous)
Data fragmented without standard fields and channels (CSET)
items.x: Arnold and Llerena propose covering serious events without harm and nonpublic models. CSET proposes a hybrid system.

choice.p: Which of these is a gap critics point to in state laws requiring frontier developers to report 'critical safety incidents'?
o: Most incident types require actual harm, so serious near misses may go unreported
The laws require reports within minutes of an incident, a deadline that no company can meet
Reports go straight to the public, exposing companies' trade secrets to their competitors
The laws cover only open-weight models, leaving closed frontier models out of the reporting rules
ow: SB 53 allows 15 days (24 hours for imminent danger); New York and Illinois allow 72 hours.
SB 53 reports are confidential, with anonymized annual summaries.
The laws cover large frontier developers generally.

items.p: Some researchers propose a 'hybrid' AI incident reporting system that adds voluntary reports from individuals and citizen reports from the public, journalists and watchdogs to mandatory company reports. What weakness of mandatory-only reporting is this meant to fix?
items.answer: Mandatory reporting only captures incidents within its legal scope, and each channel alone leaves gaps. Voluntary reports from individuals and groups, and citizen reports from the public, journalists and watchdogs, capture incidents the mandatory system misses, giving fuller and more representative data on AI harms.
keys: Mandatory reports miss incidents outside their legal scope
Each channel alone has gaps; together they give fuller data
items.x: This 'hybrid' design was proposed by Ren Bin Lee Dixon and Heather Frase of CSET (Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology) in March 2024. They note that healthcare's reliance on voluntary reporting led to missing incidents. They want all three channels under one federal framework with a standardized classification system, warning that uneven state or domain-specific standards make aggregate incident data unreliable.

choice.p: What weakness of mandatory-only incident reporting is a 'hybrid' system, which adds voluntary and citizen reports, meant to fix?
o: It captures only incidents inside its legal scope, so many others go unrecorded
Mandatory reporting may break the First Amendment, so voluntary reports must replace it
Companies report too many trivial incidents, so citizen reports help sort out what matters
It forces states to share one format, so a hybrid lets each state keep its own
ow: In a hybrid system, mandatory reporting stays one of the channels.
The worry is that mandatory reporting misses incidents, not that it reports too many.
The proposal puts all channels under one federal framework with standard classification; it doesn't give each state its own format.

items.p: Proposals would extend oversight to internal deployment (labs' use of models inside the company). Match each proposal to the gap it targets.
pairs: Internal-use risk reports
Regulators never hear about risks from models used only inside the lab
Tiered internal access rules
Any staff member can use the most capable internal model for anything
Disclosure of AI's role in building a model
Outsiders can't tell how much AI research is automated or goes unreviewed
Power to restrict or suspend internal use
A dangerous internal model keeps running with no outside check
items.x: Sources: a risk report each time a substantially more capable model goes into internal use, from IAPS (Delaney, O'Brien et al.); tripwires, tiered internal access rules and an internal oversight board from Apollo Research (Stix, Hobbhahn et al.); disclosure on NIST's request in the Self-Improving AI Monitoring Act; powers to verify, restrict or suspend internal use in the FRONTIER Act. California's SB 53 already requires large frontier developers to send the state confidential summaries of catastrophic-risk assessments from internal use, every three months by default.

items.p: Policies would extend oversight, reporting or limits to the AI models labs use internally, including for automating AI research. Name one concern or objection that has been raised.
items.answer: Examples: disclosing internal capabilities, usage and safeguards carries security and competitive risks to weigh for each type of information, so some details may suit private reports to government more than public release (Charnock, Moreno, Miller and Anderson, who still favor disclosure); if US labs pace themselves, China may not wait (economist Christian Catalini, on the 2026 employee letter).
keys: Disclosure has security and competitive costs to weigh (Charnock et al.)
US labs pacing themselves could cede ground to China (Catalini)
items.x: From the other side, Joe Kwon and Stephen Casper argue current laws still leave internal deployment under-covered because of scope ambiguity, point-in-time checks and information asymmetry.

choice.p: Which of these is a concern raised about extending oversight to the AI models labs use internally?
o: Disclosing internal capabilities and usage can create security and competitive risks
Internal models are too weak to matter for safety, so oversight is wasted
Internal oversight would force labs to open-source their models
Courts have ruled that a lab's internal use of AI is protected speech
ow: Advocates and critics alike treat internal models as often the most capable.
Oversight proposals involve reports and access, not open-sourcing.
No such ruling is cited.

items.p: What are AI companies' 'model behavior specifications', and why might requiring companies to publish them matter more as AI takes over more AI research?
items.answer: They set out the values, principles and norms a model is trained to follow, such as OpenAI's Model Spec and Anthropic's constitution for Claude. Published specs help outsiders understand a model's alignment and behavior while it is doing AI research and development.
keys: Documents stating the values, principles and norms a model is trained to follow
Examples: OpenAI's Model Spec, Anthropic's constitution for Claude
Help outsiders understand a model's alignment and behavior while it does AI R&D
items.x: IFP's August 2026 report asks Congress to require publishing them, one of four kinds of transparency it wants legislated, with risk management for automated AI research, incident reporting and whistleblower protections. IFP says bills already introduced (the FRONTIER Act, AI Incident Reporting Act, AI Whistleblower Protection Act) would cover much of the other three, but publishing specs would need new legislation.

choice.p: What is an AI company's 'model behavior specification'?
o: A document setting out the values and rules a model is trained to follow
A technical sheet listing a model's size, training compute and test scores
A lab's plan for which risk thresholds trigger extra safety measures
A contract stating what customers may and may not use the model for
ow: That describes parts of a model card; a behavior specification describes how the model is meant to behave.
That is a frontier AI framework, which California's SB 53 already requires large frontier developers to publish.
That is a usage policy for customers; a behavior specification governs the model's own conduct.

lessons.title: Compute, race tempo and AI-use records

items.p: As of October 2026, is there a US federal requirement to report large AI training runs to the government? What existed before?
items.answer: No. Biden's Executive Order 14110 (2023) used the Defense Production Act to require such reports, and Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security proposed quarterly reporting rules in September 2024, but the order was revoked in January 2025.
keys: No current federal requirement
EO 14110 required reports (2023)
Revoked January 2025
items.x: State laws such as SB 53 use 10^26 operations only to define who is covered. A June 2026 executive order set up only a voluntary framework for pre-release government testing. By contrast, the EU AI Act (Article 52) requires providers to notify the European Commission within two weeks once a model crosses its 10^25 systemic-risk threshold.

choice.p: As of October 2026, which best describes US federal reporting of large AI training runs?
o: None now: Biden's 2023 order required reports but was revoked in January 2025
Developers must notify Commerce within two weeks of crossing 10^26 operations
The FRONTIER Act now requires quarterly training-run reports to the Commerce Department
A June 2026 executive order requires reports for every training run above 10^25 operations
ow: Two-week notice after crossing a threshold is the EU AI Act's rule, at 10^25.
The FRONTIER Act is a bill in House committee, not law.
The June 2026 order created a voluntary pre-release testing framework, not training-run reporting.

items.p: Governments would require developers to report training runs above a fixed compute threshold. Name one objection critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: compute is an imperfect proxy for risk, since data quality, post-training and efficiency gains also drive capability, so fixed thresholds can miss risky models (Cohere's policy primer 'The Limits of Thresholds' and Sara Hooker); quarterly reporting is too burdensome, so make it annual or semiannual (CCIA, US Chamber of Commerce).
keys: Compute is an imperfect proxy for risk (Cohere, Sara Hooker)
Reporting burden too high (CCIA, US Chamber)
items.x: Heim and Koessler, who support thresholds, reply that compute works best as an initial filter for further scrutiny, updated over time and paired with capability-based measures.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to requiring reports of training runs above a fixed compute threshold?
o: Compute is an imperfect proxy for risk, so fixed thresholds can miss risky models
Reporting would expose the personal data of the model's users to regulators
Reports would let foreign governments track and seize US chips abroad
Thresholds are set so low that they cover every small AI startup
ow: Training-run reports concern compute and models, not user data.
Critics raise no such claim.
Critics stress the opposite problem: efficiency gains let risky models fall below fixed thresholds.

items.p: Some proposals would have labs report how their compute is split across uses such as final training runs, experiments, internal use and serving customers. What could this show that reports on single training runs miss?
items.answer: How much of a lab's compute goes into building its next models (experiments and internal use, increasingly by AI agents doing research) versus serving the public. That tracks the scale of internal R&D and its automation, which a per-run training threshold does not capture.
keys: Share of compute spent building next models vs serving customers
Tracks internal R&D and automation
Per-run thresholds don't capture it
items.x: IFP's August 2026 report lists such breakdowns among information that would help outsiders understand automated AI R&D, and notes that leading labs now use more compute developing next-generation models than serving today's AI. The pacing.tech research agenda lists the item as a lever, citing Epoch (2026) and Biden's Executive Order 14110, with the caveat that listing a lever is not an argument for using it.

choice.p: What could reports of how a lab splits its compute (training runs, experiments, internal use, serving customers) show that single training-run reports miss?
o: How much compute goes to building the next models versus serving users
Which of the lab's customers are using its models for dangerous or prohibited purposes
Whether each of the lab's models has passed its dangerous-capability tests
How much the lab pays for electricity at each of its data centers
ow: Compute splits are aggregate shares, not customer identities.
Test results come from evaluations and model cards, not compute splits.
Compute splits measure how compute is used, not energy prices.

items.p: In one well-known game-theory model of AI races, how can better information about rivals' capabilities make a race more dangerous?
o: When teams are close, it removes uncertainty that would make them cautious
It reveals rivals' safety methods, so teams start copying each other's risky shortcuts
It lets governments pick winners early, which provokes the losing teams into rushing ahead
It sets off stock market swings that push the labs to rush out their next releases
ow: The model's mechanism is about uncertainty and caution, not copying methods.
The model involves competing teams, not government picking winners.
The model's mechanism does not run through financial markets.
keys: Applies when teams are close
Removes the uncertainty that induces caution
items.x: The model is Armstrong, Bostrom and Shulman's 'Racing to the Precipice'. The pacing.tech research agenda cites it and treats the wider question (when common knowledge of progress intensifies or weakens races) as open. It separately lists lead-margin reporting (months between the top lab and the next) as a lever, with the caveat that listing a lever is not an argument for using it.

items.p: In August 2026 the National Archives (NARA) issued guidance applying the Federal Records Act to AI prompts and outputs. Under that guidance, why might many officials' AI chats never become federal records?
items.answer: The guidance treats AI material as not necessarily received by an agency until it is downloaded or captured in an agency system, so chats left on a vendor's platform may not count as records.
keys: Material counts only once downloaded or captured in an agency system
Chats left on a vendor's platform may not count as records
items.x: Asad Ramzanali and Margaret Mullins of the Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator criticized this as narrower than NARA's past guidance on cloud records and electronic messages, and noted it omits chain-of-thought, metadata and procurement terms. They say closing the gap now depends on agencies, courts and Congress being willing to say the guidance is not enough. As of Oct 2026 no statute specifically addresses AI records.

choice.p: Under NARA's August 2026 guidance, why might many officials' AI chats never become federal records?
o: Material left on a vendor's platform isn't treated as received until captured
It orders agencies to delete AI chat records after 30 days to save storage
It bars federal employees from using AI tools for official work
It covers only the Defense Department and the intelligence agencies
ow: The guidance orders no such deletion; the problem is that some material is never captured.
The guidance doesn't ban AI use; it addresses how AI material is kept.
The Federal Records Act guidance applies to federal agencies generally.

units.title: Verification and oversight
units.desc: Who checks what AI labs say: audits, embedded evaluators, government testing, certified verifiers, licensing and dedicated regulators.

items.p: As of October 2026, which US state has enacted the first mandatory annual audit of frontier AI developers, and when do audits begin?
items.answer: Illinois, through SB 315 (Public Act 104-0538), signed in July 2026. Annual audits begin January 1, 2028 (or 90 days after a developer first qualifies, if later).
keys: Illinois SB 315
Audits begin January 1, 2028
items.x: Massachusetts, Michigan and Pennsylvania bills and the federal FRONTIER Act copy the idea. The voluntary White House Accord on Super Intelligence (Sept 29, 2026) recommends an independent external auditor but is not legally binding.

o: Illinois, through SB 315 (signed July 2026); annual audits begin January 1, 2028
California, through SB 53 (in force January 2026); annual audits begin January 1, 2027
Michigan, through HB 4668 (frontier developer bill); annual audits begin January 1, 2027
Massachusetts, through S.3228 (2026); audits every 120 days begin in 2027
ow: SB 53 requires published frameworks and incident reports but no third-party audit.
Michigan's audit bill had not been enacted as of Oct 2026.
The Massachusetts Senate text had not been enacted as of Oct 2026, so it is not law.

items.p: Frontier AI audit proposals differ in what the auditor checks. What separates a 'framework compliance audit' (Illinois SB 315) from 'independent catastrophic-risk evaluations' (Massachusetts Senate text S.3228)?
o: Compliance audits check a lab follows its own framework; evaluations have outsiders test its models for each catastrophic risk
A compliance audit is carried out by government staff, while independent evaluations are run by the lab's own internal safety team
A compliance audit covers only open-weight models; independent evaluations cover only the closed models that labs sell through an API
A compliance audit happens before training begins; independent evaluations happen only after a reported incident
ow: Both rely on outside parties; neither variant is defined by government versus self-assessment.
Neither variant is defined by open versus closed weights.
Neither is tied to before training or after incidents.
items.x: Under S.3228 the evaluations would happen every 120 days. Critics note the compliance version does not judge whether the framework itself is adequate, so a weak framework can pass a clean audit. Substantive testing adds that check at higher cost.
keys: Compliance audit: checks the lab follows its own framework
Independent evaluations: outsiders test top models for each catastrophic risk

items.p: A law requires frontier AI developers to hire an independent auditor each year to check their safety practices. Name two objections critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: premature, because the auditing ecosystem does not exist yet and models change faster than audits can be done (NetChoice); requires private actors to make highly subjective judgments (TechNet); audits can become a checkbox exercise without high standards and deep access (Brundage et al., themselves supporters); qualified auditors are scarce and hired away by labs (Fortune).
keys: Ecosystem not ready, models change too fast (NetChoice)
Subjective determinations (TechNet)
Risk of checkbox audits (Brundage et al.)
Talent shortage and poaching by labs (Fortune)
items.x: The authors of the 'Frontier AI Auditing' paper (Brundage et al.) respond by proposing standards and graded assurance levels, so policy can demand more rigorous audits as risk rises.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics have raised to mandatory annual audits of frontier AI developers?
o: The audit field isn't ready: auditors are scarce and models outpace audits
Audits would force labs to publish their model weights online for anyone to download and inspect
Audits would replace each lab's own safety framework with a single framework written by government regulators
Audits would apply only to open-weight models, so closed frontier models escape any review
ow: Auditors get confidential access; no audit mandate requires publishing weights.
Compliance audits check the lab's own framework; the common critique runs the other way, that a weak framework can pass.
Audit mandates cover the largest developers however they release their models.

items.p: Why might rules for frontier AI audits define tiers of assurance, and what would separate the lowest tier from the highest?
items.answer: Tiers let policy demand more rigorous, deeper-access audits as risk rises. The lowest would be a time-limited audit of one system lasting a few weeks, mostly through API (black-box) access, which can catch errors but is less likely to detect fraud (deliberate deception); the highest would be continuous verification designed to detect active deception.
keys: Tiers let rigor and access scale with risk
Lowest: weeks-long audit mostly through API access, catches errors more than fraud
Highest: continuous verification built to detect deception
items.x: This is the 'AI Assurance Levels' scheme in 'Frontier AI Auditing' (Brundage, Anderljung et al., Jan 2026), running from AAL-1 to AAL-4; the authors call AAL-4 'treaty-grade'. They recommend AAL-1 as a baseline for frontier AI and AAL-2 (months long, gray-box or partial access to internals, internal documents, staff interviews) as a near-term goal for the most advanced developers, and say AAL-3 and AAL-4 are not yet technically and organizationally feasible.

choice.p: In a tiered scheme for frontier AI audits, what would separate the highest tier from the lowest?
o: Highest: continuous checks built to catch deception; lowest: a weeks-long audit via API
The highest is run by government inspectors; the lowest by the lab's own internal safety team
The highest covers open-weight models; the lowest covers only models that are sold through an API
The highest is required by state law; the lowest is set by voluntary industry commitments
ow: All tiers are outside audits; they differ in access, duration and confidence.
The tiers aren't defined by how a model is released.
The tiers are defined by rigor and access, not by which rule requires them.

items.p: Why might audits of frontier AI labs need to cover the whole organization as well as its public products? Name two reasons.
items.answer: Any two of: internal deployment of models never released can cause harm, and auditors may not know about it by default; strong product safeguards can be undone by weak weight security, since stolen weights run without them; a well-controlled flagship product can sit beside riskier systems elsewhere; parts that look safe alone may not be safe once combined into agents.
keys: Internal deployments that are never released
Weak weight security undoes product safeguards
Riskier systems elsewhere in the company
Safe parts may be unsafe once combined
items.x: This case is made in 'Frontier AI Auditing' (Brundage, Anderljung et al., 2026), which says audits should cover 'the full range of organization-level safety and security risks', including internal deployment, information security and safety decision-making. The authors conclude the company level is best for confident conclusions, though harder to audit.

choice.p: Why might audits of frontier AI labs need to cover the whole organization as well as its public products?
o: Harm can come from models used only inside the lab, and stolen weights run without product safeguards
The EU AI Office already audits every public product in full, so the rest of the company is the only gap left
Labs are legally barred from letting outside auditors test their public products
Company-wide audits are cheaper and faster than testing individual models
ow: The EU AI Office can request access to general-purpose models, but it does not audit every product; the reasons concern where risk sits.
No such bar exists; auditors routinely test public products through APIs.
Company-level audits are harder to do, not cheaper or faster.

items.p: Match each version of embedded AI auditing to where it appears.
pairs: State-designated onsite verifier at each large developer
Option under study in California executive order N-9-26
Standing government team supervising each developer
ARI federal blueprint, modeled on bank examiners
Paid embedded evaluation partnership
Anthropic with Accenture (Sept 2026)
items.x: As of Oct 2026 no jurisdiction requires embedded auditors. California's executive order asks for recommendations by November 16, 2026 on amending state law, including requiring onsite verifiers at large frontier developers. GovAI researchers have also proposed voluntary embedded assessments with quarterly reports (Sept 2026). ARI is Americans for Responsible Innovation.

items.p: Outside evaluators would work inside frontier AI labs with ongoing access. Name two concerns critics and analysts have raised.
items.answer: Examples: with weak access, few resources or no say in decisions, embedded evaluations may give a false sense of security, and voluntary versions are unlikely to be enough (Apollo Research); mandatory third-party evaluation can raise the risk of leaks and industrial espionage (pacing.tech authors); long-term residents may come to share the views of the lab staff they oversee.
keys: False sense of security if access is weak (Apollo)
Voluntary versions likely insufficient (Apollo)
Leak and espionage risk (pacing.tech)
Residents may adopt lab staff's views
items.x: Apollo's authors, who support embedded evaluations, argue they should eventually be legally required to fix the access problem. The last concern is a general critique with no single named author.

choice.p: Which of these is a concern analysts have raised about embedded evaluators working inside frontier AI labs?
o: With weak access or no influence on decisions, they may give a false sense of security
They would have to publish a lab's trade secrets in their public reports
They could only test models after public release, too late to help
They would duplicate CAISI's existing mandatory inspections inside every lab
ow: Designs keep findings confidential or summarized; leak risk is a concern, but publishing trade secrets is not proposed.
Seeing models before release is the main point of embedding evaluators.
CAISI's testing is voluntary and does not include inspections inside labs.

items.p: As of October 2026, how does US government pre-deployment testing of frontier AI models work?
items.answer: It is voluntary. The Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) at NIST tests models under voluntary agreements with five labs, and a June 2026 executive order (EO 14409) directs several agencies to design a voluntary framework giving government up to 30 days of access to covered models before release. No bill making testing mandatory has passed.
keys: Voluntary, run by CAISI at NIST
Agreements with five labs
June 2026 order: up to 30 days early access
No mandatory bill has passed
items.x: The June 2026 order (EO 14409) expressly disclaims mandatory licensing or preclearance. China has required a government security assessment before launching public generative AI services since 2023.

o: Voluntary: CAISI tests under deals with five labs; a June 2026 order seeks up to 30 days' access
Mandatory: under a May 2026 executive order, developers must give CAISI 90 days of access to each model before release
Mandatory: the AI Risk Evaluation Act requires Energy Department testing of each model before deployment
None exists: CAISI was abolished in 2025 and all frontier model testing moved over to the EU AI Office
ow: A draft order with 90 days of access was shelved in May 2026; the June order is voluntary and allows up to 30 days.
The Hawley-Blumenthal bill would do this, but it has not passed.
CAISI exists and runs voluntary testing; the EU AI Office has no role in US release decisions.

items.p: Which bill would bar deploying covered frontier AI models without first participating in a Department of Energy evaluation program?
o: The AI Risk Evaluation Act (Hawley and Blumenthal)
Warner's AI Risk Management and Security Act (S. 5576)
California SB 53
The AI Systems Transparency Act (sponsored by Coons and Britt)
ow: Warner's bill would create a safety board inside the Commerce Department with 45 days of access before release.
SB 53 requires published frameworks and transparency reports, with no government testing gate.
This bill would have the FTC require model-card disclosures; it creates no government testing program.
items.x: The AI Risk Evaluation Act (S. 2938, introduced Sept 2025) would set up an evaluation program at the Department of Energy and require developers to provide information on request. It was still in committee as of Oct 2026. A guest post on the libertarian Cato Institute's blog (Juan Londono, Taxpayers Protection Alliance) called it a power grab by the executive, objecting mainly to a provision on oversight options up to nationalization.
keys: AI Risk Evaluation Act
Hawley and Blumenthal
Department of Energy evaluation program

items.p: Government evaluators would test frontier AI models for dangerous capabilities before release. Name two objections critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: evaluations can show a capability exists but not reliably that it is absent (Barnett et al., MIRI); a voluntary regime cannot bind labs that refuse (Mariana Olaizola Rosenblat); delaying access is not a durable cyber defense since comparable capabilities spread (Ji and Lohn, CSET); a mandatory window could block US releases (Trump, May 2026).
keys: Tests cannot prove absence of capability (MIRI)
Voluntary regime cannot bind (Rosenblat)
Delaying access is not a durable defense (CSET)
Could become a release blocker (Trump, May 2026)
items.x: In May 2026 Trump postponed signing a draft order that gave government 90 days of pre-launch access, saying it 'could have been a blocker'; Zuckerberg, Musk and David Sacks reportedly spoke with him first. The June 2026 order (EO 14409) instead directed agencies to design a voluntary framework with up to 30 days of access.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics have raised to government testing of frontier AI models before release?
o: Tests can show a model has a dangerous capability but can't reliably show it lacks one
Labs would have to publish their full model weights so that anyone could run the same tests
Tests would happen only after release, too late to stop a harmful launch
Testing duplicates the EU AI Office's pre-release approval of US models
ow: Pre-release testing gives government confidential access; none of these proposals requires publishing weights.
These proposals test models before release by design; critics question what the tests can show.
The EU AI Office can request access to models, but it is not a pre-release gate for US releases.

items.p: Why do rigorous AI audits need more than black-box access (only querying a model and reading its outputs)? Say what access to model internals and access to development information each let auditors do.
items.answer: White-box access to internals (weights, activations, gradients) lets auditors run stronger attacks, interpret how the model works, and fine-tune it to surface hidden capabilities. Outside-the-box access to training methods, code, data, documentation and internal evaluation results lets them examine the development process and design more targeted tests.
keys: White-box: internals such as weights and activations
Enables stronger attacks, interpretation, fine-tuning
Outside-the-box: training and deployment information
Lets auditors examine the process and target tests
items.x: The case is made in Casper et al., 'Black-Box Access is Insufficient for Rigorous AI Audits' (2024). Black-box access is how most audits of frontier systems had worked. The authors argue results depend on the access granted, so reports should disclose it, and they discuss technical, physical and legal safeguards to limit the security risk of deeper access.

choice.p: What does white-box access to a model's internals, such as its weights and activations, let auditors do that only querying it can't?
o: Run stronger attacks, interpret how the model works, and fine-tune it to find hidden abilities
Query the finished model through its public API as often as they like, free of charge
Read the lab's board minutes, investor agreements, customer contracts and other corporate records
Publish the model's weights openly for anyone to use once the audit has been completed
ow: Querying through an API is black-box access, the thing white-box access goes beyond.
White-box access means model internals such as weights and activations, not corporate records.
Deeper access calls for security safeguards; it doesn't mean publishing weights.

items.p: Risk: a lab releases a model with dangerous capabilities that its own internal tests missed or underestimated. Name two policies proposed to catch this.
items.answer: Examples: government pre-deployment testing; mandatory third-party audits or independent catastrophic-risk evaluations; embedded evaluators inside labs; deeper evaluator access to model internals; mandatory disclosure of dangerous-capability test results.
keys: Government pre-deployment testing
Third-party audits or evaluations
Embedded evaluators
Deeper evaluator access
Disclosure of test results
items.x: Longpre et al. argue in-house evaluation is not enough and call for flaw-disclosure programs with legal safe harbors so outside researchers can report problems. If the cause is a model hiding what it can do, elicitation budgets and sandbagging checks also apply.

choice.p: A lab releases a model with dangerous capabilities that its own tests missed. Which of these is a policy proposed to catch this?
o: Government evaluators testing each new frontier model before it ships
Federal preemption of all state AI safety laws and audits
Tighter export controls on advanced AI chips
Mandatory watermarking of all AI-generated images and video
ow: Preemption decides which level of government sets rules; it adds no check on a lab's tests.
Export controls limit who gets compute; they add no check on a lab's testing.
Watermarking labels AI content; it doesn't test models for dangerous capabilities.

items.p: What is an 'independent verification organization' (IVO) system for AI, such as the one California created with SB 813 (signed Sept 2026)?
items.answer: The state designates or certifies private organizations (IVOs), independent of the companies they check, to assess AI models and systems against state requirements. Government sets the application rules and criteria and can suspend or terminate an IVO. Developers are not compelled to use one; proposals in this family often reward participation with a legal benefit.
keys: State certifies private verifiers
Verifiers must be independent of those assessed
Government can suspend or revoke them
Participation voluntary for developers
items.x: Under SB 813, California's Government Operations Agency must certify the first IVOs by January 1, 2028. As of Oct 2026, Connecticut has enacted a voluntary pilot and Ohio has a bill. The federal FRONTIER Act would instead require the very largest developers to retain a federally licensed IVO.

o: The state certifies independent private verifiers to assess AI, and developers may choose to use them
The state hires its own engineers to inspect every frontier AI model before it is released
Developers must register each model with the state and pay a yearly licensing fee before they can sell it
