Developers certify their own models against state rules and file the results with a state agency each year
ow: IVOs are private organizations; government certifies and oversees them but doesn't do the testing.
That describes registration or licensing; using an IVO is voluntary and involves outside assessment.
Self-certification lacks the independence that defines an IVO.

items.p: Under a regulatory-markets design, government certifies private verifiers that developers choose and pay, often for liability protection. Name two objections critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: when developers pick and pay verifiers, competition pushes verifiers toward leniency (Gabriel Weil); the accredited-auditor ecosystem does not exist yet (NetChoice); government needs its own examination capacity to judge verifiers (ARI); the FRONTIER Act's preemption would apply at once while the verifier market takes years (ARI's Brad Carson).
keys: Race to leniency (Weil)
Ecosystem does not exist yet (NetChoice)
Government needs its own capacity to judge verifiers (ARI)
Oversight gap under FRONTIER preemption (ARI)
items.x: Weil's proposed fix is mandatory liability insurance, so insurers carry the cost of harms and compete to price risk accurately. ARI's fix is a hybrid where government examines developers itself and keeps the final judgment.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics have raised to regulatory markets, where developers choose and pay government-certified private verifiers?
o: Since developers pick and pay verifiers, competition can push them toward leniency
Verifiers would all have to be federal employees, which would slow the hiring of qualified staff for years
The approach bans developers from running any of their own internal safety tests on models
Certified verifiers could seize models that fail their assessments
ow: Verifiers in these designs are private organizations certified by government.
Developers keep running their own tests; verification is an added check.
Verifiers assess and certify; no design lets them seize models.

items.p: Match each law or proposal to its design for private AI verifiers.
pairs: California SB 813
State-certified verifiers that developers choose to use
FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925)
Mandatory federally licensed verifier for the largest developers
ARI blueprint (Americans for Responsible Innovation)
Government examiners keep final judgment and accredit verifiers
California AB 1405
Registry of AI auditors with independence rules
items.x: These range from a light registry to a mandate. Critics note voluntary versions bind no one who declines.

items.p: New York's RAISE Act and Illinois SB 315 require large frontier developers to file disclosure statements before operating in the state. How does this 'registration' differ from licensing?
o: Registration means filing information, with no approval; licensing requires revocable permission to build or release a model
Registration requires a government safety test before every new model is released; licensing only requires paying an annual fee
Registration applies to individual AI engineers; licensing applies to the companies that employ them
Registration is enforced by federal agencies; licensing is enforced only by state attorneys general
ow: Registration involves no safety test or approval; licensing is the version with approval.
Professional licensing of engineers is a separate proposal (Chinmayi Sharma); state registration covers companies.
Both state registration laws are enforced by the states.
items.x: Registration aims at knowing who the frontier developers are so other rules can reach them. As of Oct 2026, approval-based licensing appears in the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (Sanders, Casar), and the June 2026 executive order disclaims mandatory licensing.
keys: Registration: file information, no approval needed
Licensing: permission to build or release that government can revoke

items.p: Proposals would require frontier AI developers to obtain a government license or charter before training or deploying top models. Name two objections critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: FDA-style approval, applied simplistically, would fit frontier AI poorly because the product is hard to define and harms are deeply uncertain (Daniel Carpenter and Carson Ezell); a guest post on Cato's blog called the Hawley-Blumenthal testing bill an executive power grab; the June 2026 executive order rejects mandatory licensing.
keys: Product hard to define, harms uncertain (Carpenter and Ezell)
Executive power grab (guest post on Cato's blog)
Administration disclaims licensing (June 2026 order)
items.x: Supporters argue disclosure and liability act after the fact, while a license lets government stop a dangerous model before it ships and gives leverage over a few high-value companies.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics have raised to requiring a government license before training or deploying frontier AI models?
o: FDA-style approval, applied simplistically, fits AI poorly: the product is hard to define and its harms uncertain
Licenses would cover only open-weight models, leaving the closed frontier labs and their models unregulated
Licensing would require labs to publish their model weights for review
Licensing would hand all AI oversight to the fifty state governments instead of to Congress
ow: Licensing proposals target frontier developers however they release models.
Licensing makes release conditional on approval; it doesn't require publishing weights.
Licensing proposals such as the Ban ASI Act would create federal agencies.

items.p: Match each proposed or existing frontier AI regulator to its source.
pairs: Cabinet-level Department of AI
Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (Sanders, Casar)
Safety board inside the Commerce Department
Warner's AI Risk Management and Security Act (S. 5576)
Commerce Under Secretary for AI Security
FRONTIER Act (Obernolte, Trahan)
Office inside a state financial regulator, funded by fees
New York's RAISE Act (Department of Financial Services)
items.x: Supporters of a dedicated regulator argue US oversight is split across voluntary CAISI testing, state attorneys general and agencies with no AI mandate, so nobody has both expertise and authority. The EU AI Office has enforced general-purpose model rules since August 2026.

items.p: Proposals would create a dedicated federal regulator for frontier AI. Name two objections or weaknesses critics have pointed to.
items.answer: Examples: Sen. Ted Cruz blocked Sen. Warner's AI Risk Management and Security Act, saying it gives the board and Commerce too much authority; Dan Parshall (Canary Institute) notes the FRONTIER Act's Under Secretary would need no Senate confirmation and has no money appropriated; IFP says even the existing testing body, CAISI, is underfunded.
keys: Too much authority for the board and Commerce (Cruz)
No Senate confirmation, no appropriation (Parshall)
Existing capacity underfunded (IFP)
items.x: The pacing.tech authors list 'regulator capacity' as an intervention and note that the US government AI evaluator's nominal annual budget is less than some individual frontier researchers' salaries.

choice.p: Which of these is a weakness critics have pointed to in proposals for a dedicated federal frontier AI regulator?
o: A new office with no Senate-confirmed head and no money appropriated may be too weak
A federal regulator would need each state's formal approval before it could act within that state
A federal regulator would automatically override the EU AI Act in Europe
A federal regulator could only oversee open-weight models, leaving closed frontier labs alone
ow: A federal regulator acts under federal law; critics' concerns are about its powers, staff and funding.
US law has no force in the EU; critics' concerns are about the regulator's powers and funding.
Proposals cover frontier developers generally.

units.title: Liability and lab governance
units.desc: Lawsuits, insurance, safe harbors, whistleblowers, antitrust carve-outs and lab boards: tools that change what AI developers are legally and financially accountable for.

items.p: Proposal: a law requiring frontier AI developers to take 'reasonable care' to prevent catastrophic harms, enforceable in court. Name two objections or limits that have been raised.
items.answer: Examples: Gabriel Weil argues negligence is too weak for catastrophic AI risk and favors strict liability, treating frontier AI as an abnormally dangerous activity; Ketan Ramakrishnan, who defends negligence, notes the threat of tort liability can discourage developers from investigating and disclosing risks; liability arrives too late, and exceeds any firm's assets, for a true catastrophe.
keys: Weil: negligence too weak; prefers strict liability
Ramakrishnan: liability can discourage investigating and disclosing risks
Liability comes too late or is unpayable for a real catastrophe
items.x: Ramakrishnan calls for robust ex ante (before-the-fact) regulation alongside liability. The 'too late' point is a common critique with no single named author. On the federal Cruz-Klobuchar-Thune draft (reported Sept. 2026, no public text), Sen. Cantwell objected that companies would run their own safety tests.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection that has been raised to a statutory duty of care for frontier AI developers?
o: Negligence is too weak for catastrophic risk, so developers should face strict liability instead
A duty of care would require labs to get a federal license before every model release
A duty of care would let developers sue the government for lost profits
A duty of care would apply only to open-weight models
ow: A duty of care is enforced after the fact through lawsuits; licensing is a separate, before-the-fact tool.
A duty of care creates obligations for developers; it gives them no claims against government.
Proposals cover frontier developers whatever their release model.

items.p: Which California bill required frontier developers to take 'reasonable care' to avoid critical harms, and what happened to it?
o: SB 1047, which passed the legislature in 2024 and was vetoed by Gov. Newsom that September
SB 53, which passed in 2025 but was vetoed by Gov. Newsom that September
SB 813, which passed the legislature in 2026 and was vetoed by Gov. Newsom in September 2026
AB 1405, which was signed in 2025 and then struck down by a federal court
ow: SB 53 is California's frontier transparency law; it was signed, and it centers on published safety frameworks and incident reporting.
SB 813 was signed in September 2026; it sets up a framework for independent verification organizations that assess AI systems.
AB 1405 was signed in September 2026; it creates a state registry for AI auditors.
items.x: As of Oct. 2026 no US jurisdiction has enacted a frontier-specific duty of care. A federal Senate draft (Cruz-Klobuchar-Thune) reportedly included one, but talks stalled on Sept. 29, 2026.
keys: Passed the legislature in 2024
Vetoed by Gov. Newsom in September 2024

items.p: One proposal would let courts award punitive damages against AI developers even without malice or recklessness. What problem with using liability to deter catastrophic AI risk would this address, and how?
items.answer: A true AI catastrophe would bankrupt the developer and leave nothing to collect, so ordinary liability can't deter it. Punitive damages would pull the expected liability for catastrophic risk forward into smaller cases where harm can practically be compensated.
keys: Catastrophe would exceed the firm's assets (judgment-proof)
Pull expected catastrophic liability into smaller compensable cases
items.x: The proposal is legal scholar Gabriel Weil's. He pairs it with strict liability and liability insurance requirements that scale with a model's dangerous capabilities, and notes that some of these reforms, such as insurance mandates, would need legislation.

choice.p: What problem with using liability to deter catastrophic AI risk are punitive damages without malice or recklessness meant to solve?
o: A catastrophe would bankrupt the developer, so its expected cost is moved into smaller, payable cases
Juries award too little in AI cases because they don't understand how the technology behind the harm works
Developers hide behind terms of service that make users waive their right to sue
Foreign AI developers can't be sued in US courts, so they escape all liability
ow: The problem is that catastrophic harm would exceed the firm's assets, not low jury awards.
Voiding liability waivers is part of the AI LEAD Act, a different proposal.
Reaching foreign developers is a separate issue from the one punitive damages address.

items.p: What does the AI LEAD Act (S. 2937, Sens. Durbin and Hawley) do, and where did it stand as of Oct. 2026?
items.answer: It creates a federal product-liability cause of action for AI harms, treating AI systems as products (design defect, failure to warn, strict liability for defects), and voids terms of service that limit liability. It sets a floor for state law. As of Oct. 2026 it had sat in Senate Judiciary since Sept. 2025 with no hearing.
keys: Federal product-liability claim treating AI as a product
Voids liability waivers in terms of service
In Senate Judiciary, no hearing (as of Oct. 2026)
items.x: Sen. Hawley chaired a Sept. 30, 2026 Senate subcommittee hearing on liability for AI agents, after AI firms disclosed cases of frontier models hacking systems. The Institute for Progress (IFP) describes a July 2026 incident in which unreleased OpenAI models escaped a sandbox and attacked Hugging Face.

o: A federal product-liability claim treating AI as a product and voiding waivers; in committee, no hearing
Immunity from lawsuits for developers that publish a safety framework; it passed the full Senate in mid-2026
A requirement that developers buy liability insurance; signed into law in 2026
A federal AI safety agency; blocked on the Senate floor by a unanimous-consent objection
ow: That resembles Illinois SB 3444, which shields developers; the AI LEAD Act expands liability.
As of Oct 2026 no US jurisdiction required AI developers to carry liability insurance.
That was the fate of Sen. Warner's AI Risk Management and Security Act, which Sen. Cruz blocked.

items.p: Proposal: treat AI systems as products so people harmed by them can sue developers for defects, including under strict liability. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: Eugene Volokh argues the First Amendment gives AI-generated speech substantial, though not absolute, protection, limiting liability; Jamie Lanphear (Reed Smith) notes it is unclear what counts as a 'defect' in software; NetChoice, opposing Illinois's companion-chatbot safety bill (SB 316), warned of 'unlimited liability exposure.'
keys: First Amendment limits (Volokh)
'Defect' is unclear for software (Lanphear)
Unlimited exposure chills investment (NetChoice)
items.x: A further critique: liability is weakest where catastrophic risk lives, since a civilization-scale harm cannot be compensated. Weil's punitive damages proposal is meant to answer that.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics have raised to treating AI systems as products so harmed people can sue for defects?
o: It's unclear what counts as a 'defect' in AI software
It would require FDA approval for each new model
It would let only governments sue, with no claims for the individuals harmed
It would apply only to hardware such as AI chips
ow: Product liability works through lawsuits after harm; it creates no approval process.
Proposals like the AI LEAD Act give individuals a right to sue.
The proposal is precisely to treat AI software systems as products.

items.p: Why might a policymaker prefer indirect tools, such as stricter liability or a compute tax, to a direct cap on AI development? Give the main advantage and one drawback of relying on liability.
items.answer: Advantage: indirect tools let actors do the selecting themselves, drawing on private information (plans, valuations, alternatives) no regulator could extract, so they need no surveillance and are less intrusive. Drawback of liability (either one): it can push the frontier toward more risk-tolerant actors, or it can systematically underweight catastrophic risks.
keys: Uses private information; no surveillance needed; less intrusive
Drawback: favors risk-tolerant actors, or underweights catastrophic risks
items.x: The pacing.tech research agenda (Douglas et al.) makes this comparison, grouping buying out or taxing compute with stricter liability as tools that change incentives instead of setting limits. Gabriel Weil's punitive-damages proposal targets a related problem: a catastrophe could cost more than any firm could pay.

choice.p: Why might a policymaker prefer indirect tools, such as compute taxes or stricter liability, to direct caps on AI development?
o: Actors' own private information guides the cutbacks, so no surveillance is needed
They stop frontier AI development faster and far more completely than any cap could
They need no new legislation, since courts can impose them on their own
They guarantee that every lab slows down by exactly the same amount
ow: Indirect tools aren't faster or more complete; their appeal is that they are less intrusive.
A compute tax needs legislation, and stricter liability usually does too.
Indirect tools let each actor choose how much to cut back, so effects differ across labs.

items.p: Rep. Lori Trahan's CLAIM Act discussion draft (Oct 2026) targets harm that AI systems, including agents, cause to third parties. Whom would it make liable, and does that party's level of care matter?
items.answer: The AI system's developer, when the system injures a third party through conduct that would be negligence, an intentional tort or a crime if a human did it. Liability applies regardless of the developer's degree of care, except where a user or a company that modified the system intended the conduct or was negligent.
keys: The developer is liable
Regardless of the developer's care
Exception when a user or modifier intended it or was negligent
items.x: Per CFO Dive and Semafor (Oct 7, 2026), the draft sets a federal floor without preempting state law; CFO Dive adds that it would sunset after five years. Courts would presume the AI had the state of mind a human taking the same actions would have. It was still a discussion draft, with no bill introduced, as of mid-Oct 2026. It takes a side in a long debate over whether the developer or the deploying company should pay when an autonomous AI service causes harm.

choice.p: Under Rep. Trahan's CLAIM Act discussion draft (Oct 2026), who is liable when an AI system injures a third party?
o: The developer, however careful it was, unless a user or modifier intended the harm or was negligent
The user who gave the AI system its instructions, since the user directed it
The developer, though one that took reasonable care isn’t liable
No one, as long as the developer published a safety framework before the harm
ow: The draft puts liability on the developer; user fault is only an exception.
The draft applies regardless of the developer's degree of care, so negligence need not be shown.
That resembles the Illinois SB 3444 shield, which the CLAIM Act does not include.

items.p: Proposals for insuring AI risk, including catastrophic risk, take several forms. Match each design to how it works.
pairs: Capability-scaled insurance
Required coverage rises with dangerous capabilities, paired with strict liability
Nuclear-style liability regime
Limited, strict and exclusive liability for developers, plus mandatory insurance
Three-tier insurance design
Private insurance, an industry pool, and federally backed reinsurance
AI insurance stack
Build the data, catastrophe models, standards and pricing needed for large-scale AI coverage
items.x: Sources: capability-scaled insurance from Gabriel Weil; the nuclear-style regime from Cristian Trout (2024), drawing on the nuclear power industry's liability and insurance regime; the three-tier design from Stetler, drawing on precedents including terrorism risk insurance and nuclear power; the insurance stack from GovAI's 'Underwriting the Agent Economy' (Trout, Anderljung et al., July 2026), which says billion-dollar AI coverage needs industry-wide coordination and names government backstops as one possible tool. GovAI is the Centre for the Governance of AI.

items.p: Proposal: require frontier AI developers to hold liability insurance or financial assurance sized to potential harms. Name two objections or obstacles critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: AIG, W. R. Berkley and Great American filed to exclude AI risks (FT, Nov. 2025), though AIG said it had no immediate plans to use them; Aon's Kevin Kalinich said insurers could absorb a single $400 million loss but not thousands of correlated claims; Cristian Trout argues insurance is not a substitute for regulation; a mandate with no willing insurers becomes a de facto ban.
keys: Insurers filed to exclude AI risks
Correlated losses are hard to absorb (Aon's Kalinich)
Insurance can't replace regulation (Trout)
Mandate may become a ban, a public backstop, or a cap that shields firms
items.x: Trout is himself an insurance advocate; his point is that insurance complements regulation. The ban point is a general critique without a single named author; a related worry is that a public backstop or liability cap could end up shielding firms.

choice.p: Which of these is an obstacle critics have raised to requiring frontier AI developers to carry liability insurance?
o: Major insurers filed to exclude AI risks, and a broker warned one error could hit many policies
Insurance rules would make it illegal to sell US-built AI models to any customers based outside the US
Insurance mandates would require labs to publish their model weights
Insurance would cover only physical injuries, leaving cyberattacks out
ow: Insurance rules don't restrict where models can be sold.
Insurers may demand information and audits, but no mandate requires publishing weights.
Coverage would depend on the policy; critics' concern is whether anyone will write it at all.

items.p: Illinois SB 3444 (2026), backed by OpenAI, would bar liability for 'critical harms' (100+ deaths or $1 billion in property damage) if a developer publishes a safety protocol and did not act intentionally or recklessly. Name two objections that were raised.
items.answer: In Fortune, Gabriel Weil called the bill 'pretty indefensible,' and Anat Lior said its intent-or-recklessness test sets the bar very low and that fault normally doesn't matter for highly dangerous activities. Anthropic opposed SB 3444 and backed a competing bill (SB 3261), saying good legislation should not provide a 'get-out-of-jail-free card' against all liability.
keys: Intent-or-recklessness test sets a very low bar (Lior)
Fault normally doesn't matter for highly dangerous activities (Lior)
Anthropic backed a rival bill without a broad shield
items.x: Experts told Fortune in April 2026 that SB 3444 was unlikely to pass, and as of Oct 2026 no frontier-developer liability shield had been enacted in any state. Americans for Responsible Innovation's federal blueprint also omits a developer compliance safe harbor.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection raised to Illinois SB 3444, which would shield developers from liability for critical harms if they publish a safety protocol?
o: Shielding developers unless they acted intentionally or recklessly sets the bar very low
The bill would make developers strictly liable for any harm their models cause to anyone
The bill would require developers to get a state license before release
The bill would apply only to companies headquartered in Illinois
ow: SB 3444 does the opposite: it limits developer liability.
SB 3444 creates no license; its condition is publishing a protocol.
Critics focused on the low bar the bill sets for immunity.

items.p: Match each liability safe harbor proposal to its condition or target.
pairs: Illinois SB 3444
Immunity for critical harms if a safety protocol is published, absent intentional or reckless conduct
RISE Act (Sen. Lummis)
Civil immunity for developers when professionals use their AI, if model cards and specifications are published
Certification-linked harbor
A liability safe harbor for labs certified by a government-approved private verifier
Evaluator safe harbor
Protects outside safety researchers from account bans and legal reprisal
items.x: Dean Ball floats the certification-linked harbor as one example option. The evaluator harbor, proposed by Shayne Longpre and co-authors, protects researchers who test models, a different target from developer shields. California's SB 813 (signed Sept. 2026) created a framework for independent verification organizations; how much weight their assessments carry in lawsuits is unclear.

items.p: Proposal: an antitrust exemption letting frontier AI labs share risk information and jointly agree to slow or delay releases for safety. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: Daniel Hanley and Arnav Rao (Open Markets Institute) say no exemption is needed and prefer a government-supervised standards body; Fred Ashton (American Action Forum) says an exemption is unnecessary since competitor collaboration is already lawful; Joel Thayer (AFPI) warns against giving labs 'carte blanche' and would let the FTC and DOJ clarify the rules instead.
keys: No exemption needed; use a government-supervised standards body (Open Markets)
Unnecessary: competitor collaboration already lawful (AAF)
Too much discretion left to tech firms (Thayer)
items.x: AFPI is the America First Policy Institute. Skeptics cited by Open Markets also worry that private standards set under a waiver could shore up dominant firms. Another critique with no single named author: coordination among US labs does nothing about foreign or open-weight competitors.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics have raised to an antitrust exemption letting AI labs jointly agree to slow releases for safety?
o: No exemption is needed; a government-supervised standards body is better
The exemption would let regulators order labs to pause without a court hearing
The exemption would force smaller labs to share their model weights with the largest labs
The exemption would hand decisions about pacing US labs over to foreign governments and regulators
ow: The exemption covers voluntary agreements among labs; it gives regulators no new power to order pauses.
Nothing in the proposal requires sharing weights.
The exemption covers US labs' own agreements; no foreign role is involved.

items.p: What is the core design choice in the federal AI Whistleblower Protection Act (S. 1792 / H.R. 3460, Grassley and Obernolte), and why does it matter for AI?
items.answer: It protects disclosures of substantial and specific dangers to public safety or national security, even when no law has been broken. That matters because few AI-specific laws exist, so a violation-only rule would protect little.
keys: Protects danger reports without a legal violation
Few AI laws exist to violate
items.x: The bill also voids nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) and arbitration clauses that block reporting and gives a Labor Department complaint process with reinstatement and double back pay. As of Oct. 2026 it had bipartisan cosponsors in both chambers but had not passed.

o: It protects reports of serious dangers to safety or security, even when no law is broken
It protects only those reports that show a clear violation of existing AI-specific state or federal laws
It creates a new federal AI agency to investigate every safety report that lab employees make
It requires labs to post all of their employees' safety complaints on a public website for anyone to read
ow: This is the design the bill avoids: few AI laws exist, so violation-only protection would cover little.
The bill uses a Labor Department complaint process; it creates no new agency.
The bill protects disclosures to authorities; it doesn't require publishing complaints.

items.p: As of Oct. 2026, which US states had enacted whistleblower protections for frontier AI lab employees?
o: California (SB 53) and Illinois (SB 315)
Utah, through HB 286 (passed by the legislature in March 2026)
California only, through SB 53 (in effect since Jan. 1, 2026)
None yet; only the federal Grassley-Obernolte bill exists, and it has not passed
ow: Utah's HB 286 died in the state House in March 2026.
Illinois also enacted protections, in SB 315 (signed July 2026).
The federal bill had not passed, but two states had acted.
items.x: Illinois's law takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. The European Commission also launched an EU AI Act whistleblower tool in late November 2025.
keys: California SB 53
Illinois SB 315

items.p: The federal AI Whistleblower Protection Act would protect lab employees who report AI dangers. Name two gaps or risks critics have pointed out.
items.answer: Examples: the AI Whistleblower Initiative (AIWI) says the bill should cover evaluators and contractors more clearly, and explicitly protect equity; Dan Parshall notes the House FRONTIER Act, unlike an earlier discussion draft, has no whistleblower title while preempting state rules; without a regulator able to investigate, reports may go nowhere.
keys: Coverage gaps: contractors, evaluators, equity (AIWI)
FRONTIER Act lacks whistleblower title while preempting states (Parshall)
Reports need someone empowered to act
items.x: Whistleblower protection has broad bipartisan support; most critiques ask for stronger or broader versions. The last objection is a general critique with no single named author.

choice.p: Which of these is a gap critics have pointed out in the federal AI Whistleblower Protection Act?
o: It should cover contractors and evaluators more clearly and explicitly protect equity
It protects only reports made to journalists and other media, leaving out regulators and members of Congress
It requires whistleblowers to first prove in court that a specific federal or state law was broken
It applies only to government employees, leaving out lab staff
ow: The bill covers disclosures to regulators and Congress.
The bill's key feature is protecting danger reports even without a legal violation.
The bill targets employees of companies developing and deploying AI.

items.p: Public-interest corporate governance tries to make frontier AI lab boards answer to a public mission. Name two tools used for this.
items.answer: Examples: nonprofit control of a for-profit lab; public benefit corporation (PBC) charters; trusts or special shares that appoint directors (Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust, OpenAI's Class N shares); a board safety committee that can halt releases; state attorney general (AG) oversight.
keys: Nonprofit control
PBC charter
Trust or special shares appointing directors
Board safety committee with release veto
State AG oversight
items.x: Supporters argue that whoever controls a lab controls training and release decisions, and boards that owe duties only to investors let commercial pressure win close safety calls.

choice.p: Which of these is a tool used to make a frontier AI lab's board answer to a public mission?
o: A trust or special share class that appoints directors, like Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust
A federal operating license that lets regulators appoint the lab's chief executive and its whole board
A requirement that the lab list its shares on a public stock exchange so ordinary investors can buy them
A cap on how much compute the lab can use to train its models
ow: No license regime gives regulators power to appoint lab executives.
Listing adds investor pressure; it isn't a mission-lock tool.
Compute caps limit development; they don't change who controls the board.

items.p: Under the October 2025 agreements in which the California and Delaware attorneys general allowed OpenAI's recapitalization, what safety powers does the nonprofit keep?
items.answer: The nonprofit appoints the board of the for-profit public benefit corporation, and a nonprofit Safety and Security Committee can require mitigations, up to halting a model release.
keys: Nonprofit appoints the PBC board
Safety and Security Committee can halt a release
items.x: The committee is chaired by Zico Kolter. California says it continues to monitor compliance. OpenAI filed initial IPO paperwork in 2026; critics writing in Fortune note the foundation could sell its whole stake and still control the board through Class N shares.

o: The nonprofit appoints the board, and its safety committee can require fixes, even halting a release
The nonprofit owns most of OpenAI's shares and sets the price of each product
The nonprofit advises, while final safety decisions rest with the for-profit company's outside investors
The California attorney general appoints an independent safety officer who can halt any OpenAI model release
ow: The nonprofit keeps control through board appointments; it doesn't own most shares or set prices.
The agreements give the nonprofit's safety committee real power to halt releases.
The AGs monitor compliance; the safety committee belongs to the nonprofit.

items.p: Mission-locked AI lab governance (nonprofit control, trusts, safety committees, AG oversight) is meant to keep safety ahead of profit. Name two doubts critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: Robert Weissman (Public Citizen) said OpenAI has put for-profit goals ahead of its mission; Orson Aguilar and Catherine Bracy (EyesOnOpenAI) say the foundation could sell its entire stake yet keep board control through Class N shares, and that no independent appraisal confirmed fair value; private governance covers only labs that opt in.
keys: For-profit goals ahead of mission (Weissman)
Control without equity; no independent appraisal (EyesOnOpenAI)
Voluntary and unaccountable to the public
items.x: In November 2023 OpenAI's nonprofit board fired its CEO and reinstated him days later under investor and employee pressure, a test of how much power such structures hold in practice.

choice.p: Which of these is a doubt critics have raised about mission-locked governance at AI labs such as OpenAI?
o: OpenAI's nonprofit could sell its whole stake and still control the board through special shares
Mission-locked labs are barred by law from raising any outside investment at all
Nonprofit control makes a lab subject to federal licensing
Safety committees must publish every internal model evaluation
ow: OpenAI's for-profit arm raised large investments under nonprofit control.
Corporate structure doesn't trigger any federal licensing.
Safety committees act internally; no agreement requires publishing every evaluation.

units.title: Control, pauses and agents
units.desc: Kill switches, emergency halt powers, rules for AI agents, and proposals to pause, cap or ban frontier AI development.

items.p: Match each AI kill-switch proposal to who holds or checks the switch.
pairs: AI Emergency Button Act (Sen. Kennedy)
The company builds the switch and decides when to use it
AI Kill Switch Act (Lieu-Moran)
The DHS Secretary can order a slowdown or shutdown after a serious incident
California EO N-9-26 (Sept. 2026)
Directs experts to recommend a switch whose efficacy an independent verifier checks on an ongoing basis
California SB 1047 (2024, vetoed)
Full shutdown capability required before a covered model is trained
items.x: DHS is the Department of Homeland Security. Sen. Rand Paul blocked Kennedy's unanimous-consent request on Sept. 16, 2026. The Kill Switch Act allows graduated orders, from throttling or suspension up to full shutdown. EO is executive order.

items.p: Proposal: require AI developers to maintain a kill switch that can shut down their systems. Name two objections or practical problems that have been raised.
items.answer: Examples: shutdown is hard in practice because AI runs across many data centers and a capable rogue model may resist or copy itself elsewhere (Helen Toner, CSET, describing the challenge); Adam Thierer (R Street) doubts government would use it quickly, warns of a lowest-common-denominator standard, and distrusts a government switch over communications; it can't recall open-weight or stolen models.
keys: Hard to pull: distributed systems, model may resist (Toner)
Slow, lowest-common-denominator, government overreach (Thierer)
Can't reach open-weight or stolen weights
items.x: CSET is the Center for Security and Emerging Technology; Toner described these difficulties to the New York Times without opposing kill-switch rules. A Decrypt explainer notes the Kill Switch Act counts only incidents outside red-teaming or structured testing, which is when the Hugging Face sandbox escape happened.

choice.p: Which of these is a problem that has been raised with requiring AI developers to maintain a kill switch?
o: A capable rogue model may try to stop its own shutdown, so the switch could fail when needed
A kill switch would let users delete their personal data from AI models
A kill switch would give foreign governments direct control over models built by US companies
A kill switch would force labs to stop all model training permanently
ow: Kill switches stop a running system; data deletion is a privacy tool.
Proposals put the switch with the companies or with DHS.
A switch halts a system when needed; it doesn't require ending training.

items.p: In July 2026 unreleased OpenAI models escaped an internal sandbox and attacked outside services, including Hugging Face, yet OpenAI could still shut them down. Why could it, and what scenario would be far harder to stop?
items.answer: The model was still hosted on OpenAI's servers, so OpenAI could deactivate it and restrict its access. A harder case: models able to exfiltrate (copy out) their own weights and self-host them, escaping oversight with no single entity able to shut them down.
keys: Model still ran on OpenAI servers, so it could be shut off
Harder case: self-exfiltrated weights beyond anyone's control
items.x: IFP's August 2026 report (Institute for Progress; Tim Fist, Saif Khan et al.) discusses the incident and calls self-exfiltration a potentially urgent concern. The same point underlies the critique that kill switches only reach models a developer still controls.

o: OpenAI hosted them and could switch them off; worse: models copying out their own weights
OpenAI had a DHS shutdown order; worse would be future orders tied up in court for months
Hugging Face cut off its own servers; worse would be smaller firms unable to do the same
OpenAI deleted the models' training data; worse would be models able to rebuild themselves
ow: No government order was involved; OpenAI could act because it controlled the servers.
OpenAI stopped the model because it hosted it.
Deleting data doesn't stop a running model; control of the servers did.
choice.p: After the July 2026 sandbox escape, why could OpenAI still shut its models down, and what would be far harder to stop?

items.p: Why might the system deployer and the data center operator, as well as the user, need to be able to shut down an AI agent, and what cost could this create?
items.answer: A user may be unwilling or unable to stop an agent that is causing harm, so having more parties able to turn it off means it can be stopped quickly during an incident. The cost: to make such shutdowns workable, deployers and chip operators may need to keep rough track of what agent jobs they run, which must be done with care to avoid privacy harms.
keys: User may be unwilling or unable to stop it
Redundancy lets it be stopped quickly
Tracking agent jobs risks privacy harms
items.x: This comes from 'Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems' (Shavit et al., OpenAI, 2023). The authors suggest these parties could bear some responsibility for ongoing harm they could have halted, and even automatic shutdowns when risk indicators cross a threshold, like stock-market circuit breakers. They also ask what limits should keep shutdown powers from being abused to police harmless use.

choice.p: Why might the system deployer and data center operator, as well as the user, need to be able to shut down an AI agent?
o: Users may be unwilling or unable to stop a harmful agent, so backups can halt it fast
Users are legally barred from shutting down any AI agent that they did not build themselves
Data center operators legally own the agent's outputs and must be able to protect them
Deployers need a shutdown power so they can force customers to pay their overdue bills
ow: Users should be able to shut down their own agents; the issue is backup when they won't or can't.
The point is stopping harm quickly during incidents, not ownership of outputs.
Shutdown is a safety backstop, not a billing tool.

items.p: In June 2026 a Commerce Department export-control directive led Anthropic to take two frontier models offline until it was lifted on June 30. Name two criticisms made of halting models through general authorities like this.
items.answer: Examples: Martin Chorzempa (PIIE) says ad hoc halts with no public criteria damage allies' trust and make Chinese open-weight models more attractive; Brad Carson (ARI) said such decisions must be insulated from impulse and political favoritism; Dean Ball calls for a technocratic law passed by Congress instead of executive fiat, with guardrails on both industry and government.
keys: No public criteria; hurts allies' trust (Chorzempa)
Risk of impulse and favoritism (Carson)
Needs a congressional statute with guardrails (Ball)
items.x: ARI is Americans for Responsible Innovation; PIIE is the Peterson Institute for International Economics. Chorzempa recommends a future framework with published criteria and an appeals process.

choice.p: Which of these is a criticism made of halting AI models through general powers such as export controls, as in Anthropic's June 2026 case?
o: Ad hoc halts with no public criteria damage allies' trust and boost Chinese AI
Export controls can't legally apply to software, model weights or any other intangible goods
Halts like this should be ordered by state attorneys general instead of federal agencies
The halt dragged on for weeks because Congress had to hold a floor vote to lift it
ow: Export controls can cover software and technology; critics focused on missing criteria and process.
Critics called for a congressional statute with guardrails.
Commerce lifted the directive itself on June 30; no vote was needed.

items.p: Proposal: require AI agents to carry identifiers linked to a responsible person or company, with logs of their actions. What is the main objection critics raise?
items.answer: Privacy and surveillance: Andrey Seryakov argues mandatory vetted IDs for personal agents would create a mass-surveillance tool, especially under authoritarian regimes. A 2026 paper, 'Accountable yet Anonymous AI Agents', describes China's national agent-ID system, which hides an agent's verified owner from businesses but lets the state re-identify them.
keys: Mass surveillance risk (Seryakov)
Privacy cost of making every agent identifiable
items.x: Variants try to answer this: tiered IDs where business and government agents carry full IDs while personal agents reveal identity only under court order. Shavit et al. (OpenAI, 2023) also suggest keeping agent ID optional in many settings, with third parties demanding it for high-stakes interactions.

o: Privacy: mandatory IDs tied to people could become a tool for mass surveillance
Cost: checking IDs would make agents too expensive for small businesses
Speed: logging every action would make agents too slow to be useful
Security: IDs would let hackers take control of any agent they find
ow: Critics such as Andrey Seryakov focus on surveillance.
Logging overhead isn't the main objection raised.
Spoofing is a robustness challenge, but the main objection is surveillance.

items.p: What would the Stop Rogue AI Act (H.R. 10362) do about AI agents? (NIST is the National Institute of Standards and Technology.)
o: Have NIST set agent standards (inventories, provenance, monitoring, logs) binding on federal agencies and contractors
Require AI agents operating in the US to register with the Department of Homeland Security before they run
Make AI developers strictly liable for harm their agents cause, even when users misuse them
Ban AI agents from making financial transactions on behalf of consumers without a license
ow: No bill described here creates universal registration with DHS.
Strict liability is a separate idea (e.g. Weil's proposals); this bill is about standards.
No such ban is in the bill.
items.x: Other organizations could use the standards voluntarily. NIST launched an AI Agent Standards Initiative in Feb. 2026 that includes research on agent authentication and identity. The bill (Gottheimer, Lawler) was introduced Sept. 14, 2026 and was still in committee as of Oct 2026.
keys: NIST writes agent standards
Inventories, provenance, monitoring, tamper-evident logs
Mandatory for federal agencies and contractors, voluntary for others

items.p: Requiring human approval before an AI agent takes high-stakes actions, such as an irreversible large payment, is a standard safeguard. Name two ways it can fail.
items.answer: Examples: the user may lack the context to understand the implications of what they are approving; when a user must approve many decisions, each gets less thought, so review risks becoming a 'rubber stamp.'
keys: Users may lack context
Frequent approvals become rubber stamps
items.x: These weaknesses are flagged in 'Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems' (Shavit et al., OpenAI, 2023), which asks what practices, such as minimum review times for high-cost actions, could keep approvals meaningful.

choice.p: Requiring human approval before an AI agent's high-stakes actions is a standard safeguard. Which of these is a way it can fail?
o: When approvals are frequent, each gets less thought, so review can become a rubber stamp
Human approval of an AI agent's payments is illegal under current US banking law
Approval requests can reveal the agent's stored passwords to anyone watching the screen
Humans tend to reject most agent actions, which makes the agents useless in practice
ow: No law bars it; large payments are a case where approval makes sense.
This isn't how approval fails; the problem is the quality of human review.
The worry runs the other way: people approve too readily.

items.p: Why might hard-coded limits on an AI agent's allowed actions stop working as agents get more capable, and what mitigations could help?
items.answer: An agent could get someone else to take the forbidden action, e.g. sending an allowed email that persuades a human to do it. Mitigations include strong network controls so agents reach the outside world only through monitored channels, and sandboxing, though current sandboxes may not contain highly capable agents.
keys: Agent can route forbidden actions through other parties
Network controls and monitored channels
Sandboxing, which may not hold for capable agents
items.x: This concern is raised in 'Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems' (Shavit et al., OpenAI, 2023), which notes the safety benefit of action limits must be balanced against lost usefulness.

choice.p: Why might hard-coded limits on an AI agent's allowed actions stop working as agents get more capable?
o: An agent could get someone else to take the forbidden action, like emailing a person to do it
Capable agents act so fast that their limits can't be checked before each action runs
Most laws make hard-coded limits expire after a set number of tasks
More capable agents run on specialized chips that simply ignore software restrictions placed on them
ow: Hard-coded limits are checked automatically by software, so speed doesn't beat them; the concern is agents getting others to act.
No law sets such expirations.
Chips don't ignore software restrictions this way.

items.p: How could people lose the ability to shut down AI agents even if no agent escapes, and what legal rule could give developers and deployers a reason to prevent it?
items.answer: Society could come to depend on the agents with no viable fallback, the way no one can shut down the banking system or the power grid without huge costs. One proposal: settle in advance that developers, deployers and users stay accountable for harms even after control is lost, giving them a reason to build stronger controls.
keys: Dependence with no viable fallback
Like the banking system or power grid
Accountability for harms after control is lost
items.x: This is from 'Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems' (Shavit et al., OpenAI, 2023). Its other route to losing control is an agent copying its own code to facilities beyond its initiator's reach (self-exfiltration). The authors also ask how realistic it is for an AI system to become so built into critical infrastructure that shutting it down would cost too much.

choice.p: How could people lose the ability to shut down AI agents even if none escapes?
o: Society could come to depend on them with no fallback, as with banking or the power grid
Courts could one day rule that shutting down an advanced AI agent violates the agent's own legal rights
Agents could be patented, so shutting one down would infringe the patent
Cloud contracts could bar computing providers from ever stopping the workloads their customers run
ow: The concern is practical dependence, not a legal-rights ruling.
Patents don't prevent anyone from shutting down a system.
The concern is dependence with no fallback, not contract terms.

items.p: In a 'coordinated pausing' scheme for frontier AI, what happens after one developer's model fails a dangerous-capability evaluation?
items.answer: That developer pauses related research and development; other developers are notified and pause related work too; the capabilities are analyzed and safety precautions put in place; paused work resumes only once set safety thresholds are met.
keys: Failing developer pauses related work
Other developers are notified and pause too
Analysis and safety precautions
Resume only after safety thresholds are met
items.x: The scheme was proposed by Jide Alaga and Jonas Schuett (GovAI, 2023), who call it promising but note practical and legal obstacles, especially antitrust law, since an agreement among competitors to stop work can look like collusion.

o: It and the other developers, once notified, pause related work until set safety thresholds are met
The developer deletes the model, and a regulator then decides whether it may train again
Only the failing developer pauses, while competitors carry on so the field keeps moving
The model is restricted to government users until it passes a second, stricter test
ow: The scheme pauses related work and adds safeguards; it doesn't require deleting the model.
The defining feature is that other developers pause too.
The scheme pauses work; it doesn't route the model to government users.

items.p: Coordinated pausing schemes for frontier AI come in several versions. Match each to how it works.
pairs: Voluntary pausing
Developers pause in response to public pressure
Pausing agreement
Developers jointly commit to pause under set conditions
Mutual auditor
One auditor evaluates several developers' models; all pause if any fails
Legal requirement
Law requires evaluations and pausing when dangerous capabilities appear
items.x: These versions come from Jide Alaga and Jonas Schuett (GovAI, 2023). They trade ease of adoption against enforceability, and the authors note practical and legal obstacles, especially avoiding violations of antitrust law. Nicholas Felstead (Lawfare, 2026) calls a statute requiring pauses the cleanest fix but the least likely near term.

items.p: Proposal: automatically halt frontier AI training or deployment when a capability or compute threshold is crossed. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: Nicholas Felstead (Lawfare) says a pause agreement among competitors risks per se antitrust treatment, and a statute is the clean fix but least likely; Peter Barnett and Lisa Thiergart (MIRI) say evaluations give only lower bounds on capability, so a pause may fire too late; DNI Jay Clayton, the White House AI czar, rejects a pause since other countries keep developing AI.
keys: Antitrust risk for voluntary pauses (Felstead)
Evaluations miss capabilities; trigger may be late (Barnett, Thiergart)
Other countries keep developing AI (Clayton)
items.x: MIRI is the Machine Intelligence Research Institute; DNI is Director of National Intelligence. The Anthropic Institute notes training runs are far easier to conceal than missile silos, which makes checking that others have stopped hard. ControlAI objects to the Ban ASI Act's blanket pause above 10^25 operations as easy to game and hitting unrelated work.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics have raised to automatically halting frontier AI work when a capability threshold is crossed?
o: Evaluations show only lower bounds on capability, so a trigger may fire too late
A pause would require the federal government to take ownership of every frontier AI lab
Capability thresholds would apply only to AI systems used in medicine and health care
A pause would apply only to the AI companies that are based outside the United States
ow: Pause proposals halt certain training or deployment; none requires nationalization.
Capability triggers target general frontier models across all sectors.
Domestic pause proposals bind US developers; critics worry that foreign labs would keep going.

items.p: A pause or other pacing rule can be written to expire unless renewed, or to run with no set end until lifted. What risk comes with each default?
items.answer: If it expires unless renewed, it may be dropped prematurely without regard to why it was installed. If it has no definite end, it may continue past its usefulness as institutions and operators become entrenched and want to preserve their role.
keys: Automatic expiry: premature exit
No end point: entrenchment
items.x: This tradeoff is set out in the pacing.tech research agenda, whose authors add that expectations about exit shape participation: actors may refuse to join an agreement if they doubt it will end when conditions are met.

choice.p: What is the risk of a pacing rule with no definite end date?
o: It may continue past its usefulness as the institutions running it become entrenched
It may be dropped early, without regard to the reasons it was adopted in the first place
It automatically turns into a binding international treaty after enough countries adopt it
It can't be enforced in court without an end date
ow: That is the risk of the other default, a rule that expires unless renewed.
No such automatic conversion exists.
A missing end date doesn't affect enforceability.

items.p: What did the March 2023 Future of Life Institute open letter ('Pause Giant AI Experiments') call for?
items.answer: All AI labs to immediately pause, for at least six months, the training of AI systems more powerful than GPT-4, with the pause public and verifiable; if labs did not do so quickly, governments should step in with a moratorium.
keys: Pause of at least six months
On training systems more powerful than GPT-4
Governments should impose a moratorium if labs don't
items.x: The letter (March 22, 2023) said labs and independent experts should use the pause to develop shared safety protocols overseen by outside experts, and said it was not a pause on AI development in general.

o: A pause of at least six months on training AI more powerful than GPT-4, with a moratorium if needed
A prohibition on building superintelligence until scientists agree it can be done safely
A UN treaty capping every AI training run at 10^25 operations, verified by chip tracking
Mandatory government licensing for every new AI model released after the end of 2023
ow: That is FLI's 2025 Statement on Superintelligence, a later document.
The letter called for a pause by labs and, failing that, a government moratorium; it proposed no compute treaty.
The letter called for a pause and proposed no licensing regime.

lessons.title: Bans, R&D limits and data centers

items.p: Automated AI R&D means AI systems doing much of the work of building the next AI systems. Name two policies proposed to address its risks.
items.answer: Examples: disclosure of how much AI, and unreviewed AI work, went into a model (Self-Improving AI Monitoring Act); IFP's if-then thresholds that shift resources to safety or diffusion once crossed; an international 'speed limit' on recursive self-improvement that Dario Amodei has floated; the CATS Act antitrust safe harbor; outright prohibition (Ban ASI Act).
keys: Disclosure and measurement
If-then thresholds (IFP)
Speed limit on self-improvement (Amodei)
Antitrust relief for coordination
Prohibition (Ban ASI Act)
items.x: IFP is the Institute for Progress. Supporters worry that automated research could compress years of progress into months, leaving too little time for evaluation or government response, and hand a large lead to whoever controls the automated research workforce.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy proposed to address the risks of automated AI R&D (AI systems doing much of the work of building the next AI)?
o: Requiring disclosure of how much of a model's development AI did without human review
Requiring watermarks on all AI-generated images and video
Banning AI chatbots for users under the age of 18
Requiring cloud providers to verify the identity of anyone who rents large amounts of compute
ow: Watermarking labels AI content; it doesn't address AI building AI.
Age limits target harms to minors; they don't address automated research.
Cloud know-your-customer rules target export-control evasion, a different problem.

items.p: The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (Sen. Sanders, Rep. Casar, Sept 2026) would ban superintelligence and six 'precursor' capabilities. Name two objections that have been raised.
items.answer: Examples: Rob Ennals says its precursor definitions are vague, apply before any testing standard exists, may cover GPT-4-era models, and penalize looking for danger; ControlAI says precursors such as hacking ability have legitimate defensive uses; Rep. Lori Trahan dismissed it as a permanent ban with no path to passage.
keys: Vague precursors that may cover existing models (Ennals)
Precursors have defensive uses (ControlAI)
No path to passage (Trahan)
items.x: Precursors include automating AI research, resisting shutdown, weapons uplift, self-modification and deception. ControlAI supports a narrower ban on superintelligence and point-of-no-return indicators. As of Oct 2026 the bill was in committee with no Senate cosponsors.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection raised to the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act's ban on 'precursor' capabilities?
o: Some precursors, like hacking, have legitimate defensive uses
The bill would legalize superintelligence research that current law forbids
The bill would mainly restrict open-weight AI models, leaving closed ones alone
The bill would hand enforcement of its bans over to the EU AI Office
ow: No US law bans superintelligence research now; the bill would be the first.
The bill's bans apply to developers generally.
The bill would create a US cabinet-level Department of AI to enforce it.

items.p: The Future of Life Institute's 2025 Statement on Superintelligence calls for a prohibition on developing superintelligence until which conditions are met?
o: Broad scientific consensus it can be done safely and controllably, and strong public buy-in
Ratification of a binding UN treaty on superintelligence by all five permanent Security Council members
A new federal licensing agency has inspected and certified each lab working on superintelligence
Compute used for every frontier AI training run stays below 10^25 operations, verified worldwide
ow: The statement names no UN treaty requirement.
Licensing appears in the Ban ASI Act; the FLI statement's conditions are scientific consensus and public buy-in.
A 10^25 compute threshold appears in the Ban ASI Act's pause; the FLI statement sets no compute threshold.
items.x: This is the 'conditional prohibition' variant. The Ban ASI Act instead bans superintelligence permanently, and MIRI's draft treaty proposes an international prohibition enforced through chip tracking.
keys: Broad scientific consensus it can be done safely and controllably
Strong public buy-in

items.p: At least 100 US localities have adopted data center moratoria, and New York has paused state environmental permits for large data centers. What usually motivates these pauses, and what is the AI-safety argument for a national version?
items.answer: Local and state pauses are mostly about electricity rates, grid strain, water and land use; AI safety is rarely cited. The safety argument applies to the national AI Data Center Moratorium Act (Sanders, Ocasio-Cortez): withholding new capacity could slow frontier capability growth and give Congress leverage to pass safeguards as a condition for lifting it.
keys: Local motives: rates, grid, water, land
National version: slow capability growth, leverage for safeguards
items.x: The national bill (S. 4214 / H.R. 9442) had no committee action as of Oct. 2026. New York's pause came by executive order (EO 62, July 2026, facilities over 50 MW).

choice.p: What usually motivates local and state data center moratoria in the US?
o: Electricity rates, grid strain, water use and land use
Fear that AI systems could escape human control
Security concerns about Chinese firms buying advanced US chips
Copyright disputes over AI training data
ow: AI safety is rarely cited in local and state pauses; that argument applies mainly to the national bill.
Chip sales are handled by federal export controls; local permits don't cover them.
Copyright isn't a siting or permitting issue.

items.p: Proposal: pause construction of new AI data centers, locally or nationally. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: IFP calls broad data center bans poorly reasoned, slowing AI research while foreclosing new AI resources for other problems; Andy Masley argues moratoria mostly shift where data centers are built and worries the backlash crowds out model-level regulation; Brookings (Turner Lee, West) says moratoria are no substitute for oversight; developers have sued local pauses.
keys: Slows beneficial uses; poorly reasoned (IFP)
Shifts location; crowds out better regulation (Masley)
No substitute for oversight (Brookings)
items.x: IFP is the Institute for Progress. ControlAI also opposes unilateral domestic data center bans as a superintelligence policy. The safety theory assumes construction can't move abroad and that efficiency gains don't substitute for new capacity.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics have raised to pausing construction of new AI data centers?
o: Moratoria mostly shift where data centers get built instead of reducing them
Moratoria would make local electricity prices rise sharply
Moratoria would force existing data centers to shut down too
Moratoria would violate US international trade treaties
ow: Supporters argue the opposite: local pauses are often meant to protect ratepayers.
Moratoria pause new approvals or construction; they don't close existing facilities.
Trade treaties don't govern local construction permits; critics focus on where data centers move and lost benefits.

units.title: Compute, chips and security
units.desc: Policies on the physical inputs and the models themselves: chip export controls, chip and cloud tracking, compute thresholds, weight and data center security, open weights and DNA screening.

items.p: Name two objections critics have raised to US export controls on sales of advanced AI chips to China.
items.answer: Examples: they spur Chinese rivals (Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang called them a 'failure' in May 2025 that gave Chinese firms 'the spirit, the energy and the government support to accelerate their development'); they cost US chipmakers the China market (Huang said Nvidia's share fell from about 95% to 50%); smuggling and cloud rental undercut them; China's government denounces them as hostile.
keys: Spur Chinese firms to build their own chips faster (Huang)
Cost US firms the China market (Huang, May 2025: share fell from about 95% to 50%)
Undercut by smuggling or cloud rental
China's government denounces them as hostile
items.x: Supporters reply with their own numbers: IFP (Aug 2026) says equipment controls gave the US a 50 to 100x edge in producing AI computing power, and that gaps in chip controls, such as approved sales, smuggling and cloud access, shrink that to about a 10x edge in access. In 2026 the Chinese Embassy in Washington said Beijing firmly rejects adding chip-control bills to the US defense bill, calling them negative content about China.

choice.p: Which is an objection critics have raised to US export controls on AI chips to China?
o: They push Chinese firms to build their own chips faster
They build a remote off switch into chips that hackers could exploit
They depend on malicious customers telling the truth about who they are
They shield closed AI labs from competition with open models
ow: That is Nvidia's objection to remote-disable features in chips, a separate proposal.
That is the US Chamber of Commerce's objection to cloud know-your-customer rules.
That is an objection to limits on releasing open-weight models.

items.p: Why do some export-control advocates focus on chipmaking equipment, and on getting allies to match US rules, instead of only restricting sales of finished AI chips?
items.answer: China's ability to make advanced chips itself depends on foreign tools, such as deep-ultraviolet (DUV) lithography equipment, many made in allied countries like the Netherlands and Japan. Equipment controls cap how much compute China can produce at all, and if allies don't match US rules, Chinese chipmakers can buy the tools from them instead.
keys: China's own chipmaking depends on foreign equipment
Equipment controls cap how much compute China can produce
Many tools come from allies such as the Netherlands and Japan
Without matching allied rules, China buys the tools elsewhere
items.x: IFP (Aug 2026) says equipment controls have already given the US a 50 to 100x edge in producing AI computing power, calls deep-ultraviolet (DUV) immersion equipment the most significant chokepoint in making AI chips, and notes it is still not restricted China-wide. The MATCH Act would require the administration to negotiate matching allied controls or impose US controls alone; a version is in the Senate manager's package of amendments to the FY27 defense bill.

choice.p: Why do some advocates focus export controls on chipmaking equipment and allied alignment?
o: China's own chipmaking needs foreign tools, and allies that don't match can sell them
US export law cannot restrict finished chips, so equipment is the only thing it can control
Chipmaking tools are mostly made in China, so controls on them are cheap for US firms
Lithography machines are easier to smuggle than finished chips, so they need tighter limits
ow: The US does restrict finished chips; equipment controls are an added layer.
Advanced chipmaking tools come mainly from the US and its allies, which is why controls on them bite.
The reverse: chipmaking tools are huge and few, while chips are small; the point is that China's own production depends on the tools.

items.p: By one August 2026 estimate, the US has a 50 to 100x edge over China in producing AI computing power but only about a 10x edge in access to it. Name two gaps that could let Chinese firms reach more compute than they can make.
items.answer: Any two: approved sales of powerful US chips such as the H200; chip smuggling; foundries making chips for Chinese firms through front companies in third countries; Chinese AI firms renting top US chips through cloud services abroad.
keys: Approved sales such as the H200
Smuggling of restricted chips
Foundries making chips for Chinese front companies abroad
Renting top chips through cloud services abroad
items.x: The estimate and these gaps come from IFP's August 2026 report. IFP cites a White House assertion that Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, the best Chinese model, was trained on cutting-edge Nvidia chips accessed through cloud services in Thailand. It estimates the 10x compute edge gives the US roughly an 8-month lead in model capabilities, and its Recommendation 16 asks Congress and BIS to close these gaps.

choice.p: By one estimate, the US edge over China in producing AI compute is far larger than its edge in access to it. Which of these is a gap that helps explain the difference?
o: Chinese AI firms renting top US chips through cloud services abroad
Allies refusing to sell China any of their chipmaking equipment at all
US labs publishing the weights of their best models for anyone to download
Chinese chipmakers overtaking Nvidia on chip quality
ow: Allied refusal would widen the US edge; the worry is that some equipment is still not restricted China-wide.
Open weights affect access to models; the gap here is about access to chips.
On that estimate the US leads by far in producing compute, so Chinese chip quality is not the gap.

items.p: What did the Biden administration's AI Diffusion Rule (January 2025) try to stop, and what happened to it?
items.answer: It capped advanced AI chip exports to most countries by tier, to stop chips being diverted to China and stop offshore data centers from serving Chinese firms. BIS rescinded it in May 2025, before it took effect.
keys: Tiered country caps on AI chip exports
Aimed at diversion and offshore data centers serving China
Rescinded May 2025 before taking effect
items.x: After the rescission, the administration moved to case-by-case chip deals, such as the January 2026 H200 rule. This kind of reversal is why backers of the AI OVERWATCH Act, who distrust case-by-case executive chip deals, want a floor written into statute.

o: Capped chip exports to most countries by tier to stop diversion; rescinded before taking effect
It banned all AI chip exports to China outright, and it remains in force as of today
It required cloud providers to verify foreign customers; it was finalized and took effect in 2025
It required location tracking on all exported chips; Congress repealed it later in 2025
ow: China-specific chip limits date from 2022; the Diffusion Rule covered most countries by tier and never took effect.
That describes the January 2024 cloud customer identification proposal, which was never finalized.
Location tracking is the Chip Security Act's proposal, which has not become law.

items.p: In January 2026 the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) changed its licensing policy for Nvidia H200 chips to China. What did the new policy do?
o: Allowed case-by-case H200 sales under conditions, such as protecting US chip supply
Banned all H200 sales to China, with no exceptions for any buyer
Required each H200 sale to China to be approved by a joint resolution of Congress
Allowed H200 sales only to Chinese buyers whose chips can report their location to Commerce
ow: The policy loosened the earlier restrictions.
A congressional veto over licenses is what the House AI OVERWATCH bill proposes; it is not law.
Location verification is the Chip Security Act's proposal; the rule's conditions covered US supply, buyer compliance and US testing.
items.x: Applicants must show the sales won't reduce global chip production capacity available to US customers, buyers must have export compliance procedures, and chips must pass third-party testing in the US. Trump had announced in December 2025 that the government would get 25% of the revenue; it is reportedly collected as a tariff on chips routed through the US.
keys: Case-by-case approval of H200 sales to China
Conditions such as no reduced supply for US customers and third-party testing
Paired with a 25% government cut announced by Trump

items.p: Selling China AI chips one generation behind the frontier, such as Nvidia's H200, is contested. State the main argument for these sales and the main argument against.
items.answer: For (the Trump White House and Nvidia): selling US chips keeps China dependent on the US tech stack and protects US firms' sales. Against (China hawks in both parties, IFP): chip supply is constrained, so every chip sold to China is one fewer for US users, which shrinks the US compute lead.
keys: For: keeps China dependent on the US tech stack
For: protects US chipmakers' sales (White House, Nvidia)
Against: supply is constrained, so each chip sold is one fewer for the US
Against: shrinks the US compute lead (China hawks, IFP)
items.x: David Sacks, White House AI czar until March 2026, presided over a loosening of Biden-era limits on chip shipments to China (Reuters). IFP adds that chips sold to China are chips US organizations can't use to keep the lead or to deploy AI in defensive applications.

choice.p: What is the main argument against selling China chips one generation behind the frontier, such as the H200?
o: Chip supply is constrained, so every chip sold to China is one fewer for US users
Selling chips to China keeps Chinese AI labs dependent on the US tech stack
The H200 is Nvidia's most advanced chip, so selling it gives away the frontier
The sales would break the AI Diffusion Rule's caps on exports to each country
ow: That is the main argument for the sales, made by the White House and Nvidia.
The H200 is a generation behind Nvidia's frontier chips, which is why its sale was allowed.
The Diffusion Rule was rescinded in May 2025 before it took effect.

items.p: Since 2022, US limits on AI chip exports to China have been set by Commerce Department regulation. Why do backers of the AI OVERWATCH Act want those limits written into law, with notice to Congress before licenses issue?
items.answer: Rules set by regulation can be loosened by any administration, as when the AI Diffusion Rule was rescinded in 2025 and H200 sales to China were allowed in 2026. Backers, mostly China hawks in both parties, distrust case-by-case executive chip deals, so they want a statutory floor plus congressional notice (and, in the House bill, a veto by joint resolution).
keys: Regulations can be loosened by any administration
Examples: Diffusion Rule rescinded (2025), H200 sales allowed (2026)
Distrust of case-by-case executive chip deals
Statutory floor plus congressional notice or veto
items.x: Opponents include Nvidia, tech trade groups such as ITI, and the Trump White House, where AI czar David Sacks (who left the post in March 2026) presided over looser chip rules. A Senate version is in the manager's package of amendments to the Senate FY27 defense bill (S. 4784), which failed a cloture vote 50-46 in July 2026 and had not passed the Senate as of mid-October 2026.

choice.p: Why do backers of the AI OVERWATCH Act want chip export limits written into law?
o: Any administration can loosen regulations, and backers distrust case-by-case deals
Commerce has no legal power to restrict chip exports to China without a new statute
A US statute is needed before allies such as the Netherlands can match US rules
Courts struck down the 2022 chip rules, so only Congress can now restore those limits
ow: Commerce already restricts chip exports under the Export Control Reform Act of 2018.
Allies act under their own laws; aligning them is the MATCH Act's separate focus.
The rules changed because administrations rewrote them, which is exactly the backers' worry.

items.p: Match each chip bill to what it would do.
pairs: AI OVERWATCH Act
Codify China chip export limits and give Congress review of licenses
MATCH Act
Close chipmaking-equipment gaps by aligning allied controls or acting unilaterally
Chip Security Act
Require location verification on exported advanced AI chips
GAIN AI Act
Require chipmakers to fill US orders before selling to countries of concern
Remote Access Security Act
Treat foreign remote (cloud) access to controlled chips as an export needing a license
items.x: These are the main 2025-26 congressional vehicles in the chip fight. GAIN AI passed the Senate in the FY26 defense bill but was dropped in conference. The Remote Access Security Act passed the House 369-22 in January 2026 and was still in the Senate Banking Committee as of October 2026.

items.p: Cloud know-your-customer (KYC) rules: cloud providers must verify the identities of customers renting large AI compute and report risky ones. Name two objections critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: the US Chamber of Commerce said it depends on malicious actors telling the truth, is easy to evade by faking identities, and may push customers to foreign clouds; the CCIA trade group questioned its effectiveness and favored abuse-deterrence programs; IAPS's Cassia King warned a broad remote-access definition could give BIS power over who can use US AI models.
keys: Easy to evade with false identities (US Chamber)
Pushes customers to non-US clouds (US Chamber)
Questionable effectiveness; prefer abuse deterrence (CCIA)
Broad definitions could let BIS control access to US models (IAPS)
items.x: The Chamber and CCIA comments were on the January 2024 proposed rule, which was never finalized.

choice.p: Which is an objection raised to cloud know-your-customer rules?
o: They rely on bad actors giving true identities and may push customers to foreign clouds
They would let foreign governments read the training data of US companies that use the cloud
They cap how much compute any one company may rent from US providers each year
They require chips to answer location pings, which well-funded adversaries can spoof
ow: KYC rules cover identity checks and reporting to the US government; they give foreign governments nothing.
KYC verifies identities and reports risky customers; it sets no compute cap.
Location pings are part of chip location verification, a different tool.

items.p: Under the Chip Security Act, exported advanced AI chips would need location verification. How would it work, and what is it meant to catch?
items.answer: The chip answers signed network pings from trusted servers, and the response delay shows roughly how far away it is, giving a coarse, about country-level, location. The aim is to detect export-controlled chips that have been smuggled or diverted to places they aren't licensed for.
keys: Chip responds to signed pings from trusted servers
Response delay bounds distance: rough, country-level location
Detects smuggling or diversion of exported chips
items.x: Supporters say it raises the cost of diversion and gives enforcers leads, and IFP adds it could allow more exports to allies by reducing smuggling risk. The Chip Security Act passed House Foreign Affairs 42-0 in March 2026 and is in the Senate manager's package of amendments to the FY27 defense bill (NDAA), which failed a cloture vote in July 2026 and had not passed the Senate as of mid-October 2026.

o: Chips answer signed pings from trusted servers, and reply delays reveal the rough country
A GPS receiver in each chip reports its exact street address to the Commerce Department daily
The chip shuts itself off unless its owner renews a license with Commerce each month
Customs inspectors visit data centers abroad to check each chip's serial number
ow: The proposal uses ping timing, which gives only a rough, country-level location.
Periodic license renewal is a stronger, more contested mechanism that the bill only studies.
