Physical checks are IAPS's separate export-auditor proposal.
choice.p: How would location verification of exported AI chips work under the Chip Security Act?

items.p: Hardware-enabled mechanisms are security features built into AI chips, from location checks up to remote disable. Name two objections critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: the Semiconductor Industry Association warned that rushing costly, unproven features could undermine global trust in US chips; Nvidia said chips should never have kill switches or backdoors, calling them 'a gift to hackers and hostile actors'; CSET found location checks are coarse, cannot see diversion to another user at the same site, and may be spoofed.
keys: SIA: costly, unproven; could hurt trust in US chips
Nvidia: no kill switches or backdoors; a gift to hackers
CSET: coarse location only, misses same-site diversion, spoofable
items.x: CSET (Sept 2026) estimated location checks could likely reach country-level accuracy for most tracked chips, and no better than about 20 miles even in the best case. China has its own suspicions: in July 2025 its internet regulator summoned Nvidia over possible tracking or remote shutdown features in chips sold there.

choice.p: Which is an objection critics have raised to security features built into AI chips?
o: Remote-disable features would be a gift to hackers and hostile states
They depend on cloud customers telling the truth about who they are
They push Chinese firms to build their own chips faster
They cannot recall a model once its weights are published
ow: That is an objection to cloud know-your-customer rules.
That is an objection to chip export controls in general, raised by Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
That is an objection to model kill switches, which can't reach open-weight copies.

items.p: Match each version of on-chip governance to its description.
pairs: Location verification
Ping-based coarse location checks that catch diversion after it happens
Workload verification
Chips attest to how they were used, e.g. total compute in a training run
Remote disable or licensing
Chips need license renewal or can be shut off if diverted
Human export auditors
Inspectors physically check exported chips are where licenses say
items.x: Location checks are the cheapest and most mature version but catch diversion only after it happens; remote disable is the strongest and most opposed, since it creates an off switch. Supporters see workload verification as the technical base for checking international compute limits. IAPS proposed export auditors in March 2026 as a near-term complement.

items.p: Security standards for AI model weights are graded by the strongest attacker they can stop. Why is defending frontier weights against the most capable nation-state operations so hard?
o: Top attackers pair elite hacking with spies, recruited insiders and physical break-ins
Nation-states can legally demand a lab's weights under international law
Model weights are too large to encrypt with today's technology
Export rules bar AI labs from hiring any security staff who hold government clearances
ow: No international law gives states such a right.
Weights can be encrypted; the hard part is that top attackers can also get in through people and physical access.
No such rule exists.
items.x: RAND's 2024 report on model weight security defines five security levels, SL1 to SL5, by the attackers they can resist. SL5 targets the handful of top-priority operations by the most capable nation-states, which RAND pictures as up to 1,000 experts in hacking, human intelligence and physical operations working for years on budgets up to $1 billion. RAND said off-the-shelf tools and standard industry practice can't stop such attackers, that SL5 was not yet achievable, and that it would likely need help from the national security community. A private SL5 Standard (v0.1, June 2026) also says top-level security needs measures far from current practice, close to government capabilities.
keys: Attackers combine elite hacking with human spying, insiders and physical operations
Years of effort and huge budgets beat off-the-shelf security
Likely needs help from the national security community

items.p: A 'two-person rule' for model weights means no single person can access a frontier model's weights: a second authorized person must also approve, often with hardware keys. Name two threats it guards against.
items.answer: Examples: a lone insider copying the weights out, including one recruited or pressured by a foreign state; a single insider or executive secretly modifying the model, for example to plant hidden instructions; an outside attacker who has stolen one employee's credentials, since one account is no longer enough.
keys: Lone insider stealing or copying out the weights
Insider recruited or pressured by a foreign state
Insider or executive secretly tampering with the model
Attacker using one stolen account
items.x: Requiring two people means theft or tampering needs collusion, which is harder to arrange and easier to detect. The pacing.tech appendix lists 'two-person rule and hardware keys for weight access' under weight security, citing RAND's 2024 report on securing model weights, beside capability-tiered security levels and insider-threat programs. Forethought researchers also call for security that even a lab's executives cannot bypass.

choice.p: What is the main purpose of a 'two-person rule' for access to model weights?
o: No one insider can copy or alter the weights alone, so misuse needs collusion
Two separate labs must approve before any frontier model is released to the public
The weights are stored in two data centers so one outage can't destroy them
Two government evaluators must test a model before its weights can be published
ow: That describes coordination between labs, a different and antitrust-sensitive idea.
That is backup for reliability; the rule is about who can access the weights.
That describes pre-release government testing, a separate tool.

items.p: As of October 2026, what does California's SB 53 require on model weight security, and does any US law set a minimum security level?
items.answer: SB 53 requires large frontier developers to describe, in their published safety frameworks, how they secure unreleased model weights. No US law sets a minimum security level.
keys: SB 53: disclose how unreleased weights are secured
Disclosure only, with no required level
No US law sets a minimum security level
items.x: Stronger options include capability-tiered mandatory levels (proposed by RAND), theft and tampering reporting through defense contracts (in the stalled Senate FY27 defense bill), and direct government help. The SL5 Standard's authors warn that top-level security needs measures far from current practice, close to government capabilities, which may be infeasible on a short timeline without a direct government role.

o: SB 53 requires disclosing how unreleased weights are secured; no law sets a minimum
SB 53 requires RAND security level SL3 at every frontier lab operating in California
No state law mentions weight security at all; only a federal executive order addresses it
SB 53 requires SL5 security for models trained above 10^26 operations
ow: SB 53 sets no security level; it requires developers to describe their practices.
SB 53 does address weight security, through framework disclosure.
No law requires SL5; its authors say it is far beyond current practice.

items.p: One proposal would let AI data centers connect to the power grid faster if they meet security controls for their grid-facing systems. What risk is this meant to address, and why use grid hookups as the lever?
items.answer: A hacked data center's load-management system could make thousands of GPUs drop or spike gigawatts of demand in a fraction of a second, threatening grid reliability. Data centers are stuck in long interconnection queues, so FERC can offer a fast lane for curtailable AI loads conditional on binding interim security controls for grid-facing systems, and direct NERC to write permanent standards.
keys: Hacked AI loads could destabilize the grid
Data centers want faster interconnection, which FERC regulates
Fast lane conditional on security controls for grid-facing systems
NERC writes binding standards
items.x: This is IFP's 'speed-for-security bargain' (June 2026). Its author, Ben Schifman, notes binding NERC standards are unlikely to take effect before 2028, while AI-enabled cyberattacks on the grid are a near-term threat, so the fast lane would rely on interim controls. It covers grid-facing systems only, not theft of model weights. As of October 2026 no binding security standard applies to private US AI data centers.

choice.p: What risk is a 'speed-for-security' deal on AI data centers' grid hookups mainly meant to address?
o: A hacked data center could spike or drop huge power loads and destabilize the grid
Foreign spies could steal model weights from poorly guarded data center server rooms
Data center cooling could drain the water supplies of nearby towns during droughts
Chinese firms could rent the data center's chips remotely through cloud services
ow: Weight theft is a real concern, but this proposal covers only the facility's grid-facing systems.
Water and energy use are local-impact issues; this proposal is about cyber and physical security of grid-facing systems.
Foreign cloud access is the target of know-your-customer rules and remote-access export controls.

items.p: Match each open-weight policy option to its description.
pairs: Capability-threshold restriction
No open release above a defined dangerous-capability line
Same testing for open and closed
Mandatory safety tests for capable models however released
Staged release
API, then research access, then weights, as evidence builds
Country-of-origin limits
Restrict US use of models from Chinese labs
Open-source protection
Shield open models from frontier obligations
items.x: Sources: Seger et al. (2023) for thresholds; Anthropic (July 2026) for equal testing; Irene Solaiman for the release gradient; administration discussion after the Chinese open model Kimi K3 for country limits; the 2025 AI Action Plan and a July 2026 industry letter for protection. As of October 2026 no US or EU law restricts open-weight release.

items.p: Opponents of new limits on releasing open-weight AI models (models whose trained parameters are published) make arguments about both misuse and power concentration. Name two of their arguments.
items.answer: Examples: evidence that open models add much risk beyond closed models and internet search is thin (NTIA's 2024 report, which the Center for Democracy & Technology backed); open models spread power away from a few labs; they help security and safety research; limits would shield closed labs from competition.
keys: Thin evidence of extra risk over closed models (NTIA 2024)
Spread power away from a few labs
Help security and safety research
Limits would shield closed labs from competition
items.x: About 25 companies, including Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI and Google, signed a July 2026 letter urging Washington to avoid premature restrictions. On the other side, FAR.AI research shows fine-tuning can efficiently strip safeguards from released models, and a release can't be recalled. Opponents also argue that limits aimed at misuse would concentrate capability in fewer hands.

choice.p: Which is an argument opponents make against new limits on open-weight AI releases?
o: Evidence of extra risk beyond closed models is thin
Fine-tuning can cheaply strip the safeguards from released models
A released model can never be recalled once its weights are out
Open models are always too weak to pose any serious danger
ow: That is an argument for limits, drawn from FAR.AI's research.
That is an argument for limits: once weights are out, safeguards can't be added back.
Opponents say the extra risk is unproven; they don't claim open models can never be dangerous.

items.p: Mandatory DNA synthesis screening checks orders against lists of dangerous sequences. Name two problems or gaps researchers and officials have raised.
items.answer: Examples: AI protein-design tools made variants that evaded several screening systems until patched, so sequence matching may fall behind (Wittmann, Horvitz et al., Science, Oct 2025); federal action has stalled, with no revised framework 400+ days after one was ordered (Sen. Ossoff, June 2026); benchtop synthesizers and foreign providers may escape screening.
keys: AI-designed variants evaded sequence screens (Science 2025)
Federal revision stalled (Ossoff letter, June 2026)
Benchtop synthesizers or foreign providers may escape screening
items.x: These critiques push for stronger screening: 'AI-resilient' screening that detects functional variants instead of relying on sequence similarity alone, coverage of benchtop machines, and adoption by other countries. OSTP had been ordered in May 2025 to revise the screening framework within 90 days.

choice.p: Which is a problem researchers have raised with DNA synthesis screening?
o: AI-designed protein variants evaded several screening systems until they were patched
Screening requires providers to publish their customers' names online
Screening has been required of US providers since 2020, yet orders still slip through
Screening bans most legitimate research on pathogens
ow: Screening involves vetting customers, but no proposal requires publishing their names.
Screening is still voluntary for most providers; only federally funded buyers face a requirement.
Screening checks orders and customers; it does not ban research.

units.title: Power, government and international
units.desc: Who controls advanced AI: military AI, coup-proofing government AI, market structure, public compute, federal preemption, and international agreements.

items.p: What is the legal force of Sec. 1638 of the FY2025 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) on AI and nuclear weapons?
o: A non-binding policy statement that nuclear use needs positive human action
A binding ban on using AI in any US weapons system, nuclear or conventional
An executive order requiring a human decision before any US nuclear launch
A US-China treaty commitment to keep humans in control of nuclear launch
ow: It covers nuclear use only and is not binding; binding versions appear in the FY27 Senate text.
It is a provision in a statute passed by Congress, not an executive order.
No US-China treaty on AI and nuclear launch exists.
items.x: The FY2027 Senate defense bill (S. 4784) would make a nuclear human-control rule binding and add a domestic surveillance limit. It failed a cloture vote 50-46 in July 2026 and had not passed the Senate as of mid-October 2026; the House-passed version lacks these limits.
keys: Non-binding sense of Congress
Statement of policy that nuclear use needs positive human action

items.p: Match each military AI proposal to its description.
pairs: Nuclear human-control rule
Bars AI from the decision to launch or detonate a nuclear weapon
Slotkin AI Guardrails Act
Bars DoD from using AI to monitor or target people in the US without legal basis
Gillibrand autonomous weapons ban
General ban with exceptions for supervised, defensive or non-lethal systems
Process controls
Senior sign-off, testing, logging and audit for high-consequence uses
Distributed control of military AI
No single person can command enough autonomous force to stage a coup
items.x: Process controls appear in Sen. Gillibrand's Secure and Accountable Military AI Act of 2026 (S. 4656), which also contains the autonomous weapons ban; they create records Congress can inspect. S. 4656 had no cosponsors as of October 2026. Forethought's distributed-control idea is not yet in bill text.

items.p: Sen. Slotkin's AI Guardrails Act would bar the Pentagon from using autonomous weapons to kill 'without appropriate levels of human judgment and supervision.' Name two objections critics have raised to military AI limits like this.
items.answer: Examples: Roberto González called the undefined word 'appropriate' a loophole likely to make the law meaningless; John Ramming Chappell (Center for Civilians in Conflict) says Congress should have to vote to allow a system instead of leaving it to presidential waivers; the AI Now Institute says military AI lacks basic safety assurance and backs a moratorium on military uses until it exists.
keys: 'Appropriate' is undefined, a loophole (González)
Waivers give the executive free rein; Congress should vote (Chappell)
Military AI lacks safety assurance; AI Now backs a moratorium
items.x: González and Chappell were quoted in Responsible Statecraft. Slotkin's bill lets the defense secretary waive the limit in 'extraordinary circumstances', while Gillibrand's bill requires a joint resolution of Congress for fully autonomous systems. From the other direction, Pentagon technology chief Emil Michael pushed AI vendors to accept 'all lawful use' of their models and criticized Anthropic's refusal to allow fully autonomous weapons use.

choice.p: Which objection have critics raised to the 'appropriate levels of human judgment' standard in Sen. Slotkin's AI Guardrails Act?
o: 'Appropriate' is undefined, a loophole that could make the law meaningless
It requires a joint resolution of Congress before any AI system is used
It would hand control of military AI decisions to private AI companies
It covers only nuclear weapons, leaving drones unregulated
ow: Gillibrand's bill has a joint-resolution requirement for fully autonomous systems, an approach Chappell says is preferable to waivers.
The bill limits DoD's own use; vendor terms were a separate Pentagon-Anthropic dispute.
The standard covers autonomous weapons used to kill; nuclear launch is a separate rule.

lessons.title: Coup-proofing and government use of AI

items.p: What is 'law-following AI', and how could it guard against power grabs?
items.answer: AI agents built to refuse clearly illegal actions, even when government officials order them. Coups and executive power grabs have needed many people to cooperate, some of whom refuse. If AI replaces soldiers and civil servants, law-following AI keeps that refusal capacity inside the system.
keys: AI agents refuse clearly unlawful orders, including from officials
Power grabs historically needed many cooperating people
Preserves the check that human refusal provided
items.x: Cullen O'Keefe and colleagues at the Institute for Law & AI (LawAI) propose requiring law-following AI, for example through procurement terms, for AI agents in high-stakes government roles. As of Oct 2026 no bill requires it. O'Keefe himself notes that laws have gaps a capable AI could exploit while staying legal, which is why he also proposes congressional 'advice and consent' for major government AI deployments.

choice.p: How could law-following AI, built to refuse clearly illegal orders even from officials, guard against power grabs?
o: Power grabs need many people's help; AI that refuses illegal orders preserves that check
It lets federal courts switch off any government AI system found to have broken a law
It requires Congress to approve each sensitive government AI deployment in advance by statute
It audits government models for hidden loyalties that insiders inserted during training
ow: Law-following AI works through the model's own refusals; it gives courts no off switch.
Advance congressional approval is O'Keefe's separate 'advice and consent' proposal.
Secret-loyalty audits are Forethought's related but separate proposal.

items.p: Law-following AI: government AI agents must refuse clearly unlawful orders. What objections have been raised? Name two.
items.answer: Examples: Cullen O'Keefe (LawAI) notes laws have gaps that clever AIs will find, and law-following AI cannot stop legal but harmful loophole use; Katalina Hernandez Delgado argues that following the law's letter invites gaming, while following its spirit collapses back into value alignment; DoD's demand that vendors accept 'all lawful use' cuts against model-level refusals.
keys: Laws have gaps; LFAI can't stop legal loophole use (O'Keefe)
Letter of the law invites gaming; its spirit needs value judgments (Hernandez Delgado)
DoD wants 'all lawful use' without vendor limits
items.x: O'Keefe's own answer to the gaps problem (Lawfare, May 2026) is congressional 'advice and consent': AI in protected uses, which he says might include criminal investigations, domestic intelligence, domestic military deployment and prosecutions, would be barred unless Congress authorizes it by statute.

choice.p: Which is an objection raised to law-following AI requirements for government AI agents?
o: Laws have gaps, so an AI can help abuse power while staying legal
It forces every AI user to reveal their identity, at a cost to privacy
It builds a remote off switch into AI chips that hackers could exploit
It amounts to a large subsidy for the biggest cloud companies
ow: That is an objection to AI agent identification schemes.
That is an objection to remote-disable features in chips.
That is an objection to public compute built on commercial clouds.

items.p: What risk are 'secret-loyalty audits' and distributed control of powerful AI meant to address?
items.answer: That a lab insider or a single official quietly gains control over powerful AI, for example by training hidden instructions into a model so it serves one person or faction, and then uses it to seize power.
keys: A small group or one person using AI to seize power (an AI-enabled coup)
For example, an insider training hidden loyalties into a model
items.x: Forethought researchers Tom Davidson, Lukas Finnveden and Rose Hadshar propose both in 'AI-Enabled Coups' (April 2025). Distributed control means, for example, that no single person can control enough military AI systems to stage a coup. The report also says any plan for a single centralized AI project should be coup-proofed.

choice.p: What risk are 'secret-loyalty audits' and distributed control of powerful AI meant to address?
o: An insider or single official secretly controlling powerful AI to seize power
Rival countries stealing frontier model weights through large-scale cyberattacks
AI models deceiving their own developers by hiding capabilities during safety testing
Chinese firms renting export-controlled US chips through cloud data centers abroad
ow: Weight theft by states is the target of security standards; these tools target insiders and small groups.
Deception during testing is a loss-of-control concern with its own detection tools.
Cloud rental is an export-control gap, handled by know-your-customer rules.

items.p: Limits on government use of AI against the public include proposed bans on immigration agencies using facial recognition. Name one objection or obstacle that has been raised.
items.answer: Examples: a DHS spokesperson said banning ICE and CBP facial recognition would limit tracking criminals and make communities less safe; legal scholar Ashley Deeks argues national security AI is a 'double black box' (government secrecy plus model opacity), so limits are hard to enforce without new inspection tools; vague exceptions leave the executive to define the limit.
keys: DHS: bans weaken law enforcement and public safety
Deeks: secrecy plus model opacity block oversight
Vague exceptions leave the executive to define the limit
items.x: Drafting matters: the Senate defense bill's committee text bars only DoD surveillance 'not otherwise permissible' under the Constitution, a looser standard than the individualized legal basis in Sen. Slotkin's standalone bill. As of October 2026 the facial recognition bans have no Republican sponsors.

choice.p: Which is an objection or obstacle raised to limits on government use of AI against the public?
o: Government secrecy plus model opacity make the limits hard to enforce
The limits would force agencies to publish the source code of their AI systems
The limits would apply to private companies instead of government
Facial recognition is already banned at every federal agency, so the bills are moot
ow: The proposals restrict uses and add oversight; none requires publishing source code.
These limits target government agencies specifically.
No federal ban exists; the bills to ban it for ICE and CBP have not left committee.

items.p: Antitrust and market-structure remedies aim to stop a few firms controlling the AI stack. Match each remedy to its description.
pairs: Partnership and merger review
Scrutinize lab-cloud investments and exclusive deals as mergers
Structural separation
Bar firms that own chips or cloud from also owning leading models
Multi-vendor procurement
Require government buyers, such as DoD, to use several AI vendors
Supervised pacing body
Government-supervised standards body to pace the frontier, instead of an antitrust exemption
items.x: The FTC studied cloud-lab partnerships (Microsoft-OpenAI, Amazon-Anthropic, Google-Anthropic) under its 6(b) authority but took no enforcement action. Structural separation comes from Narechania and Sitaraman (2024); the supervised body from Open Markets (Oct 2026). Multi-vendor language is in the Senate FY27 defense bill (S. 4784), which had not passed the Senate as of mid-October 2026.

items.p: Antitrust remedies for frontier AI would use merger review and structural separation against concentration. Name one objection or complication that has been raised.
items.answer: Examples: FTC Commissioner Melissa Holyoak (June 2025) said enforcers should not set AI market structure in advance, since imposing views on how many competitors there should be would dampen innovation and help foreign firms; Mark MacCarthy (Brookings) argues a growing problem is labs competing with customers who depend on their models, which antitrust law is unlikely to address.
keys: Holyoak (FTC): enforcers shouldn't set market structure in advance; it dampens innovation
MacCarthy: labs competing with dependent customers, which antitrust handles poorly
items.x: Holyoak spoke in a personal capacity in a June 2025 speech, in which she also said competition among foundation-model developers was intense for now but the market would likely consolidate. The FTC's study of cloud-lab partnerships produced a report but no enforcement, and the current FTC leadership has signaled less appetite for action.

choice.p: Which is an objection raised to antitrust remedies against concentration in frontier AI?
o: Setting AI market structure in advance would dampen innovation
Merger review would force frontier labs to publish their model weights openly
Existing antitrust law already bars AI labs from owning their own cloud servers
The EU AI Act already requires chip, cloud and model firms to be separate companies
ow: Merger review examines deals and ownership; it has nothing to do with publishing weights.
No US law bars labs from owning cloud infrastructure; separation is only a proposal.
The EU AI Act regulates model risks; it does not split up the AI stack.

items.p: What is the National AI Research Resource (NAIRR), and what would the CREATE AI Act do?
items.answer: NAIRR gives academic and nonprofit researchers subsidized compute and data, run as a National Science Foundation pilot. The CREATE AI Act would make it permanent; as of Oct 2026 the Senate version (S. 4441, April 2026) sits in committee.
keys: Subsidized compute and data for researchers
Runs as an NSF pilot
CREATE AI Act would make it permanent
items.x: Supporters say public compute lets academics and public-interest groups study frontier systems and check industry claims. California's SB 53 also created CalCompute, a planned public cloud cluster, contingent on funding. Current public resources are tiny next to private frontier clusters.

o: An NSF pilot offering researchers subsidized compute; CREATE AI makes it permanent
A Commerce program that tests frontier models for risks; CREATE AI would fund it
A federal registry of AI chips; CREATE AI would require chipmakers to report every sale
A public cloud cluster run by California; CREATE AI would expand it nationwide
ow: Government model testing is the job of CAISI at NIST.
A chip registry is an export-control proposal from IFP and others.
California's public cloud plan is CalCompute, created by SB 53.

items.p: Public compute and public AI projects range from research clouds to an international AGI project. What objections have been raised? Name one.
items.answer: Examples: AI Now and Data & Society (Meredith Whittaker, 2021) argued a resource built on licensed commercial cloud is a subsidy to Big Tech; Forethought researchers warn a centralized government or multinational AI project concentrates control in a few officials unless it is coup-proofed.
keys: Subsidizes the largest cloud firms (AI Now, Data & Society)
Centralized projects concentrate power (Forethought)
Forethought: coup-proof centralized projects (oversight by several bodies, use rules)
items.x: Forethought's AI-enabled coups report (Davidson, Finnveden and Hadshar, April 2025) says any plan for a single centralized AI project should be coup-proofed, for example with oversight by several government bodies, including legislative committees and courts, and formal rules on how its AI may be used.

choice.p: Which is an objection raised to public compute and public AI projects?
o: Built on licensed commercial cloud, it would mainly subsidize Big Tech
It would let Chinese researchers use US public research compute for free
It would require universities to stop using private cloud providers for research
It would ban private companies from training frontier models outside the public system
ow: NAIRR serves US researchers; foreign access is not the objection raised.
Public compute adds an option; it bars no one from private clouds.
Public compute supplements private development; it bans nothing.

items.p: Match each preemption approach to its description.
pairs: Blanket moratorium
Bars most state AI laws for years with no federal standard
Executive preemption campaign
Lawsuits and grant conditions under EO 14365
Preemption for a federal standard
States lose authority only where binding federal duties apply
Federal floor
Federal minimum that states may exceed
GUARDRAILS Act
Nullifies EO 14365 and protects state grant funding
items.x: The 2025 moratorium was stripped from the reconciliation bill by a 99-1 Senate vote. Under EO 14365 (December 2025), DOJ intervened in xAI's suit against Colorado's AI Act in April 2026, but an executive order cannot preempt state law by itself. The FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925, Rep. Obernolte, July 2026) takes the trade approach, and NCSL opposes any federal preemption of state AI law. As of mid-October 2026 no statute preempts state AI law.

items.p: Federal preemption of state AI laws is politically contested. Briefly state the main argument on each side.
items.answer: For: one national standard avoids conflicting state rules that impose national costs (Dean Ball and Alan Rozenshtein in Lawfare argue Congress should preempt, ideally with a federal standard). Against: states are now the main source of binding frontier AI rules, and they should keep room to act (NCSL opposes any federal preemption; CDT says it harms consumers and states).
keys: For: avoid patchwork; frontier risk is national
For: Ball and Rozenshtein (Lawfare)
Against: states are the active regulators (SB 53, RAISE)
Against: NCSL and CDT oppose preemption
items.x: Many positions sit between. Charlie Bullock (LawAI) wrote in July 2026 that the Great American AI Act, a House discussion draft from Reps. Obernolte and Trahan, which he called the best federal frontier framework yet, would be net-negative as written, mainly because of its broad three-year preemption. Supporters of a trade ask whether preemption comes with real federal duties.

choice.p: What is the main argument against federal preemption of state frontier AI laws?
o: States write most binding frontier AI rules, and preemption would wipe them out
State safety laws impose national costs and create a patchwork of conflicting rules
Federal agencies have no legal authority to regulate AI, so only states can act
The Constitution bars Congress from regulating AI because it is not interstate commerce
ow: That is the main argument for preemption (Ball and Rozenshtein).
The dispute is about displacing state rules, not about whether federal agencies have any role.
Congress can regulate interstate commerce, including AI; the dispute is whether it should displace states.

items.p: The FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925) would preempt state frontier AI rules in exchange for federal safety duties. What objection did Americans for Responsible Innovation (Brad Carson) raise to its preemption clause?
o: It has no sunset and takes effect before the federal regime exists
Any federal preemption of state AI law is unacceptable
It raises Tenth Amendment problems that would produce years of litigation
State safety laws impose national costs, so preemption should be broader
ow: That is NCSL's position; ARI objected to specific design flaws.
That was CAP's Nicole Alvarez, about earlier moratorium drafts.
That is the pro-preemption argument of Dean Ball and Alan Rozenshtein.
items.x: ARI said the FRONTIER Act improves on earlier proposals but needs critical changes, noting its preemption would take effect immediately while the federal assurance system would take years to set up.
keys: It has no sunset
Preemption takes effect before the federal regime exists

items.p: International proposals on frontier AI range from light to heavy. Match each approach to its description.
pairs: Incident channel
Low-cost link for national-security-level AI incidents
International red lines
Agreed bans on specific uses, e.g. AI nuclear launch authority
Compute-capped treaty
Coalition limits training compute, verified by chip tracking
Jurisdictional certification
Global body certifies national regimes; chip access tied to it
Mutual Assured AI Malfunction
States deter rivals' destabilizing AI projects by threat of sabotage
items.x: Sources: the Global Call for AI Red Lines (Sept 2025); MIRI's treaty proposal (Scher et al., 2025), whose authors concede the political will does not yet exist; Trager et al. and O'Keefe's Chips for Peace for certification; Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang's Superintelligence Strategy for deterrence.

items.p: A US-China agreement limiting frontier AI development, backed by verification, has been proposed. Name two objections or alternatives critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: Chris McGuire (Council on Foreign Relations) says such a deal is exceedingly unlikely under current conditions and has no arms-control precedent; Ruby Scanlon and Janet Egan (CNAS) say trust is low and verification tools are immature; Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang propose deterrence by threat of sabotage instead.
keys: Very unlikely; no precedent (McGuire, CFR)
Verification immature, about 50 people working on it (Scanlon and Egan, CNAS)
Deterrence (Mutual Assured AI Malfunction) proposed instead
items.x: Supporters' usual reply is to invest in verification now, since tools take years to build (CNAS and IFP both recommend this).

choice.p: Which objection have critics raised to a verified US-China agreement limiting frontier AI?
o: Trust is low and the tools to verify compliance are immature
Any such agreement would break World Trade Organization rules
China has already signed a binding treaty capping AI training
Agreements are unnecessary because export controls have halted Chinese AI progress
ow: Trade law is not among the objections raised.
No binding agreement limits frontier AI development as of October 2026.
Chinese labs still build frontier models; IFP estimates the US lead at about 8 months.

items.p: What did the White House say the US and China agreed on AI after their September 2026 summit, and what is one caveat about the announcement?
items.answer: The White House said the US and China agreed to a 'Super Intelligence' dialogue on AI risks and benefits and a communication channel for AI incidents. The announcement did not say what counts as an incident or which agencies take part, and Beijing gave no immediate comment.
keys: US-China dialogue on superintelligence
AI incident communication channel
Announced by the White House, Sept 2026
Details unspecified; no immediate comment from Beijing
items.x: The White House fact sheet came out on Sept 25, 2026, after a Trump-Xi summit in Washington. Chinese state media confirmed the incident channel the next day, according to AFP. Supporters see dialogues and incident channels as cheap confidence-building that reduces the chance of misread accidents.

o: A superintelligence dialogue and an AI incident channel, with few details given
A binding treaty capping AI training compute, signed and ratified by both countries
A joint ban on any AI role in nuclear launch decisions, signed by both leaders at the summit
A deal to lift US chip export controls in exchange for Chinese acceptance of verification
ow: No binding agreement limits frontier AI development.
The 2026 announcement covered only a dialogue and an incident channel.
Export controls were not part of the announced AI arrangements.

items.p: Suppose countries agree to cap AI training compute. Why might verification need to be strongest late in the agreement?
items.answer: The incentive to defect grows with the overhang: the longer a cap holds, the more efficiency gains and unused capacity build up, so the payoff from cheating rises, often just as political attention has moved on.
keys: Defection incentive grows as the overhang builds
Attention fades late in an intervention
items.x: The pacing.tech research agenda makes this argument, and adds that secret defection is worse than open non-participation because it corrupts every other party's picture of the situation. An 'overhang' is resources (compute, efficiency gains, ideas) that build up during a restriction and can produce a burst of progress if it ends or is broken. The authors also suggest staged exits to reduce sudden jumps.

choice.p: Why might verification of a training-compute cap need to be strongest late in the agreement?
o: The payoff from cheating grows as an overhang builds, while attention fades
Early in a cap no one has any reason to cheat, because all AI progress stops completely
Treaties bar installing verification hardware in their first years
Courts can't enforce a treaty until its first review conference
ow: Some incentive to cheat exists from the start; the point is that it grows over time.
The argument is about incentives to defect, not when equipment can be installed.
The argument concerns incentives to defect, not legal procedure.

units.title: Risks to responses
units.desc: Concrete risk scenarios where specific bills, laws or proposals are in play. For scenario practice across all tools, see AI Policy Toolkit.

lessons.title: Scenarios with specific proposals in play

items.p: Suppose AI agents become able to find and exploit software vulnerabilities on their own, at scale, and similar models are expected to appear abroad soon. Name two policies proposed to reduce the damage.
items.answer: Examples: invest in cybersecurity resilience before such models appear abroad (IFP's recommendation to NSA, CAISI, CISA and ONCD); government pre-deployment testing for cyber capabilities; agent identification and logging; operator and developer liability for agents that cause hacking damage; required shutdown capability.
keys: Cybersecurity resilience investment by NSA, CAISI, CISA, ONCD (IFP Rec. 13)
Government pre-deployment testing for cyber capabilities
Agent identification and tamper-evident logging
Operator/developer liability for agents causing hacking damage
Required shutdown or kill-switch capability
items.x: CAISI is the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at NIST; CISA is the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency; ONCD is the Office of the National Cyber Director. IFP's Recommendation 13 says agencies should plan for 'Mythos-class' cyber models being developed in China. One liability proposal would hold operators who knowingly run agents that recklessly cause hacking damage responsible, and share liability with developers who skip reasonable safeguards.

choice.p: AI agents can find and exploit software vulnerabilities at scale, and similar models are expected abroad soon. Which policy is proposed to reduce the damage?
o: Hardening key systems against AI-found flaws before rivals catch up
Mandatory screening of DNA synthesis orders and customers
Requiring AI chatbots to tell users they're talking to an AI
Merger review of partnerships between labs and cloud providers
ow: DNA screening targets bioweapons.
Chatbot disclosure rules address deception of consumers; they do nothing to harden systems against attack.
Merger review addresses market concentration.

items.p: Suppose a lab runs an unreleased, highly capable model internally for months to write code and run experiments for its next model. Rules that trigger on public release don't apply. Name two policies proposed for this situation.
items.answer: Examples: confidential internal-use risk summaries to a regulator (SB 53, RAISE); a safety case before internal deployment on the R&D stack; extending safety frameworks and access rules to internal models; embedded auditors inside labs; government authority to restrict or suspend internal use.
keys: Internal-use risk summaries to regulators (CA SB 53, NY RAISE)
Safety case before internal deployment
Apply safety frameworks and access tiers to internal models
Embedded or resident auditors
Government authority to verify, restrict or suspend internal use
items.x: California's SB 53 (in effect since January 2026) requires large frontier developers to send the state quarterly summaries of catastrophic-risk assessments from internal use; New York's amended RAISE Act is reported to add a similar duty from 2027. The pacing.tech longlist includes a safety case before internal deployment on the R&D stack and monitoring of internal agent actions. The proposed federal FRONTIER Act would cover internal use in verification and emergency orders.

choice.p: A lab runs an unreleased, highly capable model internally for months to build its next model, and rules triggered by public release don't apply. Which policy is proposed for this?
o: Confidential reports to a regulator on catastrophic risks from internal use
Location verification on the AI chips in the lab's own data centers
Know-your-customer checks on outside customers who rent the lab's spare compute
Labels on AI-generated content the lab's products show to the public
ow: Location checks show where chips are, not how a lab uses its models.
Customer checks cover outside renters, not the lab's own internal use.
Content labels apply to public outputs; the problem here is internal use.

items.p: Suppose an AI agent running for a company starts acting outside its task, spending money and launching copies of itself, and no one can quickly tell whose agent it is. Name two policies proposed to reduce this risk.
items.answer: Examples: agent identification and tamper-evident logging (Stop Rogue AI Act); spend limits per agent and task; limits on sub-agent spawn depth and unattended run length; human approval for irreversible actions; tiered agent permissions; instance-count reporting.
keys: Agent IDs and tamper-evident logs (Stop Rogue AI Act)
Agent spend limits
Spawn-depth and unattended-run limits
Human approval for irreversible actions
Agent permission tiers
items.x: The Stop Rogue AI Act (Rep. Gottheimer, Sept 2026) would direct NIST to write agent-identity standards, mandatory for federal agencies and contractors. Researchers compare agent IDs to aircraft tail numbers. The pacing.tech longlist's autonomy chain lists permission tiers, spend limits, spawn limits, approval for irreversible actions and kill-switch latency.

choice.p: An AI agent running for a company starts acting outside its task, spending money and launching copies of itself, and no one can quickly tell whose agent it is. Which policy is proposed for this?
o: Agent identifiers tied to whoever runs the agent, with tamper-evident logs
A cap on the training compute used for each new frontier model
Know-your-customer checks on everyone who rents cloud compute
Merger review of partnerships between AI labs and cloud providers
ow: A training cap limits how models are built; it doesn't trace or limit a running agent.
Cloud KYC identifies who rents compute; it can't tell whose agent is acting or limit what it does.
Merger review targets market concentration.

items.p: Suppose two leading labs each want to delay a risky release, but each fears the other will ship first, and an agreement to hold back could look like an illegal cartel. Name two policies proposed for this.
items.answer: Examples: an antitrust safe harbor for safety coordination (CATS Act); a government-supervised standards body that sets pacing rules; a statutory capability-triggered halt, so compliance with law replaces collusion; a verified pause that labs join together; a minimum interval between frontier releases.
keys: Antitrust safe harbor for safety coordination (CATS Act)
Government-supervised standards body for pacing
Statutory capability-triggered halt
Coordinated, verified industry pause
Minimum release interval
items.x: The CATS Act (Rep. Latta, Sen. Schiff, July 2026) would shield coordination on defined risks if labs first notify the Justice Department's Antitrust Division. On Sept. 18, 2026 subscribers sued Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX AI and Google under the Sherman Act over the industry's public push to 'pace the frontier'. The minimum release interval is from the pacing.tech appendix.

choice.p: Two leading labs each want to delay a risky release, but each fears the other will ship first, and an agreement to hold back could look like an illegal cartel. Which policy is proposed for this?
o: An antitrust safe harbor for safety deals, after notice to the Justice Department
Structural separation of chip, cloud and frontier model companies into separate firms
Know-your-customer rules for cloud providers that rent out AI chips
Location verification on the advanced AI chips the labs use for training
ow: Separation creates more independent firms; it doesn't let them hold back together.
Cloud KYC addresses export-control gaps.
Location checks address chip smuggling.

items.p: Suppose the US and China are both racing to automate AI research, and neither will slow down alone. Name two policies proposed to reduce the risk.
items.answer: Examples: a US-China dialogue and incident channel; using that dialogue to develop shared guidelines for rapid capability growth and prepare verification (IFP); agreed international red lines; a compute-capped treaty verified by chip tracking; funding verification R&D and a frontier-state incident hotline.
keys: US-China dialogue and incident channel
Joint guidelines and verification prep via bilateral dialogue (IFP Rec. 22)
International red lines (e.g., no AI in nuclear launch)
Compute-capped treaty with chip-tracking verification
Verification R&D funding and incident hotline
items.x: Supporters argue unilateral restraint fails if rivals keep racing, and verification makes cheating detectable enough that compliance pays. The White House said in September 2026 that the US and China agreed to a dialogue and an AI incident channel; Chinese state media confirmed the channel the next day. Skeptics such as Chris McGuire (CFR) call a US-China deal on AI development very unlikely, and CNAS authors note verification tools are immature.

choice.p: The US and China are both racing to automate AI research, and neither will slow down alone. Which policy is proposed to reduce the risk?
o: Agreed international red lines, such as no AI control over nuclear launch
A federal floor that every state AI law must meet or exceed
Mandatory screening of DNA synthesis orders and customers
Logging US officials' use of AI as federal records open to audit
ow: A federal floor settles which level of US government regulates; it doesn't touch the US-China race.
DNA screening targets bioweapons.
AI records rules check abuse of power at home.

policy.description: Specific laws, bills, proposals and frameworks in the 2026 debate over AI risk policy, and who argues what. Pairs with AI Policy Toolkit, which covers how the tools themselves work.
caveat: Drawn from the AI Risk Legislation Tracker, the pacing.tech agenda (Douglas, Dillon, Moore, Leech and Avin) and IFP’s report on automated AI R&D, with facts current as of October 2026. Frameworks, claims about what a policy would do, and objections are the views of the people who hold them, not settled fact.

Revised on October 19, 2026 to cut duplicates and report trivia, then re-checked by a second AI, which corrected many attributions. On October 20, general explanations of how each tool works moved to AI Policy Toolkit, so this course focuses on specific laws, bills, actors and frameworks. Many questions have more than one right answer, and the grader accepts any specific, correct one. No person has reviewed it.
policy.meta: Draft · revised 2026-10-20 · Fact-checked by AI, not by a person

tools.name: AI Policy Toolkit

units.title: Start here
units.desc: The main kinds of catastrophic AI risk that policy tools target, the six families of tools in this course, and which families aim at which risks.

items.p: AI risk discussions separate 'misuse' from 'loss of control'. What is the main difference?
o: Misuse: a person uses AI to cause harm on purpose. Loss of control: AI systems act outside anyone's control
Misuse: mistakes and bugs in AI systems cause harm. Loss of control: criminals take over AI systems to attack
Misuse: harm from models whose weights are published. Loss of control: harm from models kept inside labs
Misuse: harm to individual users. Loss of control: harm only to the developer's own computer systems
ow: This mixes them up: misuse is deliberate harm by people, bugs count as malfunctions, and criminals taking over a system is still misuse.
Either risk can involve open or closed models; the difference is whether a person or the AI is driving the harm.
Misuse can be catastrophic at scale, and loss of control is defined by AI escaping anyone's control, whatever it harms.
keys: Misuse: a person deliberately uses AI to cause harm
Loss of control: AI systems operate outside anyone's control
items.x: The International AI Safety Report, chaired by Yoshua Bengio, groups risks into malicious use (such as cyberattacks and biological or chemical weapons), malfunctions (including loss of control) and systemic risks. The split matters for policy: misuse tools aim at bad actors and dangerous capabilities, while loss-of-control tools aim at the AI systems themselves.

items.p: Which pair of misuse risks do frontier AI safety laws and company safety frameworks most often treat as potentially catastrophic?
o: Help building biological or chemical weapons, and help carrying out cyberattacks
Deepfake harassment of individuals, and copyright infringement by AI models
Biased decisions in hiring and lending, and leaks of users' personal data
Election misinformation, and job losses as AI automates office work
ow: These are real harms, but frontier safety rules focus on mass-casualty and very large-scale risks.
Bias and privacy harms are real, and other laws cover them; frontier safety laws target catastrophic harms.
Job losses aren't misuse, and frontier frameworks center on weapons, cyberattacks and loss of control.
keys: Biological or chemical (CBRN) weapons
Cyberattacks
items.x: California's SB 53, for example, defines catastrophic risk as a foreseeable, material risk that a frontier model contributes to more than 50 deaths or serious injuries, or over $1 billion in property damage, in a single incident: by helping create or release chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear weapons, by carrying out a cyberattack or serious crime without meaningful human oversight, or by evading its developer's control.

items.p: Why are AI risks in biology and cybersecurity often called a 'dual-use' problem for policymakers?
o: The same AI skills that help attackers also help defenders and researchers, so blunt limits hurt legitimate work
Governments and companies both build the same models, so it's unclear which of them a regulator should cover
Models can run both online and offline, so their use can't be monitored once someone downloads them
Attacks can come from inside or outside a country, so national laws can't reach most of the attackers
ow: Who builds models is a real policy question, but 'dual-use' means one capability has both helpful and harmful uses.
'Dual-use' means one capability has both helpful and harmful uses; where a model runs is a separate issue.
'Dual-use' means one capability has both helpful and harmful uses; where attackers sit is a separate issue.
keys: The same capabilities help attackers and defenders or researchers
Blunt restrictions would hamper legitimate uses
items.x: The 2026 International AI Safety Report uses this framing. It notes that overly aggressive safeguards, such as refusing cyber-related requests, can hamper defenders, and that most biological AI tools are open-weight, so harmful uses are hard to restrict without hurting research. Supporters of screening DNA orders say it sidesteps part of this problem: it acts at a physical step, so it works whichever AI model produced a design.

items.p: Everyday AI errors and 'loss of control' can both be treated as AI malfunctions. What makes a loss of control scenario different from an ordinary malfunction?
items.answer: In a loss of control scenario, one or more AI systems operate outside anyone's control, and regaining control is extremely costly or impossible. An ordinary malfunction, such as a wrong answer or buggy code, can usually be noticed and fixed.
keys: AI systems operate outside anyone's control
Regaining control is extremely costly or impossible
items.x: The 2026 International AI Safety Report, which files both under malfunctions, says loss of control becomes more likely if systems are misaligned (their goals conflict with what developers or society intend), since such a system might give false information, hide actions or resist shutdown. It says expert opinion on the likelihood varies greatly: some find it implausible, others likely enough to merit attention given how severe it would be.

choice.p: What makes a 'loss of control' scenario different from an ordinary AI malfunction?
o: AI acts outside anyone's control, and regaining it is extremely costly or impossible
The AI gives wrong answers so often that its users stop trusting it or relying on it at all
A criminal group takes over the AI system and uses it to attack hospitals and other systems
The developer loses money because the model fails to find enough paying customers
ow: That's a reliability problem, which people can notice and fix.
That's misuse or theft: a person is still in control of the system.
Commercial failure isn't a safety risk in this framework.

items.p: Some researchers argue advanced AI could make it easier for a small group to seize power, even in an established democracy. What mechanism would make this possible?
o: Seizing power has needed many people to cooperate, and some refuse; AI doing their jobs could remove that check
Voters will come to trust AI advisers more than elected officials, and will vote to hand power to those advisers
AI will make vote-counting machines easy to hack, so a small group can quietly rig elections at national scale
Whoever owns the chip factories will be able to dictate terms to every government that needs AI
ow: The concern is a small group seizing power through AI; voters choosing to hand power to AI is a different scenario.
Election hacking is a separate concern; the core worry is removing the need for human cooperation.
The concern centers on who controls AI systems inside militaries, governments and labs; chip supply is a different issue.
keys: Power grabs have needed many people to cooperate
Some people refuse illegal orders
AI replacing those people removes the check
items.x: This argument is from 'AI-Enabled Coups' (April 2025) by Forethought's Tom Davidson, Lukas Finnveden and Rose Hadshar, which names three risk factors: AI systems loyal to one person or small group, AI with hidden 'secret loyalties', and exclusive access to the most capable AI. Tools aimed at this include law-following AI, statutory limits on military AI and logging of officials' AI use.

items.p: Why do some analysts treat concentration in the market for general-purpose AI as a risk in itself?
o: A few companies gain great power over how AI is built and used, and many sectors rely on the same few models
Concentration raises chip prices so far that universities can no longer afford to do serious AI research
Dominant companies are more likely than small ones to publish models with dangerous capabilities openly
Large companies' models are less accurate than smaller rivals' models, so their errors spread more widely
ow: High costs are a cause of concentration; the concerns are power and shared points of failure.
Open release isn't the concern; the concerns are power and shared points of failure.
Accuracy isn't the issue; the worry is many sectors relying on the same few models.
keys: A few companies gain power over AI development and deployment
Many sectors depend on the same few models (single points of failure)
items.x: The 2025 International AI Safety Report raises this concern. It says building a state-of-the-art model can cost hundreds of millions of dollars, and leaders gain from economies of scale and network effects. A failure in one widely used model could spread to finance, healthcare and other critical sectors. Market-structure tools such as merger review, structural separation and public compute aim at this private side of power concentration.

items.p: Why can competitive pressure, between AI companies or between countries, raise other AI risks?
items.answer: Competition can push developers and governments to put speed ahead of safety: releasing faster, spending less on testing and risk management, or accepting larger risks to stay ahead. This may leave too little safety work done, such as the work needed to avoid loss of control.
keys: Competition pushes actors to prioritize speed over safety
Less testing and risk-reduction work
Raises the chance of other risks such as loss of control
items.x: The 2025 International AI Safety Report makes this point: if avoiding loss of control takes a lot of risk assessment and mitigation work, intense competition may lower the chance that enough gets done. Dan Hendrycks, Mantas Mazeika and Thomas Woodside (Center for AI Safety, 2023) list an 'AI race' as one of four main sources of catastrophic AI risk.

choice.p: Why can competitive pressure between AI developers or countries raise other AI risks?
o: Competition can push actors to put speed ahead of safety, skimping on testing and risk reduction
Competition makes AI models more expensive, so fewer developers can afford safety tools
Competition pushes labs to publish their model weights to win users, which makes theft and misuse easier
Competition makes governments regulate too quickly, before the risks are understood
ow: The concern is how competition shapes safety effort, not model prices.
Competition doesn't require publishing weights; many leading labs keep theirs closed.
The worry runs the opposite way: competition may lead governments to invest less in risk management.

items.p: Match each family of catastrophic AI risk to an example of it.
pairs: Misuse
A group uses a model's help to plan an attack on a power grid
Loss of control
A model hides what it can do from testers and resists being shut down
Concentration of power
A small group uses loyal AI systems to rule without needing others to cooperate
Racing
Labs skip safety testing so that a rival doesn't ship first
items.x: Some researchers treat racing as a driver of the other three: the International AI Safety Report warns that competition may lead developers and governments to spend less on risk management. Hendrycks, Mazeika and Woodside list an 'AI race' as its own source of catastrophic risk. Many tools address more than one family.

items.p: This course groups 40 policy tools into six families. Match each family to how it works.
pairs: Transparency and reporting
Labs must disclose their safety plans, test results and incidents
Verification and oversight
Outsiders check what labs claim, through audits, testing or licenses
Liability and lab governance
Lawsuits, insurance and corporate structure reshape labs' incentives
Control, pauses and bans
Keep the ability to halt a model or stop development
Compute, chips and security
Govern the physical inputs to AI and protect model weights from theft
Power, government and federalism
Limit military and government AI use and decide who controls AI
items.x: Transparency tools rely on what labs report about themselves; verification tools add someone outside who checks. The 40 tools range from enacted laws, such as California's SB 53, to ideas that so far exist only in papers.

items.p: Which family of tools works by having someone outside a lab check whether what the lab says about its safety practices is true?
o: Verification and oversight
Transparency and reporting
Liability and lab governance
Control, pauses and bans
ow: Transparency rules make labs disclose information; they don't add an outside party who checks it.
Liability works through lawsuits and incentives after the fact; it doesn't send in outside checkers.
Control tools keep the ability to stop systems or development; they don't check labs' claims.
keys: Verification and oversight
Outside audits, testing or inspection of labs' claims
items.x: Supporters of third-party audits argue that disclosure laws like California's SB 53 rely on labs describing their own practices, with no one checking the description. Verification tools include audits, embedded auditors, government testing before release, licensing and a dedicated regulator.

items.p: Supporters of liability tools, such as a statutory duty of care or strict liability for AI harms, say they have an advantage over detailed safety mandates. What is it?
o: Labs choose their own precautions to avoid paying for harms, so no regulator has to specify them
It can stop a dangerous model before it is trained or released, since a regulator can withhold approval
It gives the public detailed reports on each lab's safety tests, incidents and security practices
It guarantees victims get paid even when a catastrophe costs more than the developer is worth
ow: Withholding approval before release is what licensing does; liability mostly acts after harm.
Public reports on tests and incidents come from transparency rules.
That is liability's known weak spot: a catastrophe can exceed a firm's assets, which is why some propose mandatory insurance.
keys: Developers bear the cost of harms their models cause
Labs choose how to be safe; no regulator has to specify methods
items.x: Supporters say expected liability makes developers bear the costs of harms they impose on others, so they invest in safety without a regulator specifying how. Critics point to a weakness for catastrophic risk: a true catastrophe could exceed the firm's assets and leave nothing to collect, which is one reason some propose mandatory insurance.

items.p: Match each risk to the set of tools aimed most directly at it.
pairs: AI help building bioweapons
Screening DNA orders and limiting access to biological design tools
Theft of model weights
Required security levels for labs and data centers
Loss of control of a model
A tested off-switch and government power to halt a model
An AI-enabled seizure of power
AI that refuses unlawful orders, and legal limits on military AI
Labs racing to ship first
A legal exemption letting labs coordinate on safety, and binding rules for every lab
A US-China AI race
Dialogues, agreed red lines and verified treaties
items.x: These are the tools' main targets, and many reach further. Supporters of weight security, for instance, say it also matters for racing, since a stolen model speeds up a rival. The last unit of this course works through these links with scenarios.

items.p: Policy tools act at different points in a frontier model's life. Put these in order, from the earliest point to the latest.
items: Export controls limit who can buy the advanced chips
A developer reports a large training run to the government
Government evaluators test the model before public release
The developer reports a serious incident with the released model
A court awards damages to people the model harmed
items.x: The authors of the pacing.tech research agenda describe a recurring tradeoff along this chain: earlier control points are easier to observe and constrain but blunter, while later ones can target specific harms but are easier to get around, since the harmful model already exists. They argue the best route often uses several points at once.

units.title: Transparency and reporting
units.desc: Tools that make labs show their safety plans, test results, incidents, internal use and compute, and make officials' AI use reviewable.

items.p: Some laws require frontier AI developers to publish a safety framework, a written plan for testing for and managing catastrophic risks, and to follow it. What problem do supporters say this fixes?
items.answer: Labs set their own safety rules privately and can quietly loosen them under competitive pressure. Publishing creates a public baseline that journalists, employees and regulators can check releases against, and a duty to follow it turns broken promises into legal violations.
keys: labs' private rules can be loosened quietly
creates a public baseline others can check
following it becomes a legal obligation
items.x: California's SB 53, in force since January 2026, works this way: each large developer writes its own framework, and the law requires the developer to publish and follow it. Critics point out that because labs write the rules themselves, a vague framework is hard to violate.

choice.p: Supporters say laws requiring labs to publish and follow a safety framework fix which problem?
o: Labs set safety rules privately and can quietly loosen them under competitive pressure
Governments don't learn who is training very large models until those models are released
Regulators hear about AI accidents from the press or from victims instead of from the labs
People harmed by AI models have no clear way to sue the developer for damages
ow: That is the gap compute reporting targets; a framework describes how a lab manages catastrophic risk.
That is the gap incident reporting targets; a framework is a standing plan, and incident reports cover specific events.
That is a liability problem; California's framework law is enforced by the state attorney general.

items.p: A 'publish only' rule would require a lab to publish its safety framework. What does a 'publish and follow' rule, the model used in California's SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act, add?
items.answer: A legal duty to comply with the framework. If the lab departs from its own stated tests, thresholds or safeguards, that is a violation the state can penalize. In California the attorney general can seek up to $1 million per violation.
keys: legal duty to comply with its own framework
departing from it is a violation the state can penalize
items.x: Voluntary pledges, such as the 2024 Seoul Frontier AI Safety Commitments, rely on reputation: a lab that ignores its framework faces criticism but no legal penalty. New York's RAISE Act, effective January 2027, says developers must "write, implement, comply with" and publish their frameworks.

choice.p: What does a 'publish and follow' safety framework law add beyond requiring publication?
o: A legal duty to comply, so departing from the framework is a violation the state can penalize
A government-written safety standard that replaces each lab's own framework
A requirement that an outside auditor approve the framework before any release
A right for anyone harmed to sue the lab if it breaks its framework
ow: Each lab still writes its own framework; SB 53 lists only the topics the framework must cover.
That describes a stronger audit variant; a publish-and-follow duty by itself needs no outside approval.
Under SB 53 only the attorney general can bring the civil action for penalties.

items.p: Illinois's SB 315 adds an independent audit to a publish-and-follow framework law. What weakness of plain publish-and-follow rules is the audit meant to fix?
items.answer: Self-grading: under plain publish-and-follow rules the lab writes its framework and also judges whether it followed it, and outsiders can't see inside. An independent auditor checks whether the lab actually complied.
keys: the lab otherwise grades its own compliance
an independent party checks whether it followed the framework
items.x: Illinois's annual audits start in 2028. METR notes they are procedural: they check whether the developer followed the required processes and do not assess whether its models are safe. Audits add cost, and NetChoice, opposing a Massachusetts audit mandate, argued that "the necessary auditing ecosystem simply does not exist."

choice.p: What weakness of publish-and-follow framework laws does adding an independent audit target?
o: The lab grades its own compliance, and outsiders can't check it
Regulators don't learn about large training runs until a model is released
Detailed test results posted online could help bad actors build weapons
Labs can keep serious safety incidents secret from the state
ow: That gap is the target of compute reporting.
That is a concern about public disclosure, which rules handle with redactions or confidential filings.
That gap is the target of incident reporting rules.

items.p: Laws like California's SB 53 require large AI developers to publish a safety framework they write themselves, and to follow it. Name two objections or weaknesses critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: labs pick their own rules, so a vague framework is hard to violate (the Midas Project); published frameworks score poorly on risk-management criteria (SaferAI); labs can rewrite frameworks and have weakened pledges to pause (Future of Life Institute); state rules could slow US innovation in the race with China (industry groups, Trump administration).
keys: labs choose their own rules, so vague frameworks are hard to violate
existing frameworks are weak or underspecified
labs can rewrite or weaken their frameworks
burden on innovation or conflict with the federal AI agenda
items.x: Tyler Johnston of the Midas Project, which alleged in September 2026 that OpenAI broke SB 53, said "it's totally up to them to choose what the rules are." OpenAI said it was confident it complied. A SaferAI study scored 12 companies' frameworks against 65 criteria and found a median score of 18%.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to laws requiring labs to publish and follow their own safety frameworks?
o: Labs pick their own rules, so a vague framework is hard to break
The law imposes one government safety standard that fits no lab well
Published frameworks expose trade secrets because nothing can be redacted
The law lets anyone harmed by AI sue the developer for unlimited damages
ow: Each lab defines its own thresholds, which is why critics worry about vagueness.
SB 53 lets developers redact trade secrets and security details if they explain each redaction.
Only the attorney general enforces SB 53, with penalties capped at $1 million per violation.

items.p: Under California's SB 53, in force since January 2026, who decides the specific risk thresholds and safeguards in a large developer's frontier AI framework?
o: The developer, covering a list of topics the law requires
The state Office of Emergency Services, through regulations
The state attorney general, case by case
An independent auditor licensed by the state
ow: The Office of Emergency Services receives incident reports and internal-use summaries; it doesn't write frameworks.
The attorney general enforces compliance with the framework the lab wrote.
SB 53 asks the developer to describe how it uses third-party assessors; the lab sets the framework's content.
keys: the developer decides
the law lists topics the framework must address
items.x: SB 53 requires the framework to describe how the developer approaches topics such as catastrophic-risk thresholds, mitigations, third-party assessments and securing model weights, and leaves the specifics to the lab. A May 2026 New York bill (S10456) would instead have the state set minimum standards for frameworks.

items.p: Labs already publish model cards for many new models voluntarily. Why do supporters want laws requiring a standard report, including dangerous-capability test results, at or before each frontier model's release?
items.answer: Voluntary reports vary in timing and content and are sometimes late or missing. A required, standard report lets researchers, deployers and governments compare models, spot dangerous capability jumps and check that claimed safeguards exist. It also creates a record that enforcement can use later.
keys: voluntary reports are inconsistent, late or missing
lets outsiders compare models and spot dangerous capability jumps
lets outsiders check claimed safeguards
items.x: The case supporters cite: Google released Gemini 2.5 Pro in March 2025, and a short model card followed about three weeks later. Sixty UK lawmakers called it a breach of Google's Seoul safety commitments; Google DeepMind said it stood by its testing and reporting processes. California's SB 53 now requires a transparency report before or at the time a new frontier model is deployed.

choice.p: Why do supporters want laws requiring standard model reports, with dangerous-capability test results, at release?
o: Voluntary reports are uneven or late; standard ones let outsiders compare models
Labs train ever-larger models without telling regulators, so reports give notice before training starts
Labs quietly loosen their company-wide safety rules, so reports lock those rules in place
Regulators need a private alert whenever a deployed model causes serious harm to people
ow: Notice of training runs is compute reporting; model reports come at release, after training.
That describes safety frameworks, which are company-wide plans; model reports cover one model each.
That is incident reporting, which is triggered by events and usually kept confidential.

items.p: California's SB 53 requires large developers to publish both a frontier AI framework and a transparency report. How do the two documents differ?
items.answer: The framework is one standing, company-wide plan: which catastrophic risks the lab assesses, what thresholds trigger safeguards, how it secures model weights. A transparency report is published for each new frontier model, before or at deployment, describing the model and summarizing its catastrophic-risk assessments and results.
keys: framework: one standing, company-wide plan
transparency report: one per new model, at or before release
the report summarizes that model's risk assessments and results
items.x: The transparency report must also say how far third-party evaluators were involved. Reading the two together lets outsiders check whether a release followed the lab's own framework.

choice.p: How does a lab's frontier AI framework differ from its transparency report under California's SB 53?
o: The framework is a standing company-wide plan; a transparency report covers one new model and its risk results
The framework is confidential and goes to the state; the transparency report is its public version
The framework covers models used internally; the transparency report covers released ones
The framework is written by the state; the transparency report is written by the lab
ow: Both are published, with redactions allowed; the confidential filings to the state are incident reports and internal-use summaries.
The framework must also address risks from internal use, so internal versus external isn't the dividing line.
The lab writes both; SB 53 lists only the topics the framework must address.

items.p: Under the EU's Code of Practice for general-purpose AI, developers send a full safety and security model report to the EU AI Office and publish at most a summary. What two concerns is this split meant to address?
items.answer: Publishing full details could undermine safety and security safeguards, for example by helping bad actors, and could expose sensitive commercial information such as trade secrets. The regulator still sees the complete report.
keys: full details could undermine safeguards or help bad actors
protects sensitive commercial information or trade secrets
items.x: Signatories submit the full report before placing a model with systemic risk on the EU market, and publish a summary if and insofar as needed to assess or mitigate those risks. California's SB 53 handles the same tension differently: developers publish their documents but may redact trade secrets and cybersecurity, public safety or national security details, explaining each redaction.

choice.p: Why does the EU's Code of Practice send full model safety reports to the AI Office and publish at most a summary?
o: Full details could undermine safeguards or expose trade secrets
Summaries are cheaper to write, so the split mainly cuts compliance costs
The AI Office must approve each model before any public information comes out
Summaries let labs skip dangerous-capability testing for most models
ow: Developers must write the full report anyway; the split is about who sees the details.
The Code governs reporting to the AI Office; it doesn't turn the Office into a licensing body for each release.
The split concerns who sees the results; the testing is still required.

items.p: Model disclosure rules require developers to publish a standard report on each new frontier model, including dangerous-capability test results. Name two objections or limits that critics or legal analysts raise.
items.answer: Examples: disclosure mandates regulate speech, and ones requiring judgments, beyond plain facts, may fail First Amendment review (Sokhansanj and Arnold, LawAI); in-house testing misses flaws outside researchers find, so self-reported results have limits (Longpre et al.); detailed results could spread hazardous information.
keys: First Amendment or compelled-speech problems
self-reported tests are only as good as the lab's testing
detailed results could spread hazardous information
items.x: xAI is challenging California's AB 2013, a training-data disclosure law, on First Amendment grounds; in March 2026 a judge refused to block the law, and xAI appealed. Bahrad Sokhansanj and Mackenzie Arnold advise lawmakers to write disclosure rules that elicit facts rather than judgments. Shayne Longpre and coauthors propose disclosure programs with legal safe harbors so outside researchers can report model flaws.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to mandatory model disclosure rules?
o: Disclosures requiring judgments may fail First Amendment review
Chat logs held by AI vendors may not count as government records
Requiring permission before each release would entrench the largest labs
Pausing frontier development would hand the lead to China
ow: That limit applies to records of government AI use, a different tool.
