Internal models get reviewed once they're released, not before
items.x: Dan Parshall of the Canary Institute says including internal use "matters a lot, since the most capable models at any moment are the ones running inside the labs." Both outside IVO review and emergency orders reach internal use as well as released models.

items.p: How often must an IVO send an assessment report?
o: At least every 6 months, or more often if needed
Once, before the model is first released to the public
Every 5 years
Only when asked by Congress
items.x: Reports go to the Under Secretary and the developer at the same time. The Under Secretary can also order ad hoc assessments, for example after an incident.

items.p: What must an IVO do if it finds a model poses an imminent catastrophic risk?
o: Refer it to the Secretary of Commerce within 72 hours
Shut the model down itself
Notify the developer and give it 30 days to fix the problem
Wait and include it in the next scheduled assessment report
items.x: IVOs can't halt models themselves. They escalate to the Secretary, who decides whether to issue an emergency order.

items.p: Under the FRONTIER Act, put the review cycle between a developer and its independent verification organization (IVO) in order.
items: The IVO sends its assessment report
The developer describes its fixes within 14 days
The IVO says whether the fixes are adequate within 7 days
The developer files a post-assessment report with the Under Secretary within 30 days
items.x: The cycle forces a written record of what the IVO asked for and whether the developer did it. The full record goes to the Under Secretary. Within the same 30 days, the developer also publishes a redacted copy of the assessment report, which goes to the Attorney General and opted-in state attorneys general too.

items.p: Can an IVO be sued if a model it reviewed causes a catastrophe?
o: Only for willful misconduct causing death or serious injury, by clear and convincing proof
Yes, by anyone for any harm the model causes, under ordinary negligence rules
Never, under any circumstances, however serious the harm
Only by the developer that hired it
items.x: Licensed IVOs get broad immunity. The one exception is a federal claim for willful misconduct causing death or serious physical injury, and acting in line with the rules counts as no willful misconduct.

items.p: Who reports annually on whether the IVO market is working?
o: The Government Accountability Office (GAO)
The developers
The White House Office of Science and Technology Policy
The IVOs themselves, through a joint industry report
items.x: GAO, Congress's watchdog, reports each year on how many IVOs exist, whether they can meet demand and whether they're truly independent of the industry.

items.p: An IVO's license is at risk if a model it verified fails anyway. When is it protected?
o: When it flagged the problem and proposed adequate fixes the developer didn't make
When the model had passed its most recent scheduled assessment
When the failure happened overseas, outside United States jurisdiction
It's never protected
items.x: That rule gives IVOs a reason to put problems on the record rather than sign off quietly.

items.p: Why does Americans for Responsible Innovation (ARI) worry about the timing of IVO review?
o: Preemption is immediate; IVOs may take years
IVO licenses expire one year after they're issued
IVOs could only review open-source models, not closed ones
The bill bars any IVO from starting work until 2030
items.x: ARI president Brad Carson said the bill's preemption "would be effective immediately," while its private assurance market "will take years to set up." Very large developers don't have to hire an IVO until a year after the first one is licensed, while the limits on state law apply once the bill is enacted.

units.title: Emergency orders
units.desc: The government's power to halt a model.

items.p: Who can order a lab to suspend or restrict a frontier model?
o: The Secretary of Commerce
The Under Secretary, without the Secretary
Any licensed IVO, on its own authority
Any state attorney general, for models used in that state
items.x: The Secretary must consult the Under Secretary but holds final authority. An order can cover development, deployment or internal use, in whole or in part.

items.p: Match each type of order to how long it lasts.
pairs: Provisional order
Up to 45 days
Final order
90 days
Renewal of a final order
Another 90 days, with a fresh finding each time
items.x: Provisional orders let the Secretary act fast on a preliminary determination. Final orders require a full written finding, and every renewal needs a new one based on current facts.

items.p: Before issuing a provisional order, what must the Secretary usually give the lab?
o: Notice and a chance to fix the problem and be heard
Nothing
A court order
Congressional approval
items.x: The Secretary can skip notice only by finding in writing that the risk is too imminent, and must then give the lab a chance to fix the problem right after.

items.p: Does an emergency order cover a fine-tuned copy of the model?
o: Yes, unless the order says otherwise, plus models trained largely on its outputs
No, only the exact model the order names, not any modified copies
Yes, but models trained on its outputs fall outside the order
Copies are covered once the Secretary names them in a separate order
items.x: Orders also bind affiliates, successors and anyone knowingly working with the developer, which keeps a lab from dodging an order by moving the model.

items.p: What can someone face for willfully violating an emergency order?
o: Up to a $1 million fine per violation and 10 years in prison
Only a warning letter from the Secretary of Commerce
Up to 6 months in prison and a $5,000 fine
A $500 fine per violation, with no prison time
items.x: That's the criminal penalty. Separately, anyone bound by an order who violates it faces civil penalties of up to $10 million per violation, with each day counting separately.

items.p: Under the FRONTIER Act, a lab contests an emergency order from the Secretary. Put the steps in order.
items: The Secretary serves a provisional order
The lab applies for an expedited hearing within 10 days
The Secretary decides within 30 days
The Secretary issues a final order
The lab sues in federal district court in D.C.
items.x: Courts can't review a provisional order until a final order exists. Then the case goes only to the federal district court in D.C., which must move fast.

items.p: Which congressional committees get notice within 3 days of an emergency order?
o: Senate Commerce, House Energy and Commerce, and both Judiciary Committees
Only the House and Senate Intelligence Committees, in a closed classified briefing
The House and Senate Armed Services Committees
The House and Senate Appropriations Committees
items.x: The Secretary also reports semiannually on every order and its outcome. Notices can include a classified annex.

items.p: What does the bill's exclusivity clause do?
o: Makes this the only federal way to halt a model over imminent catastrophic risk
Gives the Commerce Department exclusive legal rights over every frontier model built in the U.S.
Bars states from writing their own catastrophic-risk rules for frontier developers
Gives IVOs the sole right to review frontier models for catastrophic risk
items.x: Any other attempt by the executive branch to halt a frontier model on those grounds is unenforceable unless a later law expressly refers to this section. Dan Parshall of the Canary Institute reads it as Congress "trying to wrest back some control from the Executive branch." It also means other emergency powers can't be used for this purpose. The bill’s limits on state laws are in a separate section.

items.p: A lab sues over a final order. Does the order stop applying while the case goes on?
o: No, unless the court orders a stay
Yes, the order is always paused until the case ends
Only if the lab posts bond
Yes, for 30 days while the court reviews the order
items.x: The court can set the order aside only if it's arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion or otherwise unlawful, a deferential standard. Claims that the law itself is unconstitutional can still be brought.

units.title: States and the debate
units.desc: Preemption, supporters, critics and odds.

items.p: Which three areas would states be barred from adding new rules on?
o: Catastrophic-risk transparency, audits and incident reports
Children's online safety, personal data privacy and consumer protection
Election deepfakes, hiring algorithms, and housing and lending decisions
All AI regulation of any kind, from chatbots to self-driving cars
items.x: Section 9 blocks states from imposing new substantive obligations on AI developers in those three "covered subject areas," all tied to catastrophic risk.

items.p: Does the preemption clause reach only companies over the 10^26 threshold?
o: No, every AI developer
Yes, only frontier developers
Only very large developers
Only foreign AI developers
items.x: The federal duties apply only above the compute line, but the limit on states covers any AI developer's catastrophic-risk transparency, auditing and incident reporting. Section 9 defines an AI developer as any entity that builds, trains or owns an AI model, so states couldn't add rules in these areas even for developers the federal duties don't reach.

items.p: Name one kind of AI law a state could still pass under the bill.
o: Pass a law protecting minors from harmful AI chatbot content
Require AI developers to report catastrophic-risk incidents to the state
Require third-party audits of developers' catastrophic-risk safeguards
Require developers to publish their catastrophic-risk testing results
items.x: Protecting minors is one of four carve-outs, along with generally applicable laws, rules on how deployers and users use AI, and rules for state agencies' own AI use. The other three options fall in the covered subject areas.

items.p: Which existing state laws' frontier provisions would the preemption clause most directly hit?
o: California's SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act
Colorado’s 2026 automated decision-making law (SB 26-189)
Illinois's Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA)
Tennessee's ELVIS Act on AI voice cloning
items.x: Both require frontier developers to publish safety frameworks and report incidents, which falls in the covered areas. The sponsors pitch the bill as "a single, clear national standard" (Trahan's words) in place of a state patchwork. Critics such as ARI say state rules would end immediately while the federal system takes years to build.

items.p: How do state attorneys general fit into the federal scheme?
o: They can opt in to receive reports and sue to enforce federal rules
They're shut out entirely
They run the IVO licensing
They can veto any emergency order issued against a lab based in their state
items.x: This keeps a role for states in enforcement. In September 2026, 26 state attorneys general led by New York's Letitia James wrote to Congress asking for full state enforcement authority and no preemption, though their letter didn't name this bill.

news.h: 26 state attorneys general ask Congress to regulate frontier AI without preempting the states

items.p: What's the main objection from groups like Americans for Responsible Innovation?
o: Preemption ends state rules before the federal system is running
The bill is too weak on kids' safety
The bill would ban the release of open-source AI models
The bill's fees would push small AI startups out of the market
items.x: ARI president Brad Carson said the preemption clause leaves "a serious hole in regulatory oversight of AI models." ARI also noted there's no sunset on the preemption and that the bill leaves the decision to release risky models with developers.

items.p: What structural weakness has one critic flagged in how the bill sets up its new Under Secretary?
o: No Senate confirmation for the Under Secretary, and no appropriations
It creates too many new Senate-confirmed posts across the Commerce Department
The Under Secretary could halt models without the Secretary's sign-off
The office would sit in the FTC, away from Commerce's technical staff
items.x: This is a point Dan Parshall of the Canary Institute raised. The Under Secretary is appointed by the Secretary of Commerce, and the text funds only the registration system, through fees. Parshall also noted the bill has no severability clause and drops the whistleblower protections in the Great American AI Act discussion draft it grew out of.

items.p: Why did OpenAI's statement on the bill matter?
o: A top lab said it "can support" the IVO requirement
OpenAI threatened to move out of the U.S. if the bill passed
OpenAI endorsed the whole bill, including preemption
OpenAI came out against the IVO requirement
items.x: OpenAI's Chris Lehane told reporters on September 15, 2026 that the company "can support" the IVO requirement, though a spokesperson said OpenAI hadn't endorsed the whole bill. Outside industry, Foundation for American Innovation research fellow Daniel King called it "Congress's best AI bill yet," and the Institute for Law & AI's Charlie Bullock called it "by far the best AI safety bill ever introduced" in a statement released by Rep. Trahan's office.

items.p: What's the biggest obstacle to the bill passing this Congress?
o: The Energy and Commerce chair doesn't want to rush it
It already passed both chambers and was vetoed by the President
The Senate passed a rival version that House leaders reject
Its two lead sponsors are both in the minority party
items.x: Chairman Brett Guthrie said on September 16, 2026, "I'm not going to say that the bill is going to move," and that he wouldn't want to act quickly in a lame duck session. As of October 19, 2026, congress.gov showed no committee action. Any bill not passed by January 3, 2027 dies with the 119th Congress and would have to be reintroduced.

news.h: Energy and Commerce chair Brett Guthrie won't commit to moving the FRONTIER Act and warns against rushing it in the lame duck

items.p: How does the Senate's Cruz-Klobuchar-Thune draft reportedly differ from the FRONTIER Act?
o: It relies on a legal duty of care
It has nothing about preemption of state laws
It creates a new independent AI agency outside the Commerce Department
It would cover AI developers of every size
items.x: No Senate text had been made public as of mid-October 2026, so these details come from Reuters' September 11 report citing Senate aides, which said the draft would also preempt some state laws. When Cruz blocked a separate Democratic AI safety bill on September 29, he objected to its "unbounded discretion" for the federal government and suggested approaches "like involving independent judges." Any final deal would need to reconcile the two designs.

caveat: Based on the introduced text of H.R. 9925 (July 23, 2026). Status, cosponsors and reactions checked October 19, 2026. Simplified: check the bill text before relying on details, and expect changes if the bill moves in committee.
Each question was checked against the bill text by a second AI, and its corrections were applied. No person has reviewed it.

side.name: Policy Side Effects

units.title: Policy side effects
units.desc: Real laws that backfired, got routed around, or landed on the wrong people. Each card describes a policy; you guess what went wrong.

items.p: In 1989 Mexico City banned most drivers from using their car one weekday a week, based on the last digit of the license plate, to cut air pollution. Studies found air quality did not improve. Name one way drivers may have gotten around the ban.
items.answer: Researchers have proposed several: some households bought a second car, often an older and dirtier used one, with a plate allowed on their banned day; others ignored the ban or used exemptions; and some shifted driving to evenings and weekends. Which mattered most is disputed.
keys: Any one of: bought a second car with a different plate, ignored the ban or used exemptions, or shifted driving to other times
items.x: Economist Lucas Davis (2008) found no improvement for any pollutant, vehicle registration data suggesting households bought extra, often older, cars, and higher pollution on weekends and late at night. Later work with household surveys (Guerra and Millard-Ball, 2017) found few households owning two restricted cars, and argues that ignoring the ban and shifting trips explain more. Lesson: if a rule restricts one unit (one car, one account, one model), check how cheaply people can get around it.

choice.p: In 1989 Mexico City banned most cars from driving one weekday a week, by license plate, to cut pollution. Air quality didn't improve. Which explanation have researchers proposed?
o: Some households bought a second, often older, car with a plate allowed on their banned day
The city's buses switched to dirtier diesel fuel the same year, cancelling out the drop in car pollution
Factories expanded output once traffic eased, so industrial pollution replaced the cuts from cars
The city stopped testing car emissions once the ban began, so the remaining cars polluted more
ow: Researchers did not point to a bus fuel change; the proposed explanations are second cars, ignoring the ban and shifting trips.
Researchers didn't attribute the result to industry; the evidence points to how drivers responded.
Emissions testing continued; the debate is about how drivers got around the ban.

items.p: From 1696 to 1851, England taxed houses by their number of windows, because windows were easy for assessors to count and big houses had more of them. Name one thing homeowners and builders did in response, and one harm it caused.
items.answer: They bricked up existing windows and built new houses with fewer windows. That cut light and ventilation, which doctors at the time blamed for disease, and the lost light was a large cost on top of the tax itself.
keys: Bricked up windows or built houses with fewer windows
Less light and fresh air, which doctors linked to disease
items.x: Economists Wallace Oates and Robert Schwab (2015) used local tax records to measure how the tax changed window counts, and roughly estimated the extra cost (the lost light) at about 60% of the revenue raised. Bricked-up windows are still visible on old English buildings. Lesson: when a policy keys on a proxy that is cheap to change (a count, a size, a threshold), people change the proxy instead of the thing it was meant to measure.

choice.p: England taxed houses by number of windows from 1696 to 1851. What was the best-known unintended result?
o: People bricked up windows and built darker houses, cutting light and air, which doctors blamed for disease
Glassmakers raised prices sharply, so rich families paid most of the tax through costlier glass
Wealthy owners rebuilt their houses as many small rented flats, which were exempt from the tax
Assessors took bribes to undercount windows, so the tax raised almost nothing and was dropped within a decade
ow: The documented response was fewer windows, not a shift of the burden onto glass prices.
The well-documented response was fewer windows, not a shift to exempt flats.
The tax lasted over 150 years; the documented response was people reducing their window counts.

items.p: French labor law adds a bundle of obligations (works councils, union representatives, layoff-plan rules) once a firm reaches 50 employees. Researchers looking at how many firms there are of each size found something odd near that line. What was it, and why does it matter?
items.answer: Far more firms have exactly 49 employees than 50: firms stop growing just below the threshold to avoid the obligations. That means productive firms stay smaller than they otherwise would, which costs output and jobs, with workers bearing much of the cost.
keys: Firms bunch just below 50 employees (many at 49, few at 50)
Firms hold back growth, costing output or jobs
items.x: Garicano, Lelarge and Van Reenen counted 416 French manufacturing firms with 49 employees and only 160 with 50, a break in an otherwise smooth size distribution. Their cost estimates depend on assumptions and range from under 1% to several percent of GDP. Lesson: any bright-line threshold (headcount, revenue, compute) invites actors to stay just under it, or to split into smaller entities.

choice.p: France adds many labor obligations at 50 employees. What pattern shows up in the count of French firms by size?
o: Many more firms have 49 employees than 50, because firms stop growing just below the line
Firms rush past 50 quickly, because the obligations come with tax credits that make growth cheaper
Firm sizes are smooth through 50, showing the obligations cost too little to change any decisions
Firms jump from 49 straight to about 100 employees, to spread the fixed costs over more workers
ow: The obligations are costs, not subsidies, and the data show firms piling up just under 50.
The distribution has a clear break at 50, which is why researchers study it.
The data show a pile-up at 49, not a jump past the threshold.

items.p: The US Endangered Species Act restricts what private landowners can do with land that hosts a listed species. The red-cockaded woodpecker nests only in old pine trees. How did some North Carolina timber owners near woodpecker colonies respond?
items.answer: They cut their forests earlier, before trees got old enough to host woodpecker nests, so the protected bird never moved in and the land-use restrictions never applied. The law ended up reducing the habitat it was meant to protect on private land.
keys: Harvested trees earlier or younger, before they could become nesting habitat
Kept the species from arriving so restrictions never applied
items.x: Lueck and Michael (2003) studied over 1,000 forest plots and found that plots closer to woodpecker colonies were more likely to be harvested, and cut younger. It's one team and one species, but a clear example of 'preemptive' avoidance. Lesson: when a rule is triggered by finding something on your property (a species, a dangerous capability, a document), people may avoid ever creating or discovering the trigger.

choice.p: The Endangered Species Act limits land use where protected species live. How did some timber owners near red-cockaded woodpecker colonies respond?
o: They cut their pines young, before the trees could host nests that would bring restrictions
They sold their land to the government at high prices, which used up most of the budget for protection
They planted extra pines to attract the birds, hoping for federal payments for hosting them
They moved the birds to public land themselves, which caused many colonies to fail
ow: The study found earlier harvesting, not land sales.
There was no federal payment for hosting the bird, so the incentive ran the other way: avoid it.
The documented response was changing harvest timing, not relocating birds.

items.p: In August 2010 the maker of OxyContin, an opioid painkiller, replaced it with a crush-resistant version, with FDA support, so it would be harder to snort or inject. Misuse of OxyContin fell. What went wrong?
items.answer: Many people already dependent on opioids switched to heroin, which was cheap and unregulated. Heroin deaths began rising the next month, and researchers estimate each prevented opioid death was replaced by a heroin death, so total deaths did not fall.
keys: People switched to heroin or fentanyl
Heroin deaths rose, offsetting the prevented opioid deaths
items.x: Two independent teams reached this conclusion. Evans, Lieber and Power found no net drop in combined opioid and heroin deaths. Alpert, Powell and Pacula found heroin deaths rose most in states where OxyContin misuse had been highest before the change. Lesson: if you make one route to a strongly wanted good harder, ask what the next-best substitute is, and whether it is less regulated and more dangerous.

choice.p: In 2010 OxyContin was reformulated to be crush-resistant, to reduce misuse. What did researchers find happened next?
o: Many users switched to heroin, and heroin deaths rose enough to offset the drop in OxyContin deaths
Doctors stopped prescribing OxyContin altogether, leaving many pain patients without any treatment
Users found an easy way to defeat the new coating within weeks, so misuse returned to its old level
Misuse fell and overdose deaths fell with it, making it a model for other drug rules
ow: The main finding is not about prescribing; it is that people already dependent switched to heroin.
Misuse of OxyContin itself did fall; the problem was substitution to other drugs.
OxyContin misuse fell, but heroin deaths rose to offset it, so total deaths did not fall.

items.p: 'Ban the box' laws stopped employers from asking about criminal records on job applications, to help people with records get hired, a group that is disproportionately young Black men. What went wrong, according to later studies?
items.answer: Without the record, some employers appear to have guessed who had one based on race, so they called back young Black men less often. The racial gap in callbacks grew, and employment of young low-skilled Black men fell.
keys: Employers guessed at records using race
Racial gaps in callbacks or hiring grew
items.x: In a field experiment with about 15,000 fake applications in New Jersey and New York City, Agan and Starr found the white-over-Black callback gap at affected employers grew from about 7% to about 43%. Applicants with records did gain callbacks; Black applicants without records lost them. Doleac and Hansen found the laws lowered employment of young low-skilled Black men by about 3.4 points, though Rose (2021) found little effect in Seattle, so the size is debated. Lesson: hidden information gets replaced by proxies.

choice.p: 'Ban the box' laws stopped employers from asking about criminal records on applications. What did later studies find?
o: Some employers guessed at records by race, so callbacks fell for young Black men and racial gaps grew
Employers shifted to running background checks on everyone, so hiring took months longer for all applicants
Applicants with records were hired more, but they left their jobs faster than others
Employers moved jobs to states without the laws, so total hiring fell in the states that passed them
ow: Studies focused on who got called back; the key finding was a wider racial gap.
Applicants with records did get more callbacks, but Black applicants without records lost callbacks, so the racial gap grew. The studies didn't track how long hires stayed.
Neither study found this. The documented effect was employers guessing at records by race.

items.p: Chile requires firms with 20 or more female workers to provide or pay for childcare, to support working mothers. Men don't count toward the threshold. What did researchers find about women hired by covered firms?
items.answer: Once a firm crossed the threshold, the women it hired got lower starting wages (about 9% to 20% lower than women the same firm hired before crossing). Employers passed much of the cost of the benefit back to the women it was meant to help.
keys: Women got lower starting wages at covered firms
The cost of the benefit was passed back to women
items.x: Prada, Rucci and Urzúa followed firms as they grew past 20 female workers. Other studies differ: Escobar (2014) found firms bunching just below 20 women and no effect on average wages, and another found the cost spread across all workers. This fits an older US finding by Jonathan Gruber (1994) that mandated childbirth coverage was paid for mostly through lower wages for the targeted workers. Lesson: a mandate triggered by employing a group can cut that group's pay or hiring.

choice.p: Chile requires firms with 20+ female workers to provide childcare. What did researchers find about women those firms hired?
o: Their starting wages were lower, so women paid for much of the benefit themselves
They were promoted faster, because firms wanted to recover their childcare spending through higher output
Firms replaced them with men at higher wages, so the share of women in covered firms fell to almost zero
Their wages were the same, because the government reimbursed employers for the full cost
ow: The study's finding was about starting wages, which were 9% to 20% lower, not promotions.
One study found firms staying just under 20 women, but nothing close to replacing women entirely; the main finding is lower starting wages.
Employers bear the cost in Chile, and it showed up in lower starting wages for women.

items.p: The EU's 2018 privacy law (GDPR) aimed partly at the data-hungry online ad industry dominated by Google and Facebook. Websites had to answer for the data practices of the outside tech vendors they used. Which vendors gained market share?
items.answer: Google and Facebook. Websites cut their outside vendors after GDPR, but dropped smaller ones first and kept the biggest, so vendor markets became about 17% more concentrated in the short run. Most of that faded by late 2018, except in advertising.
keys: The largest vendors (Google, Facebook) gained share
Sites dropped smaller vendors, so concentration rose
items.x: Johnson, Shriver and Goldberg tracked 27,000+ top websites. Vendor use fell about 15% the week GDPR took effect, mostly among smaller vendors; concentration in ad vendors stayed about 6% above its old level. Separate studies found GDPR also led to fewer apps and less venture investment in EU tech. Lesson: fixed compliance costs and legal risk tend to favor big incumbents that can absorb them.

choice.p: GDPR, the EU's 2018 privacy law, aimed partly at the big ad platforms. What happened to the market for website tech vendors?
o: Sites dropped smaller vendors first, so Google and Facebook gained share and concentration rose
Big platforms left Europe, so smaller European vendors took over most of the market
Sites stopped using outside vendors almost entirely and built their own tools in-house
Nothing measurable changed, because most sites ignored the law in its first year
ow: Google and Facebook stayed and gained relative share.
Vendor use fell about 15%, far short of disappearing, and mostly among smaller vendors.
Researchers measured a clear drop in vendor use the week the law took effect.

items.p: After Enron, the 2002 Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) gave employees who report corporate fraud the right to file retaliation complaints, first handled by the Labor Department's OSHA. How did these complaints turn out in the first three years, and why?
items.answer: Whistleblowers almost never won: OSHA found for employees in about 3.6% of resolved cases. Many lost before the facts were weighed, on the short 90-day filing deadline or narrow readings of who is covered (for example, employees of subsidiaries), and OSHA often misapplied the burden of proof.
keys: Whistleblowers rarely won (about 4% of cases)
Lost on procedure or coverage: short deadline, narrow definitions, or the burden of proof
items.x: Law professor Richard Moberly counted 13 employee wins out of 361 resolved complaints. Employees did much better before judges than at OSHA when the facts were weighed (about 56% vs 11%), and 18% of OSHA losses came from missing the deadline. Lesson: a protection can exist on paper but fail in practice. Check who decides cases, the deadlines and the coverage rules. This matters for current proposals to protect AI lab whistleblowers.

choice.p: Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX, the 2002 post-Enron fraud law) let whistleblowers file retaliation complaints. How did those complaints fare at first?
o: Employees won only about 4% of cases, often losing on deadlines or narrow coverage rules
Employees won most cases, and the flood of claims led Congress to cap damages within two years
Most cases were never decided, because companies settled nearly all of them before any ruling
Employees won about half the time, similar to other workplace retaliation laws
ow: Employees rarely won; there was no such cap.
Settlements happened, but most resolved cases ended against employees.
The win rate was far lower, around 3.6%.

items.p: Business groups have long warned that workplace safety inspections cost firms so much they destroy jobs. California's safety agency picked some high-hazard workplaces at random to inspect. What did researchers find, compared with workplaces not inspected?
items.answer: The feared harm didn't show up. Inspected workplaces had about 9% fewer injury claims and 26% lower workers' compensation costs (about $355,000 saved on average), with no detectable drop in jobs, sales, payroll or survival.
keys: Fewer injuries and lower injury costs
No detectable loss of jobs, sales or survival
items.x: Levine, Toffel and Johnson (Science, 2012) compared 409 randomly inspected workplaces with 409 matched ones, a careful design, though for one state's program. Not every predicted backfire happens. Lesson: before believing a feared side effect, check whether the regulated party also gains from the rule (here, fewer costly injuries), and look for past cases where the same fear was tested.

choice.p: California randomly chose high-hazard workplaces for safety inspections. Compared with uninspected ones, what did researchers find?
o: Fewer injuries and lower injury costs, with no detectable loss of jobs or sales
Fewer injuries, but about one in ten inspected firms closed within four years from the costs
No change in injuries, because firms fixed problems only on inspection day
More reported injuries, because inspections made workers more willing to report them
ow: The study found no detectable effect on firm survival.
Injury claims fell about 9% and costs about 26% over four years.
Injury claims and costs fell, which is the reverse of this.

side.description: Real laws that backfired, got routed around, or landed on the wrong people. Each card describes a policy; you guess what happened.
caveat: Ten cases drawn from published research, current as of October 2026. Several findings are disputed, and the cards say so.
Drafted and independently fact-checked by AI; no person has reviewed it.
side.meta: Draft · 2026-10-21 · Fact-checked by AI, not by a person

glossary.def: Power under Section 6(b) of the FTC Act letting the Federal Trade Commission order companies to submit information for studies of an industry, separate from any enforcement case.
An activity so risky even when done carefully (such as blasting with explosives) that tort law holds whoever carries it out strictly liable for the harm it causes.
A deferential standard courts use to review a decision-maker's choice: the court overturns it only if it was clearly unreasonable, arbitrary, or unsupported by the facts or law.

A defense that raises new facts which defeat liability even if the plaintiff's claims are true. The defendant has to plead and prove it, and it is often resolved only after costly discovery, well into a case.
Artificial general intelligence: a hypothetical AI system that matches or exceeds human ability across most cognitive tasks. Definitions vary and there is no agreed test.
How much compute a training method needs to reach a given level of performance. Algorithmic progress lets the same capability be reached with less compute over time.
In AI, the problem of making a system's goals and behavior match what its developers and users intend. A misaligned model pursues goals other than those intended.

The body of law that protects competition, chiefly by banning monopolization and agreements among competitors that restrain trade, such as price-fixing. In the US, mainly the Sherman and Clayton Acts.
Legislation that provides money for federal agencies and programs. Congress separately passes authorizing laws that create programs; a program can be authorized yet receive no appropriated funds.
A standard under the Administrative Procedure Act for judging agency actions. Courts set aside an action only if it lacked a rational basis, ignored key factors or ran counter to the evidence.
A contract term requiring disputes to be decided by a private arbitrator instead of a court, which can limit a person's ability to sue.
A cryptographically verifiable statement from hardware or software about its own state or activity, such as what a chip was used for.
A stay is a court order pausing a legal proceeding or the effect of a decision while a case is pending. An automatic stay takes effect by default, without a court having to order it.
Weapon systems that, once activated, can select and engage targets without further human intervention.
Wages an employee should have earned but did not because of an employer's unlawful act, such as a retaliatory firing. Courts or agencies can order the employer to pay it.
Access to an AI model limited to sending inputs and seeing outputs, with no view of its internals such as weights, activations or training data.
A group of competing firms that agree to coordinate prices, output or markets instead of competing. Such agreements are generally illegal under US antitrust law.
The legal basis that entitles a person to sue: a set of facts that, if proven, give the plaintiff a right to a remedy from the defendant.
Chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear: the categories of weapons of mass destruction often used to group the most severe AI misuse risks.
The step-by-step written reasoning a language model produces before giving its final answer.
A narrow point in a supply chain or route, controlled by few firms or places, where restricting access can affect everything downstream.
A fine that a government agency or court imposes for breaking a law or regulation, enforced through a civil case without criminal punishment.
A standard of proof higher than 'more likely than not' and lower than 'beyond a reasonable doubt': the claim must be shown to be highly probable.
The Senate procedure for ending debate and moving to a vote. For most legislation it takes 60 votes, so a failed cloture vote usually blocks a bill from advancing.
In policy usage, to write a rule into statute, often one that previously existed only in agency policy, an executive order or court decisions, so it has the force of law.
A situation where everyone would be better off cooperating, but each actor has an incentive to hold back, so the shared goal goes unmet.
A secret or unlawful agreement between parties, such as competitors, to act together in a way that harms others, for example by fixing prices.

A contract between a developer and community groups or local government in which the developer commits to local benefits (jobs, payments, environmental protections) in exchange for support for a project.
A bill introduced in one chamber that is identical or substantially similar to a bill in the other chamber, so both can move through committees at the same time.
A temporary panel of House and Senate members that negotiates a single version of a bill when the two chambers have passed different versions. Provisions are often dropped there.
A member of Congress who formally signs on to support a bill introduced by its sponsor. Original cosponsors are those listed when the bill is first introduced.
A large electricity user that can reduce its power draw on request when the grid is strained, often in exchange for lower rates or faster grid access.
An intermediary used to hide the real party behind a transaction or operation.
An organization that puts an AI system to use in its own products or operations, as distinct from the developer that built the underlying model.
A product-liability claim that a product is unreasonably dangerous because of how it was designed, so every unit carries the flaw.
The pretrial phase of a lawsuit in which each side can demand evidence from the other, such as documents and depositions. It is often the most expensive part of litigation.
Bill text that lawmakers circulate for feedback before formally introducing it. It has no bill number and cannot be acted on until it is introduced.

Training one model to imitate another, stronger model's outputs. In US policy debates, adversarial distillation means foreign rivals, mainly Chinese AI firms, doing this with US models without permission.
Manufacturing DNA molecules to a specified sequence, usually by commercial providers who ship them to customers. It is a key step in turning a genetic design into a working organism.
A legal obligation to take reasonable care to avoid foreseeable harm to others. A statutory duty of care is one written into a statute instead of developed by courts.
In AI evaluations, the effort testers put into drawing out a model's full capabilities, for example through better prompts, tools or fine-tuning. Weak elicitation can understate what a model can do.
Unauthorized copying or transfer of data out of a system. For AI, the main concern is model weights being copied out of a lab by thieves or insiders, or possibly in future by the model itself.

Government restrictions on sending certain goods, software or technology abroad, usually for national security. In the US, the Commerce Department's BIS administers controls on dual-use items such as AI chips.
A product-liability claim that a maker did not give adequate warnings or instructions about a product's non-obvious dangers.
Further training of an already-trained model on additional data to adapt its behavior. It can also be used to remove a model's safety training.
Material, such as highly enriched uranium or plutonium, that can sustain a nuclear chain reaction; it is the essential ingredient of nuclear weapons.

Floating-point operation: one arithmetic step, such as an addition or multiplication, on numbers stored in floating-point format. The total FLOP used to train a model is a common measure of its scale, e.g. 10^26.
A large AI model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many different tasks, such as the models behind major chatbots.
A chip factory that manufactures chips designed by other companies. TSMC and Samsung are the leading foundries for advanced chips, and TSMC makes most leading AI chips.
AI models that can competently perform a wide range of distinct tasks. The EU AI Act sets specific obligations for 'general-purpose AI models'.
A technology that spreads across many sectors and spawns further innovation, such as electricity or computers.
Deliberate large-scale intervention in Earth's climate system, such as reflecting sunlight back to space, to counter global warming.
Editing genes in eggs, sperm or embryos, so the changes are inherited by future generations.
The process and approval required to connect a new power plant or large electricity user to the transmission grid, often a long queue.
Legal protection that shields a person or organization from being sued or held liable for certain acts.
Running a trained model to produce outputs, as opposed to training it. Inference compute is the computing power used for this, for example to serve customers.
A cloud service model in which customers rent computing power, storage and networking from a provider instead of owning the hardware.
The risk that someone with authorized access, such as an employee or contractor, misuses it to cause harm, for example by stealing data.

A legislative measure that, like a bill, must pass both chambers and be signed by the President (or pass over a veto) to become law. Used for continuing appropriations and to approve or block executive actions.
Rules requiring a business to verify who its customers are and watch for suspicious activity. They originated in banking and are proposed for cloud computing.
The period after a November election and before the new Congress takes office in January. A lame-duck session is Congress meeting then, including members who lost or are retiring.
The chipmaking step that uses light to print circuit patterns onto silicon wafers. Deep-ultraviolet (DUV) tools are the older generation, still essential for making advanced chips.
A Supreme Court doctrine under which courts reject agency actions of vast economic or political significance unless Congress clearly authorized them.
An agreement among competitors to divide customers, territories or products among themselves instead of competing for them. US antitrust law treats it as illegal per se.
The committee meeting where members debate, amend and vote on a bill, deciding whether and in what form to send it to the full chamber.
Government examination of a proposed merger or acquisition to decide whether it may substantially lessen competition, in which case enforcers can sue to block or reshape it.
The gradual expansion of a program or institution's activities beyond its original goals.
A document published with an AI model describing its intended uses, how it was evaluated, its limitations and safety test results. A system card covers a model plus its surrounding product.
The numerical parameters a neural network learns during training. Whoever holds a model's weights can run, copy or modify it, including stripping its safeguards.
Failure to use the care a reasonably prudent person would use in similar circumstances. A negligence standard makes a defendant liable only for harm caused by such a failure.
Describes an AI model whose trained weights are published for anyone to download, run and modify.
A buildup of unused potential, such as spare compute, efficiency gains or ideas, that could produce a sudden jump in AI capabilities once a constraint is lifted.
Latin for 'by itself.' In antitrust, a per se violation is conduct (such as price-fixing) treated as automatically illegal, with no weighing of its actual effects on competition.
The doctrine, based on the Constitution's Supremacy Clause, that valid federal law overrides conflicting state law. Congress can preempt state law expressly or by implication.
An agreement among competitors to raise, lower or stabilize prices instead of setting them independently. It is illegal per se under US antitrust law.
The legal responsibility of makers and sellers for injuries caused by defective products, usually through claims of design defect, manufacturing defect or failure to warn.
A for-profit corporation whose charter commits it to a stated public benefit, and whose directors must balance that benefit and stakeholders' interests against shareholders' financial interests.
Money a court awards on top of compensation for harm, meant to punish especially bad conduct and deter others from similar conduct.
Competition in which actors keep lowering standards, such as safety or regulation, to gain an advantage over rivals.
The degree of caution a reasonably prudent person would use in the same situation. Failing to exercise it is the core of negligence.

A fast-track budget procedure that lets certain tax, spending and debt-limit bills pass the Senate by simple majority, without a filibuster. Under the Byrd rule, provisions with no or merely incidental budget effect can be struck.
A hypothesized process in which AI systems improve the design of their own successors, which then improve further, potentially speeding progress.
Deliberately probing a system the way an adversary would, to find weaknesses before real attackers or users do.
When a regulator or monitor comes to serve the interests of the industry it oversees, at the expense of the public it is meant to protect.
A training method in which a model learns by trial and error, receiving rewards for desired behavior. It is widely used to train AI models after pretraining.
Insurance for insurers: an insurer passes part of its risk to another company, or a government backstop, to limit losses from very large or correlated claims.
A legal provision that protects a party from liability or penalty as long as it meets specified conditions.
A structured, evidence-backed argument that a system is acceptably safe in a particular context. Some regulators require them, for example for nuclear plants and offshore oil and gas in the UK.
An AI model strategically underperforming on an evaluation, hiding capabilities it actually has.
An isolated computing environment that limits what software inside it can access, used to test or contain programs.
The Senate's constitutional 'advice and consent' power to approve or reject the President's nominees for senior federal posts. Lower-level officials can be appointed without it.
A provision or resolution that states Congress's opinion. It has no binding legal effect, even when included in a bill that becomes law.
A provision stating that if a court strikes down one part of a law or contract, the remaining parts stay in effect.
A company with few or no real operations or assets, sometimes used to hide who is actually behind a transaction.
A government's ability to carry out its policies effectively, including expertise, staff, funding and administrative reach.
Liability for harm regardless of fault or how much care was taken. US courts apply it to abnormally dangerous activities and, in most states, to some defective-product claims.
A remedy that bars one company from operating in two connected lines of business, such as owning cloud infrastructure and the AI models that run on it.
Authority to issue subpoenas: legal orders compelling a person to testify or hand over documents, backed by penalties for refusing.
A clause that makes a law, program or agency expire automatically after a set period unless lawmakers renew it.
Hypothetical AI that greatly exceeds human cognitive ability in virtually all domains.
Data collected automatically from a device and sent elsewhere for monitoring, such as a chip's power draw or usage.
The constitutional amendment reserving to the states, or the people, powers not delegated to the federal government.
Computing power spent while a model is answering, for example letting it reason longer, which can improve performance without further training.
A civil wrong, other than breach of contract, that causes harm and lets the injured person sue for damages. Negligence is the most common tort.
Confidential business information, such as a formula, process or technique, that has value because competitors do not know it. The law protects it against theft and misuse.
One complete process of training an AI model on data, which for frontier models can take months and vast amounts of compute.
A way for the Senate to act quickly by setting aside its normal rules. It succeeds only if no senator objects, so any single senator can block it.
In AI safety testing, how much a model improves someone's ability to do a task, such as building a weapon, compared with existing resources like internet search.
Company shares or stock options an employee has fully earned under a vesting schedule, so they belong to the employee even after leaving the company.
Wrongful conduct done intentionally and knowingly, as opposed to by accident or carelessness. It is a much higher bar to prove than negligence.
